president-in-office of the council. – mr president, i found today’s exchange to be as colourful as i remember this plenary to be. i will try to touch on most, if not all, of the issues that have been raised by my friends. first of all, i would like to thank the leaders of the different groups for their extremely positive welcome and the extremely positive words they had for this presidency. i will start with migration once again. i know this is an extremely thorny issue – not only at european level, but in each and every one of our member states. it is an extremely emotional issue, and perhaps stirs up all the wrong sentiments. this is where the battlegrounds for the next elections in our member states and elsewhere will be played for at least the next generation. so whatever we do today has a short-term impact on the composition of the different institutions and the different governments in our member states, and it cannot be underestimated. but if we wait for a total solution – for a perfect solution with no shortcomings to be found – we are condemned to go round in circles and stay in the same rut. my point today was – and still is – that we may have ideological differences – actually, we might have moral differences – on the way we approach this issue. some of us may see it as more of a humanitarian crisis, while others see it as a security issue. maybe we are both right. my point goes beyond that. that is the ideological discourse. that is the long-term. in the long term, we are all dead. in the short term, in three months’ time, we will have another crisis. i am the first to hope that i am completely wrong on this. i am the first to hope that, come next spring, it will be business as usual with maybe a few crossings that one, two, three or a maximum of four member states can take in. but i’m afraid that i will not be wrong, and the situation is that we either take a decision now or we will have to take a much bolder decision when there is a crisis, and when there are hundreds of thousands of people putting pressure on governments, communities and our families, and when we will need to take decisions that may not be well thought out. this is really the last train we can catch to do something which is structured when it comes to the collective handling of the migration crisis. money alone will not do it. so simply thinking that migration, the impending crisis and the fact that even if we do something now it is not a long—term solution, and thinking that this can be solved by throwing more money at the problem, is delusional. that is not what this is about. this is about border control. this is about having a new system to share the burden. this is about creating humanitarian corridors where and when necessary. this is about acknowledging the fact that, if we even throw around the concept of building walls that has been used by some member states – which i personally disagree with, but i will not judge that member state for doing that – as a country with a maritime border, we cannot build a wall in the sea. i am sorry to break it to you, but when my navy people call me at night, they do not ask me whether they can turn the people back or not. they just tell me that we need to save the people from drowning. if we allow this to happen again – not hitting these criminal gangs where it hurts, not engaging with the countries on the southern littoral of the mediterranean – we are in for more trouble. we are inviting more trouble by trying to postpone the issue until there is a perfect solution. there will be no perfect solution for dublin. there will be no perfect solution for border control. there can only be progress if we really accept one another’s views. i need to accept people’s views where i might have some ideological differences, but at this point in time we need operational solutions that have been missing so far. our aim, as the maltese presidency, is to try to achieve progress. i think that we were mostly on the same page on brexit. on taxation, i would tell my colleagues that i totally refute the label of ‘tax haven’ or ‘offshore’ for my country. our country’s tax system was approved by the european commission after being thoroughly examined before membership more than a decade ago, so i do not see why things that were approved pre—membership are now a problem. i have every respect for my colleague, mr casa. i understand his speech. this concerns local politics, and i do not think that we should deal with it here, but we will have all the time in the world to have a healthy political fight back home. back here, i want to stress one final point on the issue of the social agenda, the social pillar of the commission, and the issue of free trade. i do not see these as contradictory aims. i actually see these as complementary aims. it is through free trade that we can create more growth and more jobs. usually, i have felt a bit out of tune with my social democratic family in being a very clear advocate of free trade, but seeing that even the president of china is an advocate of free trade, i feel a little bit more at ease in saying that free trade is good if it is properly regulated. i think that the main issue on which we should focus right now is not trying to be protectionist. social europe does not mean protectionist europe. it does not mean withdrawing from the world. it does not mean trying to put up barriers to what we have achieved so far. social europe means that the growth and the well-being that we create through free trade needs to be distributed in an equal – or at least a fair – manner. this was missing for many years in our member states. all the well-being that was created through the policies that were advocated, even by this institutions, did not percolate through the system, and we have to admit that the belief in only a trickle—down economic approach did not work. so, will we find a solution to all this in the next six months? obviously not. what we want to do is to set the ball rolling in the right direction and build on the good work that has been done by our predecessors. one final point to parliament, rest assured that the political presence of council within parliament will be assured as much as possible, because we want a genuine dialogue with you. in writing. the social dimension is largely absent from eu policies. the single market was built without any integration in mind, and this has created and continues to create internal dumping and risks for workers. the so-called 'european social model' which was in vogue at the end of the last century must be updated, but above all it is necessary that the social dimension should become an integral part of common policies. the report deals with important issues such as income redistribution, collective social security schemes, social assistance programmes, public services, services of general interest, social investment and the fight against tax evasion. however, these requests are being placed in a context of greater coordination at the level of european governance which, as structured today, actively contributes to the promotion of inequality and the impoverishment of the majority of european citizens, in particular through the imposition of the blockade on public spending by individual member states.
in writing. the european union must do its utmost to react quickly and visibly to the growing frustrations and concerns of a large part of the population. there are no longer any ordinary answers: the uncertain life prospects, unemployment and growing inequalities require us to take concrete and urgent action on the social side of europe. new instruments are needed, new concrete measures to support those who are most in need and to revive the whole pillar of social rights in innovative ways. the european commission has put forward a consultation and the social partners have responded with some very interesting proposals, and parliament's response is now very ambitious, with a very precise list of priorities on how to structure the european social model for the future. i would like to recall in particular the passages in the rodrigues report which stress the importance of collective bargaining as a primary fundamental right of the eu. this principle gives rise to the conviction, repeatedly expressed by this house, that it is both right and useful for growth to involve workers in the management of companies by introducing, as far as possible, measures of information, consultation and participation, especially in order to achieve new and better models of work organization and to anticipate economic changes.

and verification mechanism (cvm). i have cooperated personally with various governments, of differing compositions, and all these governments have cooperated with me personally – with the commission – mr president, i very much welcome this report. the issue of crossborder adoption has been debated in the european union for many years. i remember the debate in 2009, when the czech republic held the eu presidency, and we were debating whether to amend one european law, one european adoption or to put forward the principle of mutual recognition. i think it is right that the idea of mutual recognition has finally won out, which does not in principle promote the principle of european integration of family law, but rather believes that individual states are capable of adopting correctly within their jurisdiction. so i very much welcome the idea, in my view it is a compromise between those who want to make the cross-border aspects of adoption more efficient on the one hand, and those who do not want a single european family law. the correction is correct and i congratulate the rapporteur and hope that it will work in practice.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the best interests of the child are inherent in respect for his fundamental rights, which can only be truly respected if the perspective is reversed by changing the angle of view from the adult to the child. it is the task of the institutions and all the social actors, and above all the family, to facilitate this capacity. in international adoptions, which are a meeting of affections, but also of profoundly different cultures, the protective family nucleus develops with a trilateral relationship: the court of justice has held that the principle of non-discrimination is not applicable to the situation of a child, adoptive parent and biological parent, with the peculiar elements of alienation which are typical of private international law. in the case of crossborder adoption, there are also greater legal uncertainties, due primarily to the different national recognition procedures and the divergence of the guiding principles. the only remedy and primary reference point for any cross-border adoption procedure therefore remains substantive and non-formal compliance with article 21 of the united nations convention on the rights of the child.
in writing. there are still too many obstacles to adoption, with many crossborder cases affecting thousands of families. with mr zwiefka's report, measures are being put on the table which many european citizens have been waiting for for a long time. i appreciate the effort made to suggest homogeneous and comprehensive proposals: i too believe that introducing a general regulation can be a very effective instrument. i would like to stress in particular the provision for common minimum standards for adoption, based in particular on the belief that every adoption decision is made purely in the interests of the child, and is assessed according to the specific characteristics of each case. the exchange of information between the consular authorities responsible for the adoption of a child who is a national of another member state would already be a concrete step forward and would be immediately applicable, and i hope that the commission will be able to propose rapid and effective rules on the basis of some of the examples suggested.

on behalf of the efdd group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i too have signed this resolution to ask the commission to take action to facilitate the introduction of naturally occurring pesticides into the market. in order to reduce the environmental and health impact of industrial products, including agricultural products, we must have the courage to make it easier for companies who believe in the green economy to do so. it is not right that those who produce niche products and those who use them should face the same administrative and bureaucratic burden as those who do not pay for the passive externalities of their work. natural molecules and pesticides can reduce the overall impact of treatments, by reducing emissions of pollutants and greenhouse gases during production and by reducing the impact on biodiversity and non-target organisms and on human health. a recent stoa assessment of the pros and cons of organic farming found a positive impact of organic consumption on some childhood cognitive disorders found at current levels of exposure to synthetic pesticides. so let's do this for future generations: the problem agriculture can and must become the solution.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, an ispra report documents an increase in pesticides in surface and deep waters in italy. a legambiente study entitled 'pesticides on the plate' shows that a third of the fruit and vegetable samples analysed contain pesticide residues. samples with up to nine active substances present at the same time are increasing. italy alone accounts for about 33% of the total quantities of insecticides used in the community and there are 800 products currently on the market. the risks to human health, especially to children, are very high, think of endocrine disruptors. the damage to ecosystems, as in the case of glyphosate, the most widely used herbicide in the world, whose impact on the body is insidious and manifests itself slowly over time, is very serious. however, france legally recognised parkinson's disease as an occupational disease from pesticide exposure as early as 2012. the commission must give us answers, it must make citizens aware of what it is doing to protect their health and that of the area in which they live. we are asking for specific action within two years and not a refit procedure which could take up to 10 years and end without any decision. this would be to the detriment of farmers and consumers who have the right to produce and consume products with the lowest possible risk. the real innovation today, commissioner, is to adopt the agro-ecological approach, to improve soil fertility, to diversify production, to increase carbon sequestration capacity, to ensure adequate harvests and to tackle pest and weed control, monitoring natural dynamics.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, low-risk plant protection products of organic origin are a valid alternative to conventional plant protection products, both for conventional and organic farming. the new mechanisms of action in some of the new generation of organic plant protection products could represent an important advantage, also in the light of the evolution of resistance to conventional plant protection products. however, a number of member states refuse to authorise products containing low-risk active substances of biological origin because of their alleged lower efficacy. i am of the opinion that low-risk plant protection products of biological origin should be the preferred option for users where they have the same efficacy as conventional pesticides. the regulation on the placing of plant protection products on the market therefore needs to be revised in order to improve the current registration process for basic substances with low risk, which in fact sometimes takes the form of a patent, making it difficult to use a product with the same substance not registered.

member of the commission. – madam president, honourable members, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr de jong, for his report and work on this very important topic. i think it is a thing that we share, that these rules are of the essence for the legitimacy of the advisory and expert groups. this commission has paid very close attention to the role which expert groups play in our policy making. and we have laid down tougher internal rules in order to make sure that these groups carry out their function in full transparency and accountability exactly as asked. let me stress just one thing, because this is very basic. expert groups provide very useful contributions to the work of the commission in many different policy fields, of which many are highly technical and of a specialised nature. but i think it is very important to recall that no matter what advice is given by expert groups, they have a purely advisory role. whatever their advice may be, the responsibility for any decision or measure adopted remains the commission’s and the commission's alone. but when this commission took office we decided that the rules for expert groups needed to be reviewed so as to better reflect the commission's commitment to be more transparent and accountable. before adopting a new set of rules, we listened to this parliament, the european ombudsman and civil society organisations. after a full year of consultation and intensive preparation the commission adopted new rules in may last year. we consider these new rules, which are binding for all of the commission services, to improve significantly the management, the balance and the transparency of expert groups and we also consider that they provide a positive response to many suggestions made by this house and by the european ombudsman. just let me give you a few concrete examples. the new rules confirm – reconfirm – the commission's commitment to strive for a balanced composition of expert groups. the commission’s departments must do their utmost to guarantee a balanced representation. this does not mean balanced in a mathematical sense, which would be difficult to define and achieve in all cases; it means maximum balance in terms of expertise, interests, gender, and geographical origin. the new rules also bring significant changes to boost transparency. we have set up a new register for expert groups. this register is accessible for the public and provides more accurate information and more documents drafted and discussed by expert groups. in particular, the commission will henceforth publish the register calls for applications when it selects stakeholders’ representatives as well as expert group members appointed in their personal capacity. this is a major step forward and has been a long-standing request from this parliament. in other words, we have made the selection procedures fully transparent and inclusive, which ultimately benefits the balance of the composition of expert groups. second, registration in the transparency register has now become a precondition for stakeholders’ organisations to be appointed to an expert group. this means that where particular interests are represented in an expert group there will be full transparency as regards the nature of these interests. third, every document that an expert group produces must now be put on the register of expert groups. minutes will have to be provided, which makes complete and meaningful sense. moreover, expert groups can also decide to open up their meetings to the general public. last but not least, we have taken tough measures to avoid conflict of interest in expert groups. under the new rules, independent experts can only be appointed on the basis of standardised and detailed conflict-of-interest assessment based on the declaration submitted by these experts. only if the commission services conclude that there is no conflict of interest may those experts be appointed in their personal capacity. in addition, all declarations of interest of independent experts are published in the register of expert groups. these tougher rules we have put in place to ensure – and i do hope that you find that we, the commission and this house, share the objective – a high degree of transparency and accountability for the functioning of expert groups. the commission is committed to rigorously applying our new rules and we know of course that you will scrutinise us closely and we remain of course open to continuing the dialogue with this parliament as to how to improve and how to make sure that we follow closely this important matter.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the fight against corruption and fraud is and must increasingly be a central theme of the eu's political action, which must be equipped with the appropriate measures and instruments to enable particularly complex investigations such as those normally related to cases of corruption and financial fraud to the detriment of the union. an important resource in this respect are whistleblowers, whose contribution - as we heard from mr de jong - has brought to light cases of conflicts of interest, tax evasion and avoidance, money laundering and also infiltration by organised crime to the detriment of the union's financial interests. it is therefore desirable that the commission submits as soon as possible a legislative proposal to ensure the protection of whistleblowers in accordance with common standards in all member states and to create secure channels for reporting irregularities, allowing confidentiality and sharing of information, while ensuring adequate assistance to the whistleblower.
in writing. the role of whistleblowers in upholding the rule of law and thus also in protecting the financial interests of the union is absolutely central. the guarantee of protection for those who provide information in this respect must therefore be absolute; the protection in this sense must also extend to the economic aspects, because it is easy for whistleblowers to lose their jobs as a result of their reporting. the level of protection of such persons varies greatly from one member state to another and it is therefore necessary to introduce european minimum standards in this respect. we are therefore committed to seeking timely approval from the commission to produce a legislative proposal to this effect.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with these reports the european parliament is taking part at the highest level in the debate on the future of the union, making a contribution that is both ambitious and realistic. the reports set out a path which starts from the full use of the existing treaties and outlines the basic lines of a revision of them, while at the same time defining a vision. it does not do so by prescribing a policy, mr spinelli, but by setting out a path which will enable the european citizens to decide democratically which policies to adopt. what are the underlying concepts of this vision? the first is that it is not only possible but necessary to reconcile different rates of development with the primacy of common institutions and the community method. differentiated integration must be a tool for uniting europe and not for dividing it. the second principle is that, to be effective, european governance must be democratic and the principles of attribution, proportionality and subsidiarity must be fully integrated with that of representative democracy at national and european level. these concepts are particularly clear when we face the completion of economic and monetary union. to function well, the euro needs a third leg alongside the common monetary policy and national fiscal policies. a common fiscal capacity is needed to absorb symmetrical and asymmetrical shocks, precisely to avoid putting monetary policy and the stability pact under excessive strain and also to support economic convergence between member states. this capacity can and must be placed in the union budget and does not require a reform of the treaties. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be given the right to vote in the council of ministers. mr president, the development of a union of european states and citizens is not a federal leap, but an ongoing historical process. it's a statue already. on behalf of the efdd group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the amendment of the schengen borders code should be aimed at facilitating the identification of those who represent a threat to public policy and internal security in the european union. one of the most difficult to identify is the flow of foreign fighters. to this end, at the external borders of the european union, all persons, including european citizens, will be subject to systematic checks by means of verifications of documentary and biometric information contained in the relevant existing databases. only where systematic checks have a disproportionate impact on the flow of travellers' traffic will the member states concerned be able to carry them out in a targeted manner, provided that a risk assessment demonstrates that such derogation does not harm the internal security of the union. we wondered whether it would not be more effective to provide for targeted checks, as a rule and not as an exception, on signals shared between states as a result of intelligence activities, but unfortunately the opposite view prevailed in the committee. a focus point is the need to improve the dialogue between databases and the interconnectivity between them and the infrastructures responsible for managing the external borders, in full respect of data protection and fundamental rights rules.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, checks at the external borders of the union remain one of the main measures to safeguard the area without internal border controls. these are checks carried out in the interests of all the member states, to prevent any threat, even if, as we saw in the recent attacks in paris and brussels, the threat comes from citizens of the union. thanks to the new technologies available and the national and european databases at their disposal, border guards at the union's external borders will be able to carry out systematic and targeted checks on all european citizens. however, we still regard respect for the law as the principle of priority under this regulation. the verification of the identity and validity of the travel document should always be carried out in full compliance with union law as enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights, in particular the rights to respect for private life, to data protection and to freedom of movement and residence.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is an objective fact that europe is in the eye of the storm because of the terrorist threat. the rapporteur, mrs macovei, proposes that exit checks at the union's external borders be systematised by means of databases and biometric devices. i believe that this hypothesis should be assessed in the overall framework of the reorganization of european defence systems, coordinating it with other actions already undertaken and planned. i think it is necessary to clarify the mechanism for modulating the controls on the intensity of outbound traffic which, in addition to not hindering the fluidity of travel, must also ensure equal treatment between citizens. it is essential that europe respects the principle of proportionality and that any action to improve safety does not, as is often the case, lead to unjustified restrictions on personal freedoms. finally, the appropriateness of exit controls should be assessed in the light of concrete data, intelligence and specific research and not by relying on the fears of citizens or the still painful memory of the attacks in europe.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european council has repeatedly reaffirmed its commitment to improving the exchange of information in order to meet the current security challenges facing the european union. however, the legal framework currently in force for such exchange between designated authorities, including the exchange of information on terrorist offences, is still largely subject to instruments dating back to the lisbon treaty. the slowness with which the union is working on prevention is unacceptable, especially at a time in history when european citizens are more aware of their need for security. i think it is essential that the commission acts decisively by launching an infringement procedure against member states which are reluctant to share information which they are obliged to do under the current legal framework, and in the meantime put forward an ambitious proposal for a directive to ensure a consistent and more stringent legal framework for the exchange of law enforcement information and intelligence at union level.

the agenda includes the report by mr stefan eck, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on mercury repealing regulation (ec) no 1102/2008 (com ((2016) 0039 - c8-0021/2016 - 2016/0023 ((cod)) (a8-0313/2016)).
member of the commission. – mr president, mercury is a pollutant of global concern that enters the food chain where it accumulates, mainly in fish. the eu’s mercury policy is the most advanced worldwide, but 40-80% of the mercury deposited in the eu comes from other parts of the globe. that is why we called for global action and took on a leading role in the negotiations of the minamata convention on mercury. the convention, which was signed at the end of 2013, is to a great extent inspired by eu legislation, so it requires only limited changes to the eu acquis. consequently, the new mercury regulation aims primarily at fine-tuning eu law so as to ensure full compliance with all provisions of the minamata convention and enable its ratification by the eu and the member states. we expect that ratification by the eu and those member states that have completed their required national procedures will take place before the end of june. this should trigger the entry into force of the convention, taking us a major step closer to a safer, healthier mercury-free society. as top mercury-polluters take action to implement the convention, we expect a dramatic drop of mercury emissions to air and water worldwide, leading to reduced exposure to mercury within the eu. the entry into force of the minamata convention will help level the playing field, as all major economies will apply requirements similar to those already applying in the eu on products, industrial processes and waste management. in turn, this will support the eu’s innovative eco-industry, which will be able to make the most of their technological lead in export markets. furthermore, this regulation is a golden opportunity to complement our already advanced eu acquis with new measures going beyond the minimum of the convention. the commission is very happy that parliament fully supported our proposal to put an end to new uses of mercury in products and industrial processes. this flagship measure demonstrates the eu’s continued global leadership in this policy area. the new regulation will also ensure that all known industrial processes using mercury convert to mercury-free alternatives and that mercury waste is safely start out of reach, thereby avoiding its improper use and release into the environment. finally, the regulation sets out a clear road map for reducing the use of dental amalgam and assessing the feasibility of phasing out its use. i also draw your attention to two statements by the commission that will be appended to the minutes. the first one signals our continued engagement at international level, which will aim at further narrowing the remaining gaps between the level of protection guaranteed by the minamata convention and the stricter requirements that prevail in the eu. our second statement concerns the so-called ‘no opinion clause’ in comitology. the new mercury regulation is undoubtedly a major step forward in the eu acquis. i therefore call upon all of you to express your support for this very good outcome of the informal trilogue process. commission statement on international cooperation on mercury the minamata convention and the new mercury regulation are major contributions to protecting citizens from mercury pollution globally and in the eu. international cooperation should be sustained to ensure successful implementation of the convention by all parties and further strengthen its provisions. the european commission is therefore committed to supporting continued cooperation, in accordance with the convention and subject to applicable eu policies, rules and procedures, inter alia undertaking work in the following areas:narrowing the gap between eu law and the provisions of the convention through the review clause of the list of prohibited mercury-added products; in the context of the provisions of the convention on financing, capacity building and technology transfer, activities such as improving traceability of mercury trade and use, promoting certification of mercury-free artisanal and small-scale gold mining and mercury-free labels for gold, and increasing the capacity of developing countries including in the area of mercury waste management. commission statement on comitology the commission underlines that it is contrary to the letter and to the spirit of regulation 182/2011 (oj l 55 of 28.2.2011, p. 13) to invoke article 5 § 4, subparagraph 2, point b) in a systematic manner. recourse to this provision must respond to a specific need to depart from the rule of principle which is that the commission may adopt a draft implementing act when no opinion is delivered. given that it is an exception to the general rule established by article 5 § 4 recourse to subparagraph 2, point b), cannot be simply seen as a "discretionary power" of the legislator, but must be interpreted in a restrictive manner and thus must be justified.
i am not saying that we should not be concerned about the environment, but that we should be concerned about the environment. for this reason it is necessary to regulate their uses and movements and to decide in advance how to treat them when they become waste with the aim, where possible, of reducing or eliminating all their uses within a reasonable period of time. this is the logic we followed in the negotiations with the council and the commission, which were concluded last december with a broad consensus, which was then unanimously adopted by the committee on the environment. we hope that tomorrow the text will be adopted definitively without further amendments by the house. this will enable the union to proceed with the ratification of the minamata convention on mercury and to take part in its first conference of the parties scheduled for the end of september in geneva. but neither today's debate nor tomorrow's vote is formal. the text we are bringing to the house, which is the result of the contribution of almost all the political groups, is very different from the commission's initial proposal. i would like to mention just a few: the dental amalgam first. this is currently the first use of mercury in europe and presents several risks to the health of citizens and the environment. for this reason we wanted to see its use completely phased out in a few years' time. we have not succeeded, even with the council's resistance. however, compared with the commission's initial proposal, we have obtained: first, the ban on the use of amalgam for vulnerable populations (pregnant women, breastfeeding women, children under 15 years of age, all baby teeth) as of 1 january 2019; secondly, the development of national plans for the phasing out of amalgam use; third, a commission report by june 2020 on the feasibility of eliminating amalgam altogether. fourth, we have ensured that dental facilities using dental amalgam are equipped with amalgam separators, so that they do not discharge into municipal wastewater. other important changes compared with the initial text have been made to the mercury contaminated sites, which will finally be identified and made public, with the hope that the states can accept a legislative initiative of the union as soon as possible. in addition, we will finally be able to apply the mercury limits set for the internal market to the export of batteries and non-electronic measuring devices, thus overcoming incomprehensible double standards between what we sell within the union and what we export. unfortunately, we have not achieved the same ambition for the export of lamps: however, from 2018 onwards, many of them will be subject to mercury limits lower or equal to those defined under the minamata convention. several manufacturing processes that still use mercury will, thanks to the commitment of the european parliament, have an expiry date and companies will be encouraged to find more environmentally sustainable alternatives. finally, the waste. again, the contribution was significant, they will be solidified and put in safe places.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are starting with the scientific data. exposure to mercury has a negative impact on the nervous system, digestive system, respiratory system, kidneys, skin and eyes. mercury has also been identified as a contributor to alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis and brain damage in general. we also know that, when dispersed in the environment, it can be converted into a more complex and harmful compound, methylmercury, which also has the ability to cross the placental barrier, inhibiting the mental development of babies before they're born. furthermore, the world health organization has made it clear that its toxicity is limitless, so that even very small doses can cause serious harm to health. but despite this, the world's use of mercury remains high - some 3 600 tonnes a year - and the pollution it causes knows no borders. we support mr eck's report, which responds to these health needs of the citizens, and we have also proposed a two-line amendment, which will enable us to avoid dumping 75 tonnes of mercury into our seas from dental fillings which are still used in some countries of the european union.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the widespread use of mercury throughout the world raises serious health and environmental problems. since the industrial revolution, the amount of mercury in the sea has tripled because of man's polluting activities, and there are many diseases linked to exposure to and ingestion of mercury, with very serious complications for the brain, lungs, kidneys and immune system. the text we are going to approve will integrate into a single legal act the obligations arising from the minamata convention, which have not yet been transposed into eu law, and will allow the union to take part in its first conference scheduled for geneva. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of mercury in dental amalgams for children under 15 and for women who are breastfeeding, and to ban mercury altogether from dental amalgams by 2022. the world would have needed a more ambitious approach from the union to the minamata process.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow, tuesday 14 march 2017.

situation where companies and their managers often invest for short-term returns, for personal gain that does not correspond to the interests of the community. for this reason it is important to encourage the exact opposite: to give transparency to all that investors need and to get companies to make choices that guarantee a profit for them, but above all benefits for the community looking at the medium and long term. this was the logic that jacques delors had introduced with the 1993 white paper: we have taken this logic and this text of great cultural as well as economic value as a reference. there are a few points i would like to make quickly: stricter controls and full transparency on the remuneration of directors of listed companies, starting with the so-called say-on-pay, i.e. the shareholder vote on the directors' remuneration policy and the annual report on its implementation; the same transparency for institutional investors and asset managers, which will help to steer the action of these actors towards a more targeted approach to medium and long-term returns; the transparency requirements, a key element of the directive, including for proxy advisors; and then the right for companies to identify their shareholders. finally, transparency and control in relation to transactions with related parties. everything that can be seen and interpreted is a great advantage, both for those who decide to invest and for those who will benefit from the positive effects of these enterprises. there's one last thing i'd like to quickly point out: we have introduced the rules on country-by-country reporting into the text in committee. the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has already adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. i think it 's fair . we have made this joint effort, this responsible choice, to give the regulatory system this advantage as well. the conclusion will be close and i hope also positive as regards this additional element of a sound fiscal policy in europe.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all let me thank all the shadow rapporteurs for the close work they have done in recent months and above all for the atmosphere of cooperation which has enabled us to proceed to the adoption of more than a hundred compromises on some two thousand amendments, by a large majority in the envi committee, on a sensitive and important dossier. the package we are about to discuss and vote on today is only formally amending four waste directives. but i think it would be absolutely reductive to relegate it to the realm of environmental policy or waste policy. i think that what we have before us today is, in effect, a package which poses a very profound challenge to us, which is the challenge of setting up a new sustainable industrial model, that is to say, of making sure that environmental sustainability can be considered one of the levers of the competitiveness of our economic system. because we have to acknowledge that the current linear development model is showing all its limits: it's an inefficient model of development, it's an expensive model of development, it's a model of development that is no longer producing well-being for our citizens and that is over-exploiting the resources of the planet. so, we have the opportunity today to get out of this crisis and move towards the transition to a circular economy which, if you look closely, means not only recovering raw materials from waste but also inserting a virtuous circle such that value is created throughout the life cycle of a product. in short, this means more sustainable growth, it means jobs, it means, as i said earlier, boosting competitiveness, it also means focusing on innovation and new technologies and thus opening up our economic system to new opportunities. of course, to do this we need clear regulation, which encourages investment and ambitious policies. there are many things i would like to say about this package but i will limit myself to the most essential. i must say that we started with a good proposal from the commission, but we have improved it in two main ways: the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the raw materials it uses. why start with prevention? not only because waste prevention is the first level of the waste hierarchy, but because, in our view, waste prevention is a clear indicator of how much we are moving towards a circular economy. let me explain: to produce less waste means to have set in motion all those innovations in production processes, products, business models that tell us how far we are moving towards a circular economy system. i would like to mention among the preventive measures the clearest definition of end of waste or by-products, the minimum requirements of extended producer responsibility, specific measures throughout the product's useful life such as reuse and planned obsolescence, but also, mr president, two ambitious but very important targets: the first is the 50% reduction in food waste, which is not only an environmental policy measure but also an ethical issue, and the second is the 50% reduction in marine litter, which, i recall, are two objectives of the united nations' osh, but which were not provided for in european legislation and we have filled this void. as regards the development of the secondary raw materials market, i would like to recall the targets we have set for recycling and reducing landfilling, which are ambitious but, i must say, also very pragmatic, in line with the commission's previous proposal but also in line with the conclusions of the commission's own 2014 impact assessment. clearly, the prerequisite for an efficient market in secondary raw materials of high quality is high quality separate collection, which we have also extended to the compulsory collection of organic and textile waste. we are talking about 7% of total waste and it is clear that we must close the loop by including industrial and commercial waste. we must not hide the fact that we are facing a challenge which requires a profound paradigm shift and the involvement of all actors, not only the institutions but also businesses and consumers. but i am convinced that parliament will rise to the challenge with the proposal we are voting on today.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we support this package of legislation as approved by the committee on the environment because it improves the present situation, by introducing more ambitious targets on recycling, more ambitious targets on preparing for reuse and also more restrictions on incineration, as well as on landfilling. we would have liked to see more courageous and concrete action, such as a total ban on the incineration of waste. more bold and concrete actions, such as the elimination of all possible subsidies to fossil fuels, because that would be the only real way to achieve a transition to a truly circular economy. if we don't do these simple things, we're talking about nothing. that is why we have tabled amendments to the text on these two subjects, and we have tabled them even though we know that the majority of this house will not vote for them, because the incineration lobbies and the oil industry lobbies are still too strong in this house.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i would first like to thank my fellow shadow rapporteurs and the other colleagues with whom i have worked because in just one year the commission's proposal is from february 2016 we have come to an agreement and to agree in the trilogue a good job, i believe, which is a key step for the full achievement of the digital union. it is now clear to everyone that high-speed connectivity is fundamental to our society and our economy. it is expected that by 2021 the number of smartphones will double and by 2020 internet traffic will increase by as much as eight times compared to today. i'm just quoting these two figures to give you a measure of the increase and the rapid growth of everything that's digital. we have to be ready to respond to this growing demand for connection. i think we need to do this because consumers need it, as do businesses and public administrations, to provide better and more efficient services. i think of all the innovative services that are right in front of us all, that are being born: from connected cars, to all the remote health management, to all the services of the public administration, and also to the whole big issue of digitization of businesses. the internet of things, cloud and mobile communications services are just a few examples of connectivity that are experiencing this development on a global scale. and so there is a demand for speed but also for communication networks that can carry a lot of data, a huge and growing mass of data, reaching densely populated areas as well as remote areas. the development of the most advanced technologies requires the european legislator to ensure the best possible access to the internet for all citizens, even in remote areas, also contributing to the development of increasingly cross-border and transnational applications. radio frequencies have no borders, which is why there is a need for better spectrum coordination at european level. i have been a strong supporter of this need for european coordination for some time. the aim of the proposal is to create uniform criteria at european level for the allocation of frequencies, to overcome barriers to entry, to overcome current barriers to competition and to offer this high-speed wireless connectivity with a universal character. the availability of a broad radio spectrum is one of the essential prerequisites for the deployment of broadband services. it is managed at national level it is a national asset and the sale of rights of use for it can provide substantial revenue (some states have already done so) to the coffers of the member states. but the national management of radio spectrum creates very different conditions between the individual states, both in terms of the duration of licences, of coverage obligations, but above all the consequences of inefficient use of this precious resource. that is why the commission, but also parliament, believe that action must be taken in good time, as we are doing, to ensure that spectrum is managed and regulated more efficiently. the proposal focuses on two main elements: for the 700 band, there is a common timetable for its effective availability for use by wireless services under harmonised conditions, with coordination measures to support the transition phase. for the sub-700 band, a long-term priority for the distribution of audiovisual media services to the general public is envisaged, together with a flexible approach to spectrum use in response to the different degree of digital terrestrial television penetration in the various member states. we have reached a good compromise in the itre committee, asking for the release of this band to take place by 2020 but also for some states to allow for a small delay, motivated by certain specific conditions. and we also asked for a coordinated plan for transnational issues. i think it is a good job, balanced, that meets clear objectives and that will put us in a position to win this race for the spread of 5g and all the most advanced technologies.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to congratulate mrs toia on her excellent work. connectivity services are developing rapidly globally and require speed but also communication networks capable of carrying a lot of data and reaching the most remote areas. the availability of a broad spectrum, currently managed at national level with very different conditions between member states, is one of the essential prerequisites for the spread of broadband services. the proposal for a decision will harmonise the criteria for the allocation of frequencies at european level, obliging member states to make rights of use for spectrum for electronic communications services in the 700 mhz frequency band marketable. the implementation of the proposed measures will not only make it cheaper to develop innovative devices and services, but will also allow europe to accelerate towards the digital single market and the development of the 5g network, thus closing the gap with the leading countries in mobile broadband.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the collection of scientific data is essential for the implementation of the common fisheries policy, since it allows it to be based on the best scientific advice. the data are used to assess the state of fish stocks, the profitability of the various segments of the sector and the impact of fisheries and aquaculture on ecosystems. but data are also needed to evaluate eu policies: the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster. we need scientific data to apply good rules and effective fisheries management policies and we need data to assess whether these policies are working or whether they need to be changed and improved. for this reason, an eu framework for the collection and management of fisheries data was established in 2000, which became the data collection framework (dcf) in 2008, and represented an important step forward in the development of a harmonised set of union standards for the collection of biological, environmental, technical and socioeconomic data on fisheries, aquaculture and processing. the common fisheries policy requires us to manage fishing activities with due regard for their impact on the ecosystem. on this basis we need to build a deeper and more comprehensive understanding of marine ecosystems, so that we do not act blindly and only realise the consequences of our policies after they have emerged, often in a negative way. this is particularly important in order to achieve the maximum sustainable yield (msy) by 2020. maximum sustainable yield is a relatively new and very important concept, but it is based on numerical values which must be established in a scientific manner and on the basis of data, studies and research. the commission's proposal on this dossier was based on what was already working in the current data collection system, thus maintaining continuity but at the same time allowing for adaptation to new requirements. what we have achieved, thanks to the work we have done together with the shadow rapporteurs, with whom there has been a great deal of agreement on this report and a great deal of sharing especially in the difficult moments of the discussion with the council, is an expanded scope to include the collection of data for the protection of the marine environment, that is, data which are used to assess the impact of fishing on the marine ecosystem, including vulnerable marine areas and the most sensitive species and habitats. this, of course, together with the data needed for the sustainable management of all commercially exploited species and in particular for the achievement of good ecological status by 2020. we have included the need to cover those fisheries which are so called data deficient, i.e. without the necessary support of current scientific knowledge; we also wanted to make this data available to everyone: institutions, researchers, environmental associations and anyone interested in studying and evaluating them. but we have also set stricter deadlines for member states to respond to requests for data from end-users and other interested parties. we are moving towards regional databases, which is important because data is being collected on larger marine areas in a standardised and harmonised way. we will also collect data on aquaculture, both at biological and socioeconomic level; we're going to collect data on recreational fisheries, although in this case we've been partially defeated because it was important to include socioeconomic data, but we didn't do it. we have the environmental impact of recreational fishing. we insisted on reaching an adequate and comprehensive number of mandatory sea-based search campaigns to be established at union level and finally, after a long arm-wrestling with the council, we got most of the data collection framework, in particular the list of what data and what categories of data to collect, to be adopted by means of delegated acts. we have thus defended the prerogatives of the european parliament, which must be able to evaluate and decide on such important acts.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, a good rule is one which reconciles protection and development. to create these conditions, there is a great need to collect data, to know. we, as politicians, as representatives, cannot act if we do not know, because if a rule only acts on protection or only on development, it would create a total distinction with regard to the will of the policy. that is why i think this regulation is so important and i also thank mr affronte and all those who have worked on it, mr kuhn, because we can consider the common fisheries policy (cfp) as a great policy at our disposal. we cannot ignore the economic development in europe, especially in the coastal areas, where it is possible to combine more economic development under protection with a capacity not to undermine the harmony of such an important economy as fishing.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, this dossier is dealing with a very serious problem, especially in the mediterranean, a sea rich in resources but characterized by a serious lack of data to really know the state of health of our stocks. reform of the data collection framework is therefore crucial to achieving the objectives of the cfp and requires the efforts of member states to collect the data needed to assess the state of exploited marine biological resources, the level of fisheries and the impact of the latter on biological resources and also on marine ecosystems. the collection, management and use of data shall meet criteria of accuracy, reliability and timeliness. at the same time, it is necessary to avoid the collection of the same data for different purposes, as this would lead to an unnecessary waste of resources. in this connection, i welcome the proposal to set up a european scientific data network to use the information collected in accordance with the assessment to be made and so that it can also be exchanged with third countries. the issue is very complex and at the same time closely linked to the need to manage fisheries activities, taking into account their impact on ecosystems, and should therefore be managed according to the principle of regionalisation. in addition, there is still much to be discovered about the sea and its resources. scientific knowledge is essential for efficient and far-sighted management, but it is not enough. there is still a lot to be done on this too.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the collection of data is essential for the implementation of the common fisheries policy, because it allows it to be based on objective and scientific advice. in addition to assessing the state of fish stocks, the profitability of the various segments of the sector and the impact of fisheries and aquaculture on the ecosystem, data are needed to assess eu policies such as fisheries management and mitigation measures. the creation of supranational regional databases, through regional coordination groups, is important in order to have aggregated and comparable data. in the adriatic sea, for example, the data for italy, slovenia and croatia will be evaluated together. the data will be available to all institutions, researchers, environmental associations and anyone interested in studying and evaluating them. for the first time, data from other sectors that impact on the marine ecosystem, such as recreational fisheries and aquaculture, will also be included in the framework for data collection and management. this is an important step forward which will contribute to the sustainable development of fisheries, thus limiting the impact on the marine ecosystem.
member of the commission. – madam president, honourable members, i would like to say thank you to the parliament for prioritising the work on the recast regulation on data collection and, in particular, thank you to the rapporteur and his team for their work. i will make sure i give a full account of this discussion to commissioner vella. we provided for transitional arrangements so that immediately after adoption and publication of the recast there is no legal vacuum. the current multiannual programme for data collection will remain applicable until replaced by a new one. there have been a couple of comments about data storage. i would just record that basic storage of data will remain at member state level and member states will remain responsible for ensuring that good quality data is available for end-users. the current multiannual programme was adopted last summer and it was already updated with many of the new requirements. so, there is no need to replace it urgently. the member states’ work plans for data collection were approved last summer. member states will already have started collecting data accordingly. when important modifications are needed, member states will need to resubmit the work plans for approval in the normal way. meanwhile, member states have already started to transition from regional coordination meetings to regional coordination groups, ensuring more continuity and better involving the relevant end-users in data collection. in summary, by the end of 2017 we expect the new legal framework for data collection to be operational for collecting all data needed for what i take to be our shared objective, the effective implementation and monitoring of the cfp. thank you.

member of the commission. – madam president, let me start by expressing my thanks to all of you for this opportunity to discuss with you the very important and sensitive issue of trafficking in human beings. the european parliament has been a strong and consistent supporter of our efforts to deal with this odious and appalling crime. it is a crime that takes advantage of the vulnerability and exploits the desperation of people in need of protection and support. as you know, trafficking was and remains a priority for us as reflected both in the european agenda on migration and in the european agenda on security. europe has globally a leading role in this field. we have developed a coherent and coordinated legal and policy framework to address trafficking in human beings. the anti-trafficking directive and the 2012-2016 eu strategy has been our main instruments to develop, coordinate and implement our policy framework priorities. having delivered on the vast majority of actions envisaged in this strategy we do not feel that our job is done; quite the opposite. we cannot accept that irrespective of origin there are still and unfortunately more children, women, vulnerable people trafficked, abused and exploited. these are victims of the immoral and inhuman profit-making face of our societies. now that the 2012-2016 strategy has come to an end the time has come to step up our efforts and continue delivering more intensively and in a more focused way. to this end the support and contribution of this house, of all of you, is of utmost importance. the migration crisis and transnational security threats render people more vulnerable to criminal networks and exploitation. that is why more needs to be done to target the organised criminal networks and follow their money throughout the trafficking chain, to focus more on prevention and on better identification and protection of victims, to further strengthen coordination at eu level and to ensure more coherence in the external and internal dimensions of our anti-trafficking policy. criminal networks target and exploit the most vulnerable. recent data indicate that the vast majority of victims are female and children. the most widespread form of exploitation is sexual exploitation, with mainly women and young girls as victims. that is why the anti-trafficking directive has a strong gender-specific dimension, and that is why we have also commissioned a study on the gender dimensions of trafficking in human beings. it is also of major importance to increase our cooperation with third countries and further streamline our anti-trafficking priorities in the external dimension of our policies. the two distinct notions of trafficking and smuggling are often confused. however, it is not only a matter of the correct use of terminology. it is also about ensuring a victim-centred and human rights based approach. allow me to clarify here that smuggling is a cross-border activity while trafficking can also take place within the borders of a state. in smuggling there is consent of the smuggled person while in trafficking there is not. the exploitation of the vulnerable victim for profit making is an essential element in trafficking. these differences bear significant implications for the rights of the victims of trafficking and the respective obligations of member states. i would like to assure you that the respective eu legislative frameworks on smuggling and trafficking will remain clear and constant in any future policy initiative. regarding now the two reports based on the anti-trafficking directive presented by the commission last december we will continue to proactively monitor the situation in the member states and examine potential options. to conclude, and as far as our next steps are concerned, we are currently taking stock of the experience and achievements of the current strategy, examining trends and problems and assessing and discussing with stakeholders what future actions from all the different policy areas are needed. our aim is to address the challenges created by the changing socio-political context. but we also want to maintain a coordinated, coherent and constant approach in the continuation of the efforts to fight this extremely pernicious but highly lucrative form of crime. the reflections and contributions of this house are of great importance for our work and i am looking forward with particular interest to our discussion today.
on behalf of the ppe group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the commissioner for the commission's commitment to this very serious subject. i heard my colleagues say, quite rightly: "women and children, who are vulnerable people". no, women are not vulnerable. they're made vulnerable by men, by the criminal networks that sell them. in addition, 80% of the minors are female and the other 20% are male. so it's a huge problem, a problem that's connected to other factors as well, not just the prostitution factor. i would like to introduce another theme: it is almost a taboo, but when it comes to children, there is a real danger, even for children who disappear - we mentioned unaccompanied foreign children - from organ trafficking. we took care of it. when i was chairman of the committee on children and adolescents in the senate, we discussed this issue with the minister of the interior in italy. so it is important that everything that can and must be done be done. the economic commitment: they are often exploited people. they arrive, when they're sold, who have already been abused, abused in ways that have never been seen before. they 're in economic weakness: the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem. we have to fight this too. the last thing is bound looks unbound, but is bound: we also fight for equal economic treatment of women with men: this is slavery, too.
the european union is not a party to the conflict, but it is a party to the peace process. as already mentioned, the european parliament, together with the council, adopted a directive some time ago which aims to tackle and solve the problem through a multilateral approach, not only to combat trafficking in human beings, but also to prevent it and to ensure protection for the victims of such abuse. you see, commissioner, we agree with you on the description of the problem. where we're not is on the prescription. as you know, not all member states have fully transposed the directive and this terrible abuse continues even within our own borders. and so the task before us is very clear: the european union must be able to take action quickly to develop a new strategy which is much more effective and capable of tackling this tragic problem, while fully safeguarding human rights and human dignity.
on behalf of the enf group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, one of the most convincing definitions of human trafficking, even from a legal point of view, is contained in the additional protocol to the united nations convention against transnational organized crime, better known as the 'palermo protocol', which outlines its characteristic elements, namely the threat or use of force or other forms of coercion to recruit people for the purpose of exploiting them. today, as far as the trafficking from africa is concerned, there is a strong emergency certainly from the western part, but also from the horn of africa. it is clear that the risk of trafficking in these products is particularly high for vulnerable people, particularly children. but there is one aspect which i think has been under-emphasized, even in the commissioner's reply, and which is reflected in the data collected by the international organisation for migration (iom), which shows a worrying reality, as more than 70% of migrants in transit from north africa to europe are victims of trafficking, organ trafficking and other forms of exploitation. this is a reality that we have denounced many times, but where is europe? have you noticed that your immigration policy, your hypocritical open door policy, these disparate policies, actually encourage this trafficking? and so it is useless to debate these things here when nothing is being done to close the borders to smugglers and we are relying on certain soros-funded ngos to intervene in favour of immigrants and migrants, under who knows what conditions, and then perhaps relying on turkey to take in migrants who wanted to reach europe from other places. that's a good result.

but my joy, my friends, is not clouded. it is bitter to speak for the first time before this house, shortly after a member state has begun to withdraw from the european union. i know that you will be speaking to this house tomorrow. i find this bitter not only as a politician but above all as a citizen of europe. you should know that i am about as old as the european union. when i was born in 1956, the wounds of the war unleashed by hitler's germany were still visible in our cities throughout europe. even greater were the wounds in the hearts of our neighbors. and yet, at that very moment, they reached out to my country for peace and together, in rome 60 years ago, they laid the foundations for a new europe. when i went to school, young people were already symbolically sawing at the battlements of europe's borders to show that we wanted more europe. what we have achieved is not enough! in 1968 the customs barriers within europe were removed, the long lines for lorries at the toll booths were history and the queues for cars were at least shorter. when i came to university, the pull of europe was already so great that the people of southern europe - in greece, in spain, in portugal - were not only sweeping away dictatorships, but were paving the way for freedom and democracy in the common europe. in 1989, i was in the final stages of my doctoral thesis, the berlin wall fell, brought down by the brave men and women of eastern europe who had peacefully won freedom and democracy. it was they who made possible not only the unity of my country but the reunification of europe. all of this and much more is meant when the rome declaration says: 'we are united in our happiness!' all this is the great legacy that the mothers and fathers of europe have entrusted to us and on which our children are building. we must not give up this precious heritage and leave it to the enemies of europe. we must preserve, maintain and improve it - this is our common historical mission! (applause from the centre) when i look back on the 60 or so years of my life and the same period of time as the european union, i see the growth, the development and the success of the new europe - the path from the organisation of the deficit economy in post-war europe to a beacon of hope for a more just and peaceful world. it seemed to some - and i'm not excluding myself - that this was guaranteed forever. but in my biography i have also experienced the struggles of europe: the crises, the contradictions, the setbacks. i had to learn: my belief, and the belief of many in my generation, that the path of europe, the path of european unity, was irreversible, was wrong. no, europe's future is not a certainty - it never was, and we haven't known that since brexit. i remember 2005. i had just become foreign minister of my country, and the dream of the european constitution had just been shattered. i remember how disappointed many of us were back then. but i know just as well as we do that - and i suspect many of you in the chamber have done that - that we have come together again and done what europe does best: get back on our feet and get on with it. we picked up the phone, listened to each other, spent nights at the negotiating table and forged, piece by piece, the treaty of lisbon. what i'm saying is that europe has never been a walk in the park. europe is a complicated, indeed, a strenuous project. but it's worth it! we can and must counter europe's bad guys: cooperation, growing prosperity and, above all, 70 years of peace - that is europe's promise to its citizens. but never in its history has that promise been fulfilled on its own. it has only been fulfilled when the actions of the actors have been guided not by national narrow-mindedness but by european reason. that is the standard we must meet! (applause from the centre) that's why i came to you today. i would like to make my first speech as president of the federal republic of germany outside germany nowhere else than here in this parliament. (applause from the centre) i am not saying that the european parliament should be the only one to be able to do this. as a citizen, i say, as many citizens have said in recent weeks: yes, i want europe! and as president of the federal republic of germany, i can say that the overwhelming majority of germans want europe! we do not want a return to an unpleasant past, but a common path towards a better european future! that's the perspective! (applause from the centre) if we say yes to europe, we do not have to flatter ourselves and we do not have to be afraid of contradiction. if we say yes to europe, we also say yes to the complicated, the strenuous and also the unfinished aspects of europe! how complicated political solutions are, how tedious the process - who knows this better than you here in the european parliament? it is not only a meeting of conflicting interests, but also of different cultures, languages and traditions. europe's diversity is an adventure, but it is also exhausting. i think i just heard antonio and the leaders of the factions sighing about it. but that is precisely what europe needs today: that we do not entrench ourselves in a circle of opinion, that we do not simply complain about the divisions that have opened up in europe or withdraw into national recesses, but that we seriously look for ways on all sides to build bridges across these divisions. this includes - and in europe has always included - the assumption that the other party may also be right. europe was founded on the assumption that others might be right. europe's successes have always been compromises. europe's successes have been the arduous but peaceful balancing of interests. that is what this parliament stands for, that is what you stand for in 28 nations. who would ever become a member of parliament without the will to convince and at the same time the willingness to be convinced, without the passion for the complicated, for the efforts of democracy! everyone in this room who is showing this passion right now, in these difficult times, has my deepest respect and certainly my support. (applause from the centre) support because i know there are others. there are plenty of other forces that are always there with the very simple answers - answers of the strong hand, answers with clear enemy images. a new fascination with authoritarianism is spreading not only far beyond the borders of europe, to the west and east, but also, unfortunately, here in the heart of europe. populists paint the world in black and white and capitalize on fear. anyone who knows me knows i'm not one for alarmism. this parliament can tolerate dispute, and it needs it. but i also say: those who dismiss democratic institutions and parliaments as a waste of time, those who declare willingness to compromise as weakness and, above all, those who no longer insist on the distinction between fact and falsehood, are touching the very foundation of democracy and will, must, hear our resolute, our common opposition as democrats! (applause from the centre) the world we live in has become more uncertain and confusing. many people worry about the future; fear of losing control. they are becoming susceptible to the enticements of those who say: 'come back behind the familiar butts of the nation! border close, scots close! it's the only way we can regain our sovereignty! but it's not only naive, it's irresponsible to trick people into thinking that you can put walls and fences around dangers like terrorism or climate change that know no borders. it's irresponsible to tell people that in a world that's getting more complicated, the answers are getting simpler. and i believe it is wrong to say that in this world a european country can make its voice more heard or its economic interests more effective by itself and without the eu.
