(applause from the centre) the crisis gives us the opportunity to see europe as it really is - without illusions, without false optimism, with all its strengths and also its weaknesses. and the crisis forces us to answer the question: what kind of european unity do we want and how much do we want it? the commission's white paper has identified options for this. this is not the solution, but one thing seems clear to me: a permanent self-blockade in the european union is the worst possible option, it is not! if we want to move forward together, we cannot all achieve 100 per cent in the end. the problems are too complex and the expectations too different: yes, we want a stronger europe and more european solutions, but we must also make room for those members who cannot or do not want to take further steps towards integration. yes, we want to show solidarity with countries suffering from the consequences of the financial and economic crisis and having to embark on or have had to embark on tough reforms. but european solidarity can only support national efforts, not replace them. yes, we want to help people who are fleeing war and persecution. but because our collective possibilities are also finite, we must decide how and how much responsibility each of us must bear. yes, we want to keep the european union together. but we also know that europe is bigger than the european union and that without the integration of our neighbours to the east and south there will be no lasting peace on this continent. (applause from the centre) i know that, ladies and gentlemen. none of these problems is easy, and we must not ignore the concerns of the people in all of this. but those who built europe certainly had to contend with more difficult problems. you have replaced the battlefield with the negotiating table, the confrontation with a peaceful balancing of interests. they have been wise; they have shown soundness of mind. the world of today - a world full of new uncertainties - does not allow us to be less clever than our predecessors. there is no lack of clarity on the issues to be solved - they are on the table. what is lacking is the courage - and sometimes the willingness - to solve them in a european way. and we have to change that! (applause from the centre) the balance of interests is the dispute. we are fighting in europe, and in my view this is not a sign of decline. i too have been involved in political disputes in europe for the last 25 years, not just occasionally but more often, and i have met some of you in this room in the course of your disputes. but when we argue in europe, we do so on a firm normative foundation. many questions are complicated, but this must not cloud our view of the most basic and important things: freedom and democracy, the rule of law and human rights are not at our disposal. it is thus enshrined in article 2 of the treaty on european union and is binding on all member states. this is the essence of europe, so to speak, this is what europe is in the eyes of the world and what many of us may even envy. if we are to be a beacon for the rule of law and human rights in the world, then we must not be indifferent to the fact that this foundation is being shaken within europe. and then europe must not remain silent when civil society, even science - as is happening now at the central european university in budapest - is deprived of its breathing space. then europe must not remain silent! (applause from the centre) but the role of my country is also a subject of controversy. some are calling for germany to take a more leading role in europe. others warn of german dominance. and the newly elected president of our most important ally recently said that the european union is nothing more than "a means to an end for germany". i'll tell you what, that's a misunderstanding. europe's strength cannot be based on the leadership of individuals, but always on the responsibility of all. of course, germany, as the largest and most populous country, has a special responsibility. but we know our options, and we know our limitations. and we too will not forget that others in europe may be right when we argue about solutions. we know what we owe to this europe. i say that a united europe is the right answer to our history and our geography - for ourselves and for our neighbours. and we feel that a strong europe is not only in our own interest, but that it has become part of our identity. so you should know that we germans want to keep the european union together. we want to build a common future in europe, together with our partners, large and small, on equal terms and with equal responsibilities. but in the end, beyond all the state's reason, there is something quite different and perhaps something much more important: europe is a matter of the heart for the vast majority of people in germany, not for all of them. that is why i have told you my own story of europe. and that is why in the past few weeks many people, especially many young people in germany, have told me their stories about europe. the young people - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i voted in favour of this report today because it is necessary, for reasons of clarity, to revise the regulation defining the characteristics of fishing vessels. it is essential to codify all the regulations from 1986 to the present day, with the aim of simplifying this rule and making it more understandable and accessible to fishermen and citizens of the european union. i regret that the council did not consider it appropriate to protect small-scale artisanal fishing by keeping it separate from industrial fishing. in fact, a legal definition is needed as regards the characteristics of large-scale fishing and small-scale fishing in order to distinguish them from a legal point of view. this definition, which unfortunately does not appear in the regulation in question, should include, in addition to the size of the vessel, attributes such as the length of the vessels, variables relating to their range, their social role in coastal communities, the ecological impact, the fishing capacity and the economic data relating to the undertaking.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, amnesty international has denounced the fact that the world's leading brands of food and household products containing palm oil are responsible for serious human rights violations in a sector where children as young as eight are working in dangerous conditions and where discrimination against women is being committed on a day-to-day basis without guarantees of permanent employment and social benefits such as health and personal insurance. this is particularly serious when you consider that much of this product is produced on indonesian plantations owned by the world's largest oil palm grower, the agribusiness giant wilmar, which supplies 8 of the largest multinational palm oil users, which are themselves part of the rspo certification circuit. that 's right . while the world's largest companies reassure consumers to make ethical choices by buying products that claim to use sustainable palm oil, they continue to turn a blind eye to the exploitation of millions of workers in their own supply chains. that is why the report, which i voted for, finally calls for multinationals to be more transparent about what is in their products, by declaring where the raw materials in the products on the shelves of supermarkets come from.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the precious tropical ecosystems, which cover about 7% of the earth's surface, are increasingly under pressure from deforestation. about half of the area of illegally logged forests is used for the production of palm oil for the european market, which is the third largest in the world. in the report we have approved today, the european parliament calls for the introduction of minimum sustainability criteria for palm oil and the adoption of a binding regulatory framework to ensure that all the supply chains of importers of agricultural commodities are traceable back to the origin of the raw material. the report stresses the need to replace the current voluntary certification schemes, some of which have revealed limitations, with a single certification system to ensure that only sustainably produced palm oil can access the eu market. for these reasons i thought i should vote in favour.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, honourable members, as you have already highlighted, you have added the topic ‘state of play of the second review of the economic adjustment programme for greece’ to today’s agenda and you will appreciate that i will limit my intervention on this process. in line with the european legal framework, the institutions, that is the commission, the ecb, the esm and imf, are entrusted with the design and monitoring of adjustment programmes. this also includes negotiations of updated policy conditionality with the national authorities. the eurogroup is regularly informed of the state of play of the adjustment programme by the institutions and also the authorities, and on occasion the eurogroup provides political guidance on open issues. the second review of the greece programme is on the agenda of the next eurogroup meeting later this week on 7 april. the council is not intervening in ongoing programme reviews and i can confirm that it has not discussed the issue at hand either in march or at earlier meetings. the commission is also, i think, much better placed to provide you with the information on the subject than i am, and i see that commissioner moscovici is here and he will address you just after me. the commission informing the european parliament is also in line with the eu provisions, the two-pack provisions, on adjustment programmes. so for now i thank you very much and i will listen with great attention to the interventions by the honourable members and by commissioner moscovici.
member of the commission. mr president, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, it is a pleasure to be with you today to discuss the second review of the greek programme. let us start with the situation of the greek economy, which has shown resilience in the face of the turbulence of 2015 and 2016 and the effects of capital controls. as early as 2016, positive trends emerged, including the return, which surprised us, of positive growth faster than expected for some quarters and the decline in unemployment, which was at an absolutely unacceptable level and remains far too high. today, however, this positive trend - it must be admitted - is beginning to slip. why is there such hesitation? because we're closing the review late. what i have observed from my own responsibility is that there is a very close link between the return of growth in greece and success in negotiations. when the negotiation moves forward, growth and confidence restart. when negotiation is delayed, then growth is delayed, as are investors. all greece's partners must now come together to put an end to this damaging uncertainty and finally create a sustainable cycle of virtuous recovery. greece deserves it. its authorities, government and parliament have made considerable progress since the launch of the current programme. the progress made over the past 18 months must be sustained and strengthened to ensure what the country and the euro area need, namely a sustainable recovery. we remain convinced that, following substantial reforms and further implementation efforts, the greek economy, which is very flexible, very creative and very responsive, is capable of turning the page. but it must be helped and not hindered further by uncertainty. for its part, as the minister has said, the commission is doing everything in its power and is playing its part, in a way, as an honest broker to achieve a fair and balanced agreement, which we want quickly. why is this agreement possible? firstly, because the budgetary objectives have been largely achieved. i would like to reiterate that the 2016 primary surplus target of 0.5% under the programme has been very much exceeded. eurostat will publish the result at the end of april, but we expect the primary surplus to be simply above 3%. greece is also on track to meet its target of 1.75% of gdp in 2017 and 3.5% in 2018. these results don't just fall from the sky. they are the result of a series of extremely tough fiscal consolidations that include high-quality parametric measures adopted in 2015 and 2016, with a cumulative fiscal return of 4,5% of gdp, a considerable figure. what european country has experienced such an adjustment? whatever the political preferences - and the commission has no political preference - such efforts must not be forgotten or ignored, but they must be anchored, deepened and pursued. as regards the reform programme, the authorities have already implemented much of what was required. to cite a few examples that do not always get the attention they deserve: greece has for the first time a national social security net which will guarantee a subsistence or basic income and thus strengthen education and vocational training in times of high unemployment. an independent authority for public revenue has finally been established. greece needed it, among other things, to improve the collection of revenue. the legislation to reduce non-performing loans has been passed and we are now moving to implementation. a new privatisation and investment fund, hcap, is now operational and its supervisory and management boards have already started to fulfil their responsibilities. it follows naturally that important progress has already been made in major privatisation projects. i encourage the greek authorities to maintain this momentum which is essential to attract the investment and private investors that greece needs. finally, i will mention the various measures adopted in the fields of product markets, the business environment and the legal system. all these examples are in fact only a small part of the approximately 200 measures that have been taken since the programme started in summer 2015. the first months of this year were spent negotiating two critical elements. first, the measures necessary to complete the second review. the main outstanding issues are well known. first of all, it is a question of labour market reform, which is of great importance to many of you and also to the commission. it is essential that the greek labour market takes into account the difficulties on the employment front, but also the current economic challenges specific to the country, in order for reforms to support the recovery and job creation. i would like to say that the commission, committed to the european social model, continues to support fair and effective collective bargaining systems. greece should follow european best practice in areas such as collective redundancies and trade union action. in this respect, we take into account the work of the group of independent experts responsible for formulating recommendations in the light of european and international best practice. we also know that not all of them have had unanimous support. in my experience, what matters most is not necessarily how the system works on paper, but how it works in practice, i.e. how the social partners take ownership of it and commit themselves jointly, autonomously and in collaboration with the public authorities. the second major subject of negotiation is the energy market. in this sector, it is important to increase competition, taking into account european rules and, of course, recent court decisions. a more competitive and efficient market is in the interest of all consumers. i think that with some technical adjustments we should be able to agree quickly on the necessary elements of reform that are good for everyone and, first and foremost, for the greek economy. in recent weeks another item of discussion has been a budgetary arrangement which would allow the international monetary fund to participate with its own programme. i know that for many of you, for the commission and for the member states, the involvement of the international monetary fund is a major security guarantee. this is a basic condition. what is new is that this scheme would take effect in the years immediately following the end of the programme. so we are thinking not about what happens by the end of 2018, but in the years immediately after 2018, without asking for a primary effort for too long, because it is neither viable nor democratic. the objective should be to achieve a balanced package, which will ensure that greece achieves this primary surplus target in the medium term. this concept was reiterated at the february and march eurogroup meetings. it has been and is still the basis for the discussions of the last few weeks, which must be concluded very quickly because we have another eurogroup meeting in valletta in three days' time. the discussions are continuing. i would also like to apologize for leaving this house before the end of our debate and going to brussels, where important meetings with the greek authorities and the european institutions are taking place this evening. i wanted to be in strasbourg for your debate and then go back to brussels, which is never easy. i would like to emphasize that this system includes measures to further rationalize expenditure. the commission and i welcome the progress made so far, including on the issues which are necessary prerequisites for imf participation. we have already come a long way since the mandate given to the eurogroup at the end of february. we shall have the opportunity to measure it this week with the ministers in valletta. i hope that the meeting there will be a good meeting, which will show that we are really moving towards a satisfactory conclusion. i continue to believe that technical agreement at institutional level before and after a political agreement is not only possible but also imperative to limit the risks of delay and to avoid jeopardising the positive budgetary performance of last year. but this requires a genuine commitment and a willingness to conclude on the part of all, and i emphasize the word 'all'. the european union has a long history of supporting the peace process. we are aware of that. this is particularly true for greece. we therefore count on the constructive attitude of the other institutions concerned and i want to say in this forum, without any reservations, that this also includes the international monetary fund, which has been actively involved in all aspects of the negotiations since the creation of the esm programme in 2015 and which must also do its part to understand the specific difficulties of greece. the commission will therefore continue to support constructive discussions between all partners and to promote a swift conclusion of the review. finally, the commission will also continue to encourage all efforts towards a more sustainable greek debt. we have been pointing out for some time that a more realistic primary surplus pathway is needed after the end of the programme. it is not possible to demand for years and years that primary surplus levels be too high if growth is to be restarted in the country and employment is to return. without this, markets will not be willing to lend at reasonable rates and greece will continue to depend on the support of its european partners. in the end, i think it is a matter of burden-sharing between greece and the eurogroup. in short, the commission would like to highlight the progress already made. she knows that there is still some work to be done before the discussion can be successful. i repeat how much this is for us, and for me personally, something that is not only desirable but possible and necessary for our economic and monetary union, for the euro area, for greece and for the greek people, who have suffered a lot from the crisis, who must see the light at the end of this long tunnel of austerity and return to the path of growth and employment.

president-in-office of the council. thank you for inviting the presidency to give our views on how the european union can respond to hate speech, populism and fake news on social media on behalf of the council on a subject of common concern. let me start with the first part of the topic, namely hate speech. evidence from different sources such as the european union agency for fundamental rights and the council of europe confirms an alarming increase in intolerance and hatred in europe. there may be various reasons for this phenomenon, but there is certainly no justification for it. the european union has adopted specific legislation on combating intolerance and hatred, notably including the 2008 framework decision on combating racism and xenophobia. and in june last year, in 2016, the council also invited member states to ensure the effective transposition and implementation of the framework decision and other relevant laws related to hate crimes at national level in order to fight the scourge of hate crimes. and furthermore, the council also asked the member states to develop effective methods to report hate crimes and thus ensure their proper registration. there is no doubt, mr president, that the means of social communication are today one of the main means, as the honourable member fajon has also said, one of the main means by which hate speech is being spread to the greatest number of people and in the shortest possible time. and a possible remedy against this epidemic is a coordinated and determined european response. in the context of interinstitutional cooperation, the council has also already supported the ambitious plans of the commission's high level group which is trying to develop, with the member states, concrete practices and tools to improve the response to racism, xenophobia and other forms of intolerance. and so we also welcome and support the ongoing dialogue at european union level with leading it companies to address this scourge. last but not least in this respect we should also remember and commend the excellent work done by the agency to which you referred earlier. these countermeasures are all in vain, however, if we forget the important role of education and our work among young people. and more specifically the need to develop democratic resilience, media literacy, tolerance, critical thinking and even conflict resolution skills in the learning process. finally, i would also like to stress that combating hate speech online is also one of our priorities as president. in fact, just tomorrow in valletta, around 100 experts will be meeting to discuss how to effectively deliver positive narratives against hate speech online and the role of the european union and the member states in supporting civil society in this effort. a positive element of this event is, i think, the fact that social media is being seen not only as the problem but as part of the solution. i now wish to go into more detail on the second part of the debate: the manipulation and propaganda through fake news. fake news and misinformation that are considered by many to be dangerous to democracies because they threaten the very foundations of our societies: citizens elect their representatives on the basis of political views formed by open and fair debate. the rise in popularity of the internet and social media has led to a flood of news sources, which is good in itself, but many of them are not reliable. it is a reality. and so news organizations are under increasing pressure to deliver a continuous stream of news at the moment it happens, leaving less time, as time, for quality control and auditing. and so that's a challenge on the newsrooms that we understand. in addition, you also have populist actors spreading misinformation to support their narratives, which is particularly harmful in years when the people are making their democratic choices. it is not easy for citizens to identify fake news, or even to find and access reliable information. we have already heard some proposals and i imagine that other members will speak about them during this debate. the algorithms put people in bubbles: the commission has also been asked to provide a report on the implementation of the new rules on the protection of personal data. and so prejudices are reinforced as the media create bubbles that filter information. and so it takes governments, news organizations and even it companies to recognize these dangers and take action against them. the presidency uses the media, including the internet, to ensure that reliable information on our work is accessible. but we are not just talking about our work here, we are talking in a much broader sense. i also heard that some news organisations, i think in france, are also now joining social media platforms in fighting the rise of fake news online. and in some other member states, the call for legislation to protect political debate from manipulation and outright deception on social media is growing. it companies believe they have a role to play in society and so that is protecting this core element that is our democracies. president, honourable members, i would like to conclude by stressing how important it is that we do not allow our citizens to be deceived by fake news and our societies to be determined by hatred. we also use social platforms, we also see these realities and i hope that social media is the platform where one expresses positivity, the platform where one shares with one's friends, with the community in which one lives, the positive experiences, and does not have to be fooled by fake news and even dominated by hatred. our role is also to remind ourselves of our responsibilities and to be serious and responsible about everything we say. and for that reason, freedom of expression has its limits and it is our common responsibility to strike that fair balance although i know that this is difficult and often not easy.

speech. the proliferation of hate speech online is shrinking the space for democratic discussions. when ‘toxic narratives’ about migrants and religious minorities publicly incite hatred and violence, the thin line between hate speech and hate crime merges into one. where public incitement to violence and hatred is spread against groups or individuals on grounds of their race, ethnicity or religion, we have eu laws that criminalise these kinds of behaviour. the commission has engaged with the social media operators to counter illegal online hate speech. in may 2016, it companies – facebook, microsoft, twitter and youtube – agreed a voluntary code of conduct with commitments to take action and tackle illegal online content that publicly incites violence and hatred. we will present the results of this self-regulatory exercise next month. the commission’s proposal to revise the audiovisual media services directive widens the definition of hate speech by referring to ‘incitement to violence or hatred’, and includes ethnic origin, belief, disability, age or sexual orientation. it calls for a requirement for video-sharing platforms to protect people against incitement to violence or hatred. the commission is now assessing whether improved eu-wide procedures are needed for the removal of illegal content from online platforms. we will announce our conclusions on 10 may this year as part of the mid-term review of the digital single market. fake news – or simply ‘lies’ – are also a serious problem... in writing. the circulation of fake news on the internet - so-called 'fake news' - is a problem which must be tackled as soon as possible on a supranational scale and in an effective manner. the internet is an extraordinary source of information, but it can also become a dangerous tool for the artificial manipulation of reality in order to weaken and disrupt the consensus around the fundamental values on which the european union is founded. the rightful freedom to inform through the internet has highlighted the need for clear regulation that provides greater certainty about the legal responsibilities of those who, through the amplifying power of social media, leverage the creation and dissemination of slander, lies and incitement to racial and institutional hatred to generate income, unconcerned with the devastating social effects that such activities entail. since the network has no borders or barriers, the issue can only be effectively addressed at international level. i therefore welcome the debate which has opened up today in parliament on this subject and hope that this reflection will involve the other eu institutions as soon as possible in order to arrive at ready, concrete and effective responses.
in writing. a whole old information society, easily controlled and enslaved to political and economic power, is increasingly in crisis. hate speech and fake news did not come with the advent of the internet and social media, nor do they manifest exclusively through these channels. information that distorts reality, spread by the mainstream media, and that has been used to justify wars and maneuvers by certain power groups are recurrent in contemporary societies. the risk that the demands for excessive regulation of the internet will lead to a form of censorship of alternative news channels is clear. hate speech and fake news have a soft spot in all those situations where we see a lack of transparency, where there is a lack of democratic control. it is enough to think about the decision-making processes that take place in ways unknown to most people by bodies that are not elected by anyone. citizens have the right to know the truth and to have their freedom of expression protected. what they need is not a gag, but policies that can give them the tools of knowledge, that can bridge educational gaps and economic disparities, so that they feel informed, aware and fully free.

member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, mr pedicini, let me start first of all by saying that the commission has been very deeply concerned for many years about the environmental situation from which the region of campania is suffering due to the illegal treatment and mismanagement of waste, and of course about the impact on public health. the latest public health report issued by the istituto superiore di sanità, which links the abnormally high cancer rate in some parts of campania with the illegal treatment of waste, has been brought to our attention. given the systematic shortcomings in waste management in campania underpinned by organised crime, the commission has made full use of its powers over the past decade to address the situation. already in 2007 the commission initiated infringement procedures against italy for a lack of adequate disposal facilities for waste in campania, and this led in 2010 to italy being condemned by the european court of justice. then again in 2015 the court condemned italy to pay a heavy fine consisting of a lump sum of eur 20 million plus eur 120 000 every day due to insufficient follow-up measures. one year earlier, in 2014, the court of justice had already imposed heavy fines on italy for the existence of illegal disposal of waste, including hazardous waste, throughout practically all the italian territory, including campania. also in 2014, the commission suspended eu financial assistance corresponding to the financial period 2007-2013 in respect of waste management and disposal in campania. we cannot grant eu money if there are no guarantees that it will be spent well. when we received adequate assurances, eu funding was again made available in the current programing period. as regards enforcement by the commission, there was nothing more that we could possibly do according to eu law. now it is fair to say that the overall waste management situation in campania has improved since the waste crisis of 2007 and following the government’s appointment of several waste emergency commissioners for the region. for instance, separate collection of waste in the region is steadily improving, as well as recycling. at the end of last year, campania adopted a new regional waste management plan which is now being examined by the commission services. but challenges remain, and health problems caused by past practices are still making themselves felt. the health and the environmental issues in campania have their roots in the existence of organised crime and an enforcement system which is not coping with it. although the main responsibility for fighting organised crime rests with the member states, the european union has agreed to take action on a number of instruments in the field of enforcement of compliance. to address the eco-mafia, in 2011 europol created a platform for experts from law enforcement agencies, the envicrimenet, dealing with environmental crime. also to improve enforcement, the commission will adopt later this year a communication setting out an action plan with practical actions for environmental compliance assurance. this will be aimed, amongst other issues, at helping member states to combat waste crime and offences. in addition to the enforcement actions, the commission has urged the italian competent authorities to address land decontamination and rehabilitation as a matter of urgency. for the latter, eur 72 million of eu structural funds have been made available under the current financial period, that is under the period 2014-2020. of course the specific health-related aspects are of huge concern and i know that the signatories of this major interpellation, including my colleague pedicini, already met with my colleague commissioner andriukaitis here in strasbourg few weeks ago. as you know, health policy is essentially a national competence but there may be scope for reinforcing dialogue with national authorities. i can assure you that my services will keep monitoring the situation in campania. solving the problems derived from the illegal treatment of waste in campania is dependent on all relevant actors working effectively together.

governments. we are talking, as was already said in the speeches before me, of an expression, that of 'land of fire', which is becoming commonly used in the 2000s, but in reality the problem we are talking about, that of the illegal dumping of special and toxic waste in the area between the provinces of naples and caserta, dates back to at least the mid-1970s, and investigators such as roberto mancini had already highlighted the problem. i would remind you that part of the development of small and mediumsized industries in northern italy was also built on the tax-free dumping of processing waste in the soils of tierra del fuego, with the mediation of organized crime, which used land-moving companies, quarries and waste transport to organize traffic. the fact that we are still in an emergency is therefore politically and morally unacceptable. i am personally in contact, as are other colleagues here in the chamber, with the committees that are responsible for defending environmental justice in the land of fire, and which emphasize the effectiveness to date of the mapping, monitoring and remediation measures provided for by italian law 6/2014e and implemented by the government and the campania region. there are no operational plans for remediation, no thorough analysis of pollution of the groundwater, and entire areas such as the vesuvius national park are not covered by monitoring. in the molti quarry, for example, in the municipality of maddaloni, there are an estimated 200 000 cubic metres of already characterized chemical waste, but the situation is stable and there is not only no operational treatment plan, but also no safe disposal. there are also no plans for agricultural rehabilitation of contaminated land, with serious economic damage to the population. it is also necessary to concentrate epidemiological and toxicological testing on the people living within the site of national importance and not to extend it to the whole region, with the risk of minimising the impact of the results. the mothers of the committee "victims of tierra del fuego" reported the deaths of 16 children from leukemia in the last four months alone, 80% of whom were residents of tierra del fuego. we find it shameful from this point of view the words of the minister - indeed the minister - of health lorenzin in 2015, who dared to say that the higher mortality rate in campania was due to pollution from vehicles, a poor health system and wrong lifestyles and diet. we are really speechless, because that means ignoring the weight and the gravity of the problem we are talking about. i therefore thank my colleagues once again for submitting this request, which is more than legitimate, considering that the european commission fined italy 22 million last february and that, after the european court of justice's 2015 judgment precisely for the waste emergency in campania and the non-compliance with directives 98/2008 and others on the treatment and recycling of waste, it is still difficult to impose a solution to this problem. it is therefore necessary to make up for what the member state, the italian government, is still doing, precisely because the health of the citizens is at stake and the right to health is a fundamental right. i would just like to add that i do not think it is enough - indeed, i think it is profoundly wrong - to turn a problem of economic and social order, of environmental justice of national scope, into a problem of public order, into a problem simply of repression and waste management. the militarization of many of these sites has simply too often prevented committees, activists, experts from being able to properly oversee the polluted sites. i think that the solutions must be fundamental, they must be long-term solutions, but they must also be immediate solutions because we are talking about deaths, we are talking about economic damage, we are talking about social damage that persists in an area where female unemployment and youth unemployment are already at very high levels. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the fact that the community's environmental policy is not only a matter of the environment, but also of the environment.

member of the commission. – mr president, thank you for those useful comments, this rich debate, the support of so many of you for the proclamation of the european pillar of social rights, and for the support also for a broad approach to social policy. let me first address some of the key issues in this discussion. the pillar we launched today is just the start of a process. it is indeed a pillar of 20 principles and values and rights. it is something that we will use from day one as a reference framework to screen the employment and social policy in member states and at european level, and a guidance, a compass, to guide us to more convergence, to upward convergence, towards better employment and social conditions – also working conditions – for our citizens, and it is indeed more than words, words, words. that is the reason why we immediately proposed and launched today some concrete deliverable proposals for legislation or concrete starting first—phase consultations with the social partners. regarding the request of the european parliament for legislation, and also for a framework directive on decent working conditions, we agree that it is important to ensure that all forms of employment enjoy a minimum set of rights and protection. this is perhaps the main outcome from our public consultation: to adapt the social acquis to the new world of work. i want to reassure you that this objective is addressed in the two partner consultations we are launching: the one on the written statement directive, and the other one on access to social protection. if social partners cannot agree – you never know – then the commission stands ready to table proposals. you have seen now, with the proposal on the work-life balance, that we have the courage and we have the determination to do so. it is important to recognise that the commission cannot legislate on everything. in fact, the guiding principle of this commission has been that we do not legislate for the sake of it. for example, we are not reopening the working time directive: we are issuing guidance to improve its implementation. indeed, we will proceed on a two-prong approach. on the one hand, we will step up our monitoring of the existing acquis, and on the other hand, we will enhance guidance to help member states to help enterprises to implement it. on the work-live balance (i will be short on this because time is running), you will see that we go beyond maternity and beyond childcare. i see in this house that there are different opinions. we have put an ambitious proposal on the table, and i hope for quick and constructive consideration by the co—legislators so that we can soon have a good directive. we are in the midst of an economic and social transition. the social fallout from the crisis remains present, and the resulting political pressure at all political levels is massive. above all, this demands a clear and a commonly shared idea of what the european union can and cannot do in this field. there is an economic, social and political urgency to make the european pillar of social rights a success. first, the economic arguments: we need a modern labour market, we need social protection, and we need education systems to drive upward convergence, and we need to get more and better qualified people into the labour force. this is the way to build resilience, and this is the way to make our economies competitive and our welfare systems sustainable in the longer term. second, there are the social arguments. the labour market is a vehicle for inclusion, to improve people’s life chances and to help them to fulfil their potential. the best way to make people feel valued is through a high—quality job. we need to make sure that everyone can participate, and that no one is left behind. third, there is the political imperative of tackling inequalities. our political resilience – our resilience too – depends on restoring a sense of fairness, of opportunity, and of empowerment. i therefore count on your support to make the european pillar of social rights a reality. on the reflection paper, the debate on the future of europe, it is open. president juncker launched the white paper on this debate, and we are now feeding the debate with concrete reflection documents. the first one, not par hasard, is on social policy. we will have others on the deepening of the economic and monetary union, on defence, on globalisation and on the financing of the european union. so the debate is open and we will deliver more reflection papers to feed the debate – and of course we hope, thomas mann, that as many people as possible participate in this important debate, and in the one on the future of europe. thank you very much, and let us continue to work together.
in writing. following the commitments made by the leaders of 27 member states in rome last march, the european institutions are taking the first step towards the establishment of a 'social europe'. this transition is represented by the interinstitutional declaration on the european pillar of social rights. the document sets out principles and rights that are essential for the labour market and welfare in the 21st century, which we believe should be more attentive to the needs of those 'excluded' by globalisation. the pillar states that there should be equal opportunities for all in the union for work, study and learning, that gender equality and ethnic religious differences should always be respected and that adequate support for employment, especially for young people, should be ensured. there is still a lot to be done, but this declaration is the first concrete step towards giving citizens the answers they have been waiting for.

president of the eurogroup. – mr president, it is an honour once again to participate in this exchange of views on the second review of the greek adjustment programme. i regret not having been able to join you a few weeks ago; as i indicated in writing to you, mr president, domestic political obligations prevented me from accepting your previous invitation. there was certainly no ill will intended on my part, and i very much value the regular exchanges that i have with parliament and stand ready to work with you in the coming months. before turning to greece, let me shortly address the issue of my remarks in an interview with the frankfurter allgemeine zeitung last month. in this interview, i made the point that respecting our agreed framework is crucial for maintaining confidence and solidarity in the eurozone. in the days following the interview, however, my words were linked to the situation during the crisis periods in certain southern european countries. this is very unfortunate as it was not what i said, and certainly not what i had intended to say. the crisis years have impacted societies throughout the eurozone and throughout the union at great social expense, and solidarity has been justified. the way i expressed myself has caused offence, and i regret this very much. it was, of course, never my intention to insult people. i have worked for the past four years to bring the eurozone closer together, and the last thing i want is to cause new divides. as parliament stated in its recent resolution on the budgetary capacity, we can only successfully strengthen the monetary union if responsibility and solidarity are closely linked. i strongly believe in that, and i will continue to work for that. one way to move forward in strengthening the emu is to develop the esm further into a european monetary fund. on my initiative, the efsf and esm programmes are being evaluated at this moment. the report is being drawn up by an evaluation commission led by gertrude tumpel-gugerell and will be published in june, and i can imagine we will devote one of our future hearings to this report. one important lesson is that we should keep and improve on the expertise that has been acquired over the crisis period, and to anchor it at the esm. the esm, in my mind, should be in the lead in designing, negotiating and monitoring future programmes. also, the esm could in the future have a broader preventive mandate in line with how the imf does it now by developing its own country reports to assure objective macroeconomic analysis. in my view, the commission should continue in its role as keeper of the pact. having said that, now let me turn to greece. a lot has been accomplished in the first part of the current programme, such as reform in the financial sector, the setting up of an independent authority of public revenues, implementation of the first leg of an ambitious income tax and pension reform and the creation of a privatisation agency, etc. these steps proved to be instrumental in bolstering confidence, and have resulted in a return of deposits, a reduced dependency on ela and in a much better than expected fiscal performance overall in 2016. eurostat came out last monday with a primary surplus figure of 3.9% for greece. meanwhile, the second review is, admittedly, taking too much time. therefore, at my initiative in february and following intensified high-level talks in march between the institutions and the greek government, an over—arching agreement was reached earlier this month. the authorities in the institutions have agreed on the size, the sequencing and the timing of reform measures underpinning a growth-friendly rebalancing of the economy. in short, the authorities committed to legislating up-front further pension and income tax reforms, each worth about 1% of gdp. pension reforms will become effective in 2019 unconditionally. income tax reform is planned to become effective in 2020 in principle, unless front-loading is needed. we also agreed that the authorities can now legislate expansionary measures to implement as of 2019, provided of course that the medium—term targets are met. apart from possible tax measures, it provides for improvements to the modernised social safety net that greece is rightly developing. beyond this, recent discussions also concerned labour market reforms that balance the need for a flexible economy with the vital respect for workers’ social rights in line with european best practices. this approach has allowed the institutions to resume their mission in athens. they returned last tuesday, and i am confident that an agreement on the whole package will be reached very soon. the eurogroup will then also review greece’s medium—term fiscal trajectory and debt sustainability, and let me just say that i believe that the ten-year period of a primary surplus target of 3.5 per cent should be shortened. in terms of the next steps, i expect that all of this will allow all institutions to come to the conclusion that the numbers add up, and the imf to financially participate. i hope to be able to report to you the successful conclusion of the second review before the end of next month, allowing confidence to return to the greek economy and for greece to join all other eurozone countries in their ongoing process of economic recovery.

member of the commission. – mr president, i am very grateful for this opportunity to participate in this debate on the parliament’s yearly resolution on the protection of the european union’s financial interests. the fight against fraud is of the utmost importance for the commission, as it is for the parliament. protection of the european union’s budget is all the more important at a time when the trust of citizens in the european project and in its capability to bring security and prosperity is at risk. i would like to take this opportunity to thank the members of the committee on budgetary control, and in particular ms pitera, the rapporteur, for the excellent work done on this motion for a resolution. the result is a comprehensive and well-structured report which covers a broad range of issues. it is also thanks to the political pressure exercised by the european parliament in its annual resolutions that several issues highlighted in the commission reports have been addressed and progress has been made at european and at member state level. over the last five years together, we have significantly reinforced a framework for the protection of the union’s financial interests. let me recall just the most important measures that we have adopted. we have adopted several important acts modernising the legal framework for the protection of the financial interests of the european union such as the revision of the olaf regulation in 2013, the package on public procurement directives in 2014 and the four delegated and four implementing acts on irregularity reporting. the legal framework for the programming period 2014-2020 for the first time refers explicitly to the obligation for member states to put in place proportionate and effective anti-fraud measures. on the revenue side, the revised regulation on mutual administrative assistance in the customs area entered into force, creating new databases to fight better customs fraud. the last and not the least of these legal achievements is the directive on the protection of the union’s financial interests by means of criminal law, for which a political agreement was finally reached, also thanks to the persistence of the parliament. but this is not all. there are also important ongoing legal initiatives. the negotiations of the european public prosecutor’s office (eppo) have moved forward very fast in the last month, and we now have 17 member states willing to establish the eppo in enhanced cooperation and a few more making preparations to join it. like the parliament, the commission supports establishing a strong and efficient eppo with as many member states as possible and with the necessary means to effectively fight crimes affecting the union budget. we are convinced that the eppo has significant potential to improve the current situation as regards the low level of prosecutions for crimes affecting the union’s financial interests. olaf will continue to play a key role as regards non-fraudulent and fraudulent irregularities. it will complement and support the work of the eppo. beyond the protection of financial interests it will continue also investigations into serious facts by members of the institutions and staff, likely to lead to disciplinary or criminal proceedings. the commission is determined to maintain a sufficiently strong olaf which will operate across all member states and will thereby play a crucial role to ensure that an adequate protection of the european union’s budget is assured in the whole european union. over the last five years we have also made progress on concrete actions and measures. i will mention three examples for which the parliament’s support, reiterated in the pitera report, is once more important and particularly welcome. the first is the embedding of anti-fraud measures in national anti-fraud strategies. the second is to extend the use of it tools by all member states to strengthen the fight against fraud, and the third is the accomplishment of harmonised and qualitative reporting of the detected irregularities and frauds by the member states. the commission acknowledges that the reported data are still not fully comparable and takes note of the request of the parliament to improve the situation. new guidelines are being prepared in cooperation with national experts to address the most important issues to reduce disparities and standardise the reporting process. the document is expected to be finalised this year. it is by analysing such data that we can ultimately understand whether the measures we have adopted really make a difference. however, there is still much to do. the commission will keep on fulfilling its role of supporting and assisting member states where needed and of facilitating the exchange of best practices and know-how. i would like to close my intervention, stressing once more the importance of the parliament’s resolution. it is by acting together towards the same target that we have achieved all these improvements. but we are aware that we cannot rest on our laurels. we count on you to keep on stimulating, encouraging and also criticising when necessary – the commission and the member states – in their fulfilment of the treaty obligation to protect the union’s financial interests from irregularities and from fraud.
the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the commissioner for his introduction and mr pitera, the rapporteur, for his excellent work. the 2015 financial interests protection report again unfortunately shows a significant increase in fraudulent irregularities and corruption cases in several areas of interest of the european budget. in this context, the pif directive and the establishment of the european public prosecutor's office know, are often also financed through these illegal activities. however, pending the entry into force of these instruments, action is needed to strengthen the capacity for coordination between mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we believe that it is truly unacceptable that in times of economic crisis each citizen of the european union should waste on average 173 kilograms of food per year, and on the other hand, if this is an average, it means that there are poor people who waste nothing, because they have little more than nothing, and therefore there are rich people who waste twice or even much more than twice this enormous amount. we will support any proposal to reduce this waste, such as the gradual reduction in the price of foodstuffs as they approach their natural expiry date. on the other hand, at the same time, we believe that it is really unacceptable that in times of ecological crisis there is food waste. food has a negative impact on the environment when it's produced, and it has a negative impact on the environment when it's wasted, because it becomes waste and therefore has to be disposed of. our recipe is very simple: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the prevention of food waste, the promotion of responsible consumption and the absolute prohibition of landfilling and incineration of all types of food waste.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i was very surprised to read in a recent study that if food waste were represented by a single state, it would be the third largest producer of carbon dioxide on the planet, not to mention that for every undernourished person in the world, at least two are overweight. europe has committed itself, with the un sustainable development goals, to halving this, one of the most intolerable economic, environmental and ethical contradictions, but nothing, to date, is provided for in european legislation. so, number one: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. two , i 'm not . the commission has already proposed a number of measures to help achieve this objective, including the specific measures mentioned above, but also a specific food hierarchy which gives priority to human consumption through donations. waste is not just in the final consumption, but in the entire chain, from agricultural production to food processing, from distribution to catering, and that's where we need to make it more cost-effective for businesses to donate to those in need rather than waste. finally, encourage the use of organic waste that is no longer donated as a secondary raw material for new products. so my appeal here to the member states and the commission is to share this urgency which parliament is also expressing with this further and important report, to find a solution starting from the circular economy package which is being negotiated today. europe must be at the forefront of these issues, which call into question the values of solidarity and fairness.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the transition to a circular economy is weak, much weaker without common european rules to reduce food waste throughout the chain: production, distribution and consumption. it is not a question, as i would say to the honourable member who spoke earlier, of interfering with and hindering national initiatives; on the contrary, these must be supported, encouraged and coordinated, but a common european basis is needed. it is an illusion that such a gigantic problem can be solved only by national measures. we must not bury our heads in the sand. reducing food waste is an urgent necessity. we are in the midst of an incredible paradox, as other colleagues have said, of 1.3 billion tonnes of food wasted, four times the amount needed to feed the 800 million undernourished men and women. but food waste is not only an intolerable injustice, a gigantic social inequality to be ashamed of, it is also a waste of raw materials, a waste of land, a waste of water, a waste of energy, a multiplication of waste and environmental damage. that's why, again, it's a blow to the transition to a circular economy if we limit ourselves to good debates. a legislative initiative by the european commission is urgently needed.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, food waste is an unacceptable scandal of our time, as this report points out. in fact, while we need to increase food production by 70% in the next few years to feed a growing population, a third of the food produced in the world is wasted, of which 80% could still be consumed, in europe 180 kg per capita. with food thrown away, we also waste land, water and fertilizer, not to mention the greenhouse gas emissions that are necessary to produce it. reducing food waste by 50% by 2030, as set out in the circular economy package approved by parliament, requires the commitment of everyone - producers, retailers, restaurateurs, businesses, individuals and households. 42 percent of food waste in europe occurs in the home, at a cost of over 500 euros per family per year. let's start at home to promote a more socially, environmentally and economically sustainable development model through waste prevention campaigns and by encouraging food donations of unsold food.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as you all know, in europe there are no frontiers between the various countries, but only one large common frontier for all goods coming in from outside. the rules for crossing the frontier should be the same everywhere, but in some places this frontier is weaker than in others and this situation creates a distortion of trade from abroad and a detriment to the financial resources of the european union. the resolution i am writing is a parliamentary document which sets this situation in black and white and has been prepared with the valuable input of my fellow opinion-makers and the shadow rapporteurs in the inta committee, whom i would like to thank. madam president, there are european ports where customs controls are strict and careful, and others where they are less so. this situation creates unfair competition between shippers, port authorities and states, which europe cannot tolerate. i've been looking into it and i've found several different types of distortion. there is the case, for example, where the same european legislation is respected but applied differently in different countries. there are some ports which are on the verge of being legally bound by european rules and there are also those which do not comply with the rules, enjoying, for certain periods, the connivance of some of the national authorities. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the european parliament is able to exercise its right to vote and to stand as a candidate in the elections to the european parliament. this undermines the foundations of european trade policy. when we negotiate free trade agreements, when we tell our citizens that they need not fear products that are harmful to health and the environment, we must be sure that we can keep that promise and that we can control goods entering europe effectively. unfortunately, this is not the case because europe allows some countries to apply the rules differently or to turn a blind eye to parts of community law. that is why in the resolution we call for the commission to intervene to ensure the harmonisation of controls and the uniform application of the law, to identify the differences in treatment between economic operators, to continue the process of computerization and the interoperability of databases at european level. we also call on the commission to assess the impact of these different customs practices on incoming and outgoing trade flows and to work within the wto to promote the implementation of the international agreement on trade facilitation and, finally, to cooperate on customs matters with the main trading partners. ladies and gentlemen, in writing this resolution i met with the operators of many ports in europe and italy, collected their testimonies and brought their concerns to brussels. i would like to thank all the people i met on the ground, in particular the customs agency, the port authorities, but also the shippers and terminal operators in genoa, trieste, taranto, palermo and gioia tauro, and last but not least the health and plant health offices who made their contribution. finally, a special thanks goes to the guardia finanziaria, the police and all those european civil and military forces which carry out customs control activities at the frontiers. i would like to thank them very much and tell them that my resolution is intended to highlight the legislative gaps between our countries, but it is not in any way intended to call into question the excellent work that these forces are doing for the security of goods on our territory. i hope that the commission will follow the recommendations we have made, both for the protection of european citizens, for the protection of shippers, economic operators and port activities, but also for the protection of competition and for the protection of the dignity of commercial policy.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the customs union is a fundamental pillar of the european union. however, some flaws in the current system raise concerns about trade value distorting, counterfeiting, illicit financial flows and money laundering in commercial activities. differences in customs procedures, in particular as regards customs clearance, inspections, penalties and controls, create fragmentation, divergences in the collection of taxes between member states and market distortions. the customs authorities of the member states should be proactive in sharing data, cooperating with control bodies and, above all, in identifying anomalies linked to price manipulation. only closer customs cooperation can reduce the current shortcomings in customs control systems, ensuring an effective fight against illicit trade, counterfeiting and fraud and thus protecting legitimate traders, who are usually the only ones to suffer the consequences of a fragmented customs system.
the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank once again all the members who have actively contributed to this resolution. i am a little surprised at some of the positions, especially the one by my green colleague, who spoke of harmonization as a problem for the states which are already the most virtuous. i think that harmonizing customs controls is an opportunity, above all for those countries which are more virtuous today, and among them, i recall, italy, which is the first in terms of the severity of controls. the other thing i would like to point out to commissioner dombrovskis, which has not been mentioned, is that we do not only need more efficient controls, which will certainly have to be done, but above all we need to recognise that we need uniform controls. this is not only and exclusively due to problems related, as i explained at the beginning of my speech, to illegality, and therefore to corruption, but there are also different practices related to different sensitivities. as i said, during the missions i have carried out in the field, i have been able to see how there are different technical sensitivities, so operators are shopping around the fact that in certain ports some counterfeit goods would never enter, as operators are more sensitive on certain subjects, and can do so elsewhere. we need to make customs clearance procedures more streamlined and faster for the operators, but we also need to ensure that it is not possible to bring goods into a different port simply because there is no proper knowledge of certain things. i believe that this is due above all to all european citizens who have the opportunity to be defended and protected in this way, but also to economic operators who do not see the withdrawal of traffic quotas.

vice-president of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank the rapporteur, ms verheyen, and the shadow rapporteurs for a very good parliamentary report on the egovernment action plan. there is more to egovernment than just putting up websites and offering public services online. its impact is much more far—reaching. it is a key enabler in achieving the transformation of europe’s public administration, contributing to growth, competitiveness and quality of life. one major achievement of the first year is the proposed draft regulation on the single digital gateway, which also introduced the once—only principle at european level. with the addition of five new actions to the action plan, the mid-term review of the digital single market confirms this. the challenge is not to introduce digital technologies into public administrations, but rather the integration of digital technologies into public sector modernisation efforts. it is its transformative nature, impacting all levels of government and various public policy domains, that has great potential to bring significant benefits. the smart use of ict by governments can help deliver better policies and decisions to tackle the pressing social and economic challenges of our times. by becoming more open and transparent, government and public bodies become more accountable and trustworthy. this report provides an additional layer to the topic of egovernment in general. indeed, it provides further food for thought in terms of developing future actions to be included in the action plan in the coming years. i am encouraged that all eu institutions share a common vision on what the future of egovernment will look like. this vision can only be reached if all stakeholders embrace it and commit themselves to working together to make it a reality: governments, public bodies at all levels – european, national, regional and local – and also industry, business and citizens. the european parliament is uniquely placed in this mission. on the one hand, it can communicate to its constituents the benefits of this digital transformation. on the other hand, it can work together with the commission in adopting egovernment—related legislative proposals. one of the key themes of the egovernment action plan is that the commission shall lead by example in applying the underlying principles of the action plan, such as digital by default, cross—border by default, and applying the once-only principle. the commission is taking its commitment seriously and also offers member states, local and regional administrations and other stakeholders financial support to accelerate the digital transformation of government. this is being done through various programmes, including structural funds, the connecting europe facility and horizon 2020, and i am confident that parliament will also wish to lead by example and it can count on the full support of the commission in advancing the digital transformation of government.
in writing. the modernisation of the internal market is one of the key commitments of this european legislature, which is making progress in several areas and which certainly needs a strong impetus from the national public institutions themselves. this is to be achieved, first of all, by fully digitalising our internal administrations, making them more open and closer to citizens and businesses and able to respond to the challenges of competitiveness and new forms of production. e-government is not just an internal operational tool for the public administration: it is also a driving force for economic development, reducing costs and procedures and opening up new channels of financing, planning and investment. the introduction of new and simpler ways of acting for businesses should therefore be strongly encouraged as a focal point for the development of e-government, in particular through a thorough review of the rules on the digital dimension of company law. this is a subject which will be of great interest in the near future, in view of the progress which parliament is making on the reform of crossborder mergers and divisions.

επιτάχυνση και αυτών των διαδικασιών. και τέλος, όπως πολύ σωστά επεσήμανε ο κύριος κύρκος: ναι, οι ασυνόδευτοι ανήλικοι αποτελούν πράγματι την προτεραιότητά μας. αυτό το μήνυμα πρέπει να περάσει σε mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the commission for this document on globalisation, a process which is in fact the reality in which we live and which must undoubtedly be governed. it is important to understand that when we talk about globalisation, we are increasingly dealing with a world competition based on the capacity of technological innovation to meet the challenges of a linear economy that can no longer cope with the current consumption of the planet's resources and is able to put on the market products and services that can better meet the needs of consumers. in short, to grow again and to continue to guarantee our precious welfare system, we must then position ourselves in the key high-tech sectors. to do this we must focus decisively on investment, fresh resources in research and innovation and help businesses, especially small and mediumsized enterprises, the heart of our system, to renew themselves, and on the other hand, however, put in place social protection policies for those excluded from this process and policies that are able to redistribute the benefits to the whole population. europe has the size and capacity to play a leading role in this scenario if we start taking concrete action now.
in writing. humanity has often experienced forms of cultural and economic interdependence between different societies and cultures operating in very different geographical areas. the globalisation of our time, however, has taken on new characteristics due to exceptional factors such as new telecommunications, the internet and modern means of transport. economic crises, political changes, but also the rapid change of fashions and the spread of new consumer goods have the ability to spread and affect communities in every nation on the globe in an extraordinary short time. from an economic standpoint, globalization has certainly had the great credit of rescuing millions from poverty and misery. it is also true, however, that globalisation has also brought about a less equitable distribution of wealth, as well as serious disruptions in the labour market. i therefore believe that europe has an ambitious task today: to be able to steer the phenomenon of globalisation in order to derive all the benefits possible for citizens and businesses, while at the same time removing the side effects on society.

it is very difficult to talk about fraud in the european union, because what emerges from the annual report and what we wanted to stress in the regi committee is that you cannot really rely on data. there are different legal systems in europe, there is no single case of fraud at community level, and member states have full discretion in communicating the number of fraud cases detected or established. all mechanisms that complicate the picture and expose it to easy instrumentalisation. it is not that the states that report the most fraud are actually the most corrupt, for example, it often simply means that they have a more effective system of control. then there is the distinction between fraud and irregularity. in particular, in the area of cohesion policy, the difficulty of procedures and bureaucracy lead to a high number of irregularities, which are rarely found to be fraudulent. the way forward is therefore the one being pursued by olaf and the national anti-fraud coordination services, the afcos, which are making efforts to ascertain just that.
reducing food waste is a moral issue and also an economic one, because 88 million tonnes of food waste per year equals 173 kilos per european citizen, a huge amount, of which most people are not even aware. unfortunately, waste occurs at all stages of the food chain. this is why we need a coordinated action from producer to consumer, and one that is concerned above all with encouraging donations, because in the world, let us not forget, there would be food for everyone, but not everyone has food. fortunately, there are also practices that encourage donations, and in addition to this, there are experiences that minimize waste, for example through applications that some merchants use at the end of the day to send alerts and apply discounts on fresh products. but given that food waste is the work of households, of private consumption, we must put in place policies that include training and education already in school. it's our responsibility.
finally, the customs report was approved and it was not easy to get to this point, because this is an uncomfortable report, which denounces how some countries do not apply the customs controls that are required, bringing billions of euros of counterfeit or even dangerous products onto the european market. a report which has been opposed from the beginning here in parliament, first by a long conflict of attribution, then by an endless series of parliamentary backlashes and finally, last week, by the request of some parties to postpone the vote until a date to be decided. to all those who have tried to stop us, i want to say that they have failed and i want to thank all those who have supported our fight, the majority in fact. it has not been easy, but the customs report is finally a reality and i now hope that the commission will act on our recommendations without delay.
