vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, on palm sunday, as you well remember, two coptic churches were attacked in egypt as worshippers gathered for mass. forty-five people were killed and hundreds were wounded. daesh terrorists claimed responsibility for the attack, because in their minds there is no room for the peaceful coexistence of different faiths. i will start with just one of the terrible attacks on christians in the middle east and mention the response that this madness provoked, which was one of the best responses i have ever seen to one of these attacks. just a week later, on easter sunday in jordan, tens of muslim youths stood guard to protect churches and christian believers to make sure that they could celebrate their holiest festivity in peace and respect. i believe that these young people of muslim faith, these young jordanians, are daesh’s worst nightmare. they show the real face of the middle east and they honour hundreds of years of peaceful coexistence of different religious faiths in the middle east. you will remember well the message that his majesty the king of jordan delivered in this very chamber exactly along these lines. when pope francis embarked on his historic visit to egypt last month, he described christians, muslims and people of all faiths as fellow travellers. for thousands of years people of different religions have been fellow travellers in the middle east, in europe and in the rest of the word. at a time when freedom of religion or belief is coming under attack in many parts of our world, we have a duty first of all to preserve this diversity here in europe as well. religious or ethnic groups – christians and others – are being forced to flee from lands they have inhabited for centuries. we can, and must, preserve the space for people of different backgrounds to be fellow travellers, sharing their land and their lives. christianity was born in the middle east. it belongs to the middle east. yet we know that entire christian communities have been forced to leave their home countries and their region. the phenomenon is not new, but what is new is the trend that is now more worrying than ever. this is not only causing great human suffering to christians as well as to many other minorities in the region but, if the middle east loses its incredible diversity – that is a problem in itself – it would also lose its greatest richness. for this reason, the european union is engaged on a daily basis to protect all minorities and every person’s human rights with concrete actions in several fields. i will mention a few of them. first, we systematically raise freedom of religion and belief at different levels of our political dialogues, including in our human rights dialogues with countries in the middle east. together with a number of partner countries, we have developed what we call our partnership priorities in order to promote common interests. the protection of human rights is always part of our own priorities. in the second field of action we always condemn violence against religious or belief minorities with public statements and with private demarches. public advocacy is not always sufficient, but it reminds all these community groups that they are not alone in this struggle. in the third field of action we work to ensure that freedom of religion and belief remains prominently on the global agenda and specifically on the un agenda, featuring a strong human rights approach. in the fourth field of action the eu special representative, stavros lambrinidis, is doing an amazing job and keeps raising these issues in all his official visits and dialogues – most recently to egypt, just to mention one country. in may 2016, as a follow-up to the european parliament’s resolution on the systematic mass murder of religious minorities by daesh, we appointed mr figel' as the first special envoy for the promotion of freedom of religion or belief outside the european union. in the fifth field of action we are seeking the broadest engagement of relevant regional actors and international organisations. preserving diversity is, first and foremost, a middle eastern interest, so we will not stop working to protect all minorities. but we are not alone in this task and we look for cooperation with our partners. sixth, we are providing very concrete financial support to local communities and minorities through the european instrument for democracy and human rights. the 2016 global call for proposals addressed the rights of persons belonging to minorities, and the new call on freedom of religion or belief will be launched in 2017, aiming at supporting local and international civil society organisations in promoting mutual tolerance and understanding. we are also providing support to christians in countries where they are facing a precarious situation. in iraq, for example, we are making sure that our projects for stabilisation also deliver on the needs of christian communities. last, but certainly not least, we are fighting terrorism through security cooperation, with our work to end the conflicts in our region, and by addressing the social, economic and cultural roots of radicalisation. in this work we also have a duty to get the narrative right and also to represent the best face of the middle east: the face of diversity, the face of those muslim young people protecting christian churches. we must give voice, if i can quote pope francis in italian:..."non solo alla inciviltà del conflitto, ma anche alla civiltà dell'incontro". the narrative is important: to dismantle the narrative of those who believe that there is no space for living together either in the mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as many have mentioned, dadaab was established as far back as 1991 as a temporary solution for those seeking refuge from persecution, violence and instability in the east african region, including the civil war in somalia. it's the largest refugee camp in the world, according to the un, with 245,000 people, 60 percent of whom are under 18, with no education or jobs. unfortunately, the issue of somali refugees in dadaab has become the subject of an election campaign by president kenyatta, under the slogan of fighting terrorism. we have, of course, welcomed and accepted the judgment of the nairobi high court that this decision to close the dadaab camp is nothing, but unfortunately the government has also appealed and cannot, in our view, simply tell hundreds of thousands of people to return to the war, hunger and extreme poverty from which they fled. we must remember that the un refugee convention prohibits return to areas where their lives and freedom are threatened, and this is certainly the case in somalia, which is suffering from drought, famine, cholera and violence. good practices to be copied are those of uganda with its "self-reliance" strategy, where refugees can work and move freely. these are good practices to be copied, not the indiscriminate closure carried out by the current government.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the dadaab refugee camp, the largest in the world, is celebrating its 26th anniversary this year. a camp that was supposed to provide temporary accommodation, especially for somali refugees, has instead become a permanent ghetto of 260 000 people. at least two generations have been born and raised in what is a symbol of the social misery of refugees in africa, of the failure of development and pacification policies in that area and of the inability, also, to manage the global phenomenon of migration. ethiopians, eritreans, sudanese, south sudanese, somalis, they are the unrighteous inhabitants of this metropolis, forced to live a life of "no life", because they are deprived of a future and a hope. on their heads the authorities and the international community are making decisions that the supreme court itself has defined as an act of mass persecution, illegal and therefore unconstitutional. it is true that dadaab is a hub of misery, lawlessness and abuse, especially against women, children and vulnerable groups. however, it is difficult to predict the fate of these refugees if they suddenly find themselves without a roof. it is a collective responsibility to end the political instability in the region, to finally create the conditions for sustainable development and to rethink our migration policies, knowing that by embracing the challenges but also the opportunities, without peace and stability and without a holistic approach to migration, there will be no future for any refugee either in a camp or in their home countries.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, honourable members, i would like to thank you for the opportunity to intervene in this topical debate on the subject of the powers and control of the european central bank. as we all know, the treaty has bestowed independence upon the european central bank to conduct its monetary policy and to pursue its primary objective of maintaining price stability in the euro area as a whole. international experience has indeed shown that monetary policy tends to be more effective in supporting a stable price level when it is shielded from short-term political influence. the presidency believes that the accountability of the european central bank for its monetary policy is commensurate with its independence and can be inferred from the treaty. when it comes to the ecb’s accountability for its banking supervision tasks, this is specified in the regulation on the single supervisory mechanism. in this context, the presidency sees no reason to question whether the ecb adheres to the accountability obligations towards the eu legislators. similarly the presidency does not have grounds to doubt that the ecb acts within its mandate. against this background, the council has not debated the subject of the powers and control of the european central bank and the issue does not feature on any upcoming council agendas. however, i am grateful for your invitation to attend and i look forward to hearing your views – or more views – during this debate.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, minister, honourable members, you are having a debate today about the powers and accountability of the european central bank. on behalf of the commission, i would like to limit myself to a very few remarks on this matter. the ecb and the national central banks are independent when exercising the powers and carrying out the tasks and duties conferred upon them by the treaty. the principle of central bank independence is enshrined in the treaty itself. it is put there to protect the ecb and the national central banks in pursuing their primary mandate of fulfilling their price stability objective and thus creating the foundation for a healthy and stable european economy. independence and accountability are of course intertwined. the ecb presents to parliament an annual report on its activities and you hold a general debate on that basis. the quarterly monetary dialogues you organise with the ecb president provide a further forum for in—depth discussion. i understand you have regularly made use of this possibility over the past year. the commission has full trust in the ecb to exercise its mandates under the treaty. we welcome the constructive engagement that has developed between the european parliament and the ecb over the past years.
on behalf of the s&d group. – mr president, it is no surprise that mr starbatty’s positions are in a minority in this house because they are factually weak and wrong. a broad majority of this house supports the ecb, its independence and its policies because the ecb is the main pillar of emu and has been a fundamental anchor of its stability and integrity. that such a great responsibility would fall on the shoulders of the ecb was unavoidable, taking into account the peculiar construction of emu, with the explosive components of monetary policy, coordination competence on economic policy, and a small budget for the single market but not for the single currency. with the soaring debt crisis these responsibilities have been successfully honoured in full compliance with the task and the powers conferred by the treaties and the protocol in order to achieve the primary objective of maintaining price stability and to support the general economic policies of the union, which of course include the integrity of the emu. the treaties are crystal clear. in order to achieve its objectives, the ecb and national central banks can conduct open market and credit operations. so it is not surprising that the omt programme has been declared by the court of justice fully compatible with eu law. in the post-crisis phase of low growth and low interest rates, and with the additional negative impact of financial fragmentation on proper monetary policy transmission, other unconventional policy tools have proven to be necessary to meet the inflation objective. i do not need to recall them, but is important to underline that, without quantitative easing (qe), europe would have fallen into deflation. qe has been – and is – an economic success and for all stakeholders the potential negative side effects have clearly been outpaced by the positive ones. moreover, economic data clearly show that the necessary sustained adjustment in the path of inflation has not yet materialised. enhanced non-standard monetary policy measures are to continue until that time. the ecb is, and has to be, fully independent. nevertheless, we welcome and appreciate the accountability framework vis—à-vis the european parliament and the committee on economic and monetary affairs and the improvements in transparency of the ecb’s monetary policy. as far as the ssm is concerned, a stronger accountability framework is appropriate and we are in line with our interinstitutional agreement to fulfil our democratic role. it is evident that the current emu construction, while it is not unsustainable, is sub-optimal and we need to complete it. we cannot rely only on common monetary policy and national fiscal and economic policies. instead of contesting the excellent job of the ecb, it would be good if political groups and member states would contribute to providing the instruments and policies that we need in order to face our current challenges.
on behalf of the enf group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the independence of the central bank, that is to say, the fact that the executive does not have control over the money supply, is a concept which, in my view, is incompatible with democracy. to put the power to create money in the hands of an unelected authority outside any democratic control, to let it pursue a senseless goal like inflation targeting, a tool that has nothing to do with price dynamics, that is, the money supply, is insane and undemocratic. the rhetoric that has been supporting this undemocratic system for decades is based on an assumption that the crisis has refuted, that printing money creates inflation. the need to keep money creation out of the hands of politicians would arise from this, from the need to avoid that inflation which everyone now wants instead. i do not know if anyone has noticed that for some time now draghi has been printing and pouring billions of euros into the eurozone system, and what has been the result? the deflation. inflation is not mechanically dependent on printed money, but it is dependent on the demand for goods, on money spent, and in a depression like the one we are experiencing now a government can be sure that printed money is spent only if it spends it itself. without monetary financing of expenditure, which the treaties and the independence of the central bank prevent, it will be impossible to revive the economies of the eurozone countries. however, in this union of equal states, where one is more equal than the others, the powers of the state are independent but one, the power of the central bank, is more independent than the others and is therefore the one who actually commands, making and breaking puppet governments at will. if a politician talks to you about democracy without rejecting this dogma, he is lying to you. the central point for restoring a glimmer of democracy is to abolish this aberration and to take this power out of the hands of unelected bureaucrats.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr ansip, the regulation on the portability of online content is one of the first concrete measures of the digital single market strategy presented by the european commission. it is the first step in a wider process to eliminate all forms of unjustified geoblocking and will help to make the idea of a common area of rights and opportunities for european citizens a reality. the creation of a european digital dimension of the single market also starts with the recognition that online content acquired in one's country of residence can be enjoyed throughout the union, including when travelling, studying or working outside one's country of residence. although only a small proportion of the european population is currently affected, the numbers are set to increase exponentially, reaching 72 million european citizens by 2020. the legal fiction behind the regulation extends opportunities for consumers without compromising the protection of copyright and the quality of the creative industries, an important element of the european development model. our work in the committee on the internal market has focused on finding the right balance between the need to provide consumers with an agile and effective tool, strict protection of privacy, legal certainty and copyright protection. i think the final agreement sums up these considerations very well. i am sorry, mr president, commissioner, that once again the council did not have the same ambition as we did in providing for a more flexible system of verification and a faster implementation period.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, over 26 000 deaths a year across europe and a social cost of some 100 billion euro, road safety is therefore the main emergency we have to respond to in terms of mobility. we believe that the urban centres need to be decongested by introducing the use of public transport at the expense of private transport, which is responsible for about 80% of the co2 emissions produced by the entire transport sector. the rules on rest periods and the qualifications of heavy goods vehicle drivers, with checks on licences and alcohol levels, must also be enforced. we have the technology to make road checks very timely and effective, and we are helping small businesses, perhaps even giving them an economic incentive, to adopt the technological devices needed for such checks. we support the resolution, particularly as regards the part concerning emission reduction policies. for the new electricity sector, we want to invest in both the expansion of the grid and research into the sustainability of the batteries used, so that we have products with a lower impact both during construction and at disposal.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the transport sector, and road transport in particular, will be one of the most interesting areas in which to test the european union's capacity for innovation. we have spoken in detail about all the challenges of new fuels, the need to limit emissions to the atmosphere, as much as 70 per cent of the emissions generated in the transport sector take place within road transport. a lot of investment is required. the european commission has allocated 70 billion from the structural funds to this sector, 39 of which are for the identification of strategies to limit atmospheric emissions in the transport sector and, in particular, road transport. these investments are made if there is a general framework of guarantees which ensure a balanced market, where the investor's reasons are respected and the worker's reasons are respected. a general concept in which you don't make a profit by exploiting people who work, you don't create the pockets of money needed for investment by not paying people. the resolution is fairly balanced overall, but there are too many dark spots. the liberalization of cabotage will be a sham innovation, paid for by hauliers who will play a game of drawdown and we will all be blamed. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the transport of dangerous goods is not subject to any restrictions. the transport and return of empty goods is not because the cabotage is too free or too restricted, but because it is difficult to match supply and demand. we're not wrong.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the road transport sector in europe must be prepared to seize the opportunities offered by digitalisation, with the development of vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure communications infrastructure. this is the future of road mobility and the union must provide the appropriate regulatory framework, logistical support and research and innovation capacity. the future of transport certainly involves environmental sustainability, a subject on which europe is strongly committed, but the functionality and interoperability of urban public transport must also become a priority. adapting existing structures requires appropriate support policies at european level and substantial investment to transform and adapt the transport systems of european cities. the issue of illegal road cabotage must be tackled quickly, it is unfair competition which is causing considerable damage in the union. the controls themselves must be made more effective, and the sanctions system must be changed in this respect.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i will of course, as you have rightly pointed out, deal only with the question of the agreement. i am of course in full agreement with what has been said a little while ago on the question of tariffs, but i shall concentrate much more on the question of the agreement. this is an agreement on the european economic area, the so-called eea agreement, of 1994, which allows the participation in the single market of norway, iceland and lichtenstein, members of the efta. the efta countries have contributed since 1994 to reducing economic and social disparities within the eea through a dedicated financial mechanism, to which norway has added a further contribution. these financial mechanisms, which expired in 2014, need to be renewed as well as the protocols concerning fish trade. so today, at this stage, we are looking at four acts, namely two agreements relating to financial mechanisms, one between the eu and iceland, lichtenstein and norway, and one between norway and the european union, and two protocols on fisheries, one between the eu and norway and the other between the eu and iceland. these agreements will jointly provide a financial contribution to economic and social cohesion in the eea of eur 2,8 billion over the period 2014-2021. this framework, which has so far been beneficial for the european union, must be integrated into a broader political reflection on our relations between the european union and the efta countries. there are no particular problems with liechtenstein and iceland, and we will soon be discussing new agricultural agreements with iceland in the inta committee, and we must be careful here that iceland does have a free trade agreement with china, so we want to stress this aspect too. with norway, as was rightly said earlier, the question is more sensitive because of certain duties imposed on european meat and cheese. this practice has certainly slowed down the progress of the dossier and has also given rise to the oral question which is being discussed today, tabled by the president. political and economic relations between the eu and norway have always been quite good, but the question of tariffs has, as has been rightly said, been a vulnus in our trade relations in recent years. norway is the fifth largest trading partner of the european union in terms of imports and the seventh largest destination for the european union in terms of exports. strengthening our trade relations with norway is of course important, but these developments must take place in full respect of the objectives of the eea agreement. we know that negotiations are under way between the eu and norway on certain liberalizations of trade in agricultural products; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. this removal must be a priority for both sides and thus help to strengthen trade relations which are fortunately already strong. the european union exports eur 4.1 billion of agricultural products to norway and imports eur 488 million. equally important is the import of fishery products, which amounts to eur 5.6 billion. i would therefore like to conclude by thanking my colleagues for the work done in the committee on international trade and the colleagues who will now speak for their input, and i hope that we can count on a broad consensus for this agreement here too.
i believe that the agreements between the european union and norway, iceland and liechtenstein which we are to ratify tomorrow represent a good example of cooperation between our union and the countries of the european economic area. these agreements will, as mentioned above, provide a total contribution of eur 2,8 billion to the european union for the period 2014-2021, an increase of 11,3% compared to the previous period. the funds will be directed to those areas of the european union where social and economic disparities persist in a clear way, with the aim of strengthening economic and social cohesion, always favouring a better functioning of the single market, in which iceland, liechtenstein and norway participate fully. among the priority areas for investment, i would like to highlight the one on youth employment and the one on justice and home affairs, which therefore includes strategic areas such as asylum and migration. the amount of assigned revenue in accordance with article 21 (3) of the financial regulation is estimated at eur 100000. with regard to the question raised by the oral question, it will be essential to find a solution quickly, since the imposition of increased duties by norway on certain european products is clearly in breach of the spirit and the letter of this agreement. let me conclude with a comment, mr president. there has been a lot of talk in the post-brexit debates about the possibility of the uk adopting the norwegian model of participation in the european union. we agree that contributing financially to the european union and accepting its four fundamental freedoms are sufficient criteria to open the doors to our single market, as is the case with norway and other countries, but this does not seem to be the path the british government wants to take and they will soon realise that, as our dear colleague said in the aftermath of the referendum, the best possible deal for the united kingdom is the one we already have.

president-in-office of the council. – madam president, i would like to thank you for the opportunity to speak today on combating anti-semitism. it is a topic of common concern to us all. let me start by expressing my deep concern about the current situation in europe. evidence from different sources, including the eu agency for fundamental rights and the council of europe, shows an alarming increase in intolerance and hatred. there exists specific data collected by the fundamental rights agency confirming that every fourth jew in europe has experienced verbal or physical violence. it is difficult to believe and understand that so many in our society reject the fundamental values of tolerance, respect and liberty, and instead choose to hate. what can be done to address anti-semitism? this issue was discussed in more general terms during the conference on positive narratives against hate speech, which the maltese presidency organised in april this year. experts from member states, international organisations, academia and civil society agreed that there was no single perfect remedy for hatred. as is often the case, we need a complex response that starts with education, data collection and analysis, and ends with condemnation and criminal sanctions. let me start with the measures i mentioned last, condemnation and criminal sanctions. the eu has adopted specific legislation on combating intolerance and hatred, namely the 2008 framework decision on combating racism and xenophobia. this decision outlaws holocaust denial and anti-semitic hate speech inciting violence. in particular, it prohibits under criminal law condoning, denying or grossly trivialising the holocaust. in june 2016, the council stressed the importance of this legal instrument and invited member states to ensure its effective transposition and implementation, in addition to other relevant hate crime laws at national level. furthermore, the council asked member states to develop effective methods to report and ensure proper recording of hate crimes. in the context of hate speech, the council supports the commission high level group, which seeks to develop, together with the member states, concrete practices and tools to improve responses to racism, xenophobia and other forms of intolerance. this group is actually meeting today and tomorrow, and one of the items on the agenda concerns specifically the week of action on combating anti-semitism and anti-muslim hatred. there will also be an opportunity to discuss the rights of victims of hate crimes. on several occasions, the council has called on member states to ensure the full and correct implementation of the eu legislation, notably the eu directive on the rights of victims of crime. i hope that the expertise from the high level group experts will bring us closer in our common endeavour. however, let me stress that all these countermeasures will be in vain if we forget the important role of education and youth work. more precisely, it is crucial to know the history of our continent to understand the value of tolerance and to be able to counter anti-semitism when confronted with it. in the context of awareness-raising and policy advice, we are grateful to the european fundamental rights agency for its continued monitoring of, and research into, discrimination and anti-semitism and for offering evidence-based solutions and suggestions. i would like to conclude by stressing once again how important it is to combat anti-semitism. i would like to recognise the work of the first european commission coordinator on combating anti-semitism, katharina von schnurbein. we have different tools: we have knowledge, we have education, we have counter-narratives, but we also have condemnation of any form of anti-semitic violence, hate speech or discrimination. accordingly, the responsibility rests with all of us – politicians, teachers, students, parents and, if need be, also judges and prosecutors. no one can close his or her eyes or ears and pretend not to see injustice, discrimination or hatred. an important part of the exhibition in the recently opened house of european history, which was founded at the european parliament’s initiative, is devoted to the genocide of european jews. it is the duty of our continent, and our shared responsibility, to remember and not to let it happen again.
member of the commission. – madam president, combating anti-semitism is indeed a very important and alarming topic, considering the statistical evidence which the minister has just mentioned. i very much welcome parliament’s debate and the motion for a resolution. increasing fear and high rates of verbal and physical violence against ethnic, religious and other minorities across europe are a major concern, and it is our duty not only to discuss this but also to come forward with solutions. data show a clear spike in anti—semitic incidents. there was more than one incident a day in austria and three incidents per day in the united kingdom in 2016, in both cases the highest numbers ever recorded. we are particularly worried about discrimination and harassment against jewish youngsters, who are more likely to experience anti-semitism in schools and universities. a hostile environment in schools will put the next generation at risk of exclusion. all of us, collectively and individually, have the duty to fight against intolerance and hatred and reject all expressions of them. we welcomed yesterday’s joint day of action, with parliament, on combating anti-semitism and anti-muslim hatred, which brought together jewish and muslim youngsters. today we are opening two funding calls for applications, making available eur 5.5 million to support civil society and member states’ authorities in better preventing and countering racism and xenophobia, including anti—semitism and other forms of intolerance, hate crime and hate speech. particular areas of attention include hate-crime training, empowering and supporting hate-crime victims, and improving recording, as well as data collection and methodologies. also, at today’s meeting of the high—level group on combating racism, xenophobia and other intolerance i presented the results of the implementation of the code of conduct we concluded in may 2016 with major it companies to combat illegal hate speech online. i can inform you today that significant progress has been made and all it companies have been improving their reaction to notifications concerning manifestly illegal hate speech, including anti-semitic hate speech. let me also inform you that i have asked the eu fundamental rights agency to conduct a large-scale survey on the experience of jews with anti-semitism. we expect the results by early next year. it will be the first time that we have comparable data on trends around anti—semitism across the eu, following an initial survey in 2013. on the occasion of this year’s holocaust remembrance day we made the international holocaust remembrance alliance definition of anti-semitism available through our website. the commission welcomes any useful tool that helps to prevent anti-semitism. several member states, including the uk and austria, which i have already mentioned, use this definition in their policymaking and training and in data collection on anti-semitic incidents and hate crimes. as you know, following our first annual colloquium on fundamental rights, the commission appointed a coordinator on combating anti—semitism, tasked with liaising with jewish communities and with i would like to thank mr kaufmann and all the shadow rapporteurs for their commitment to the issue under discussion today, which is of great concern to the security of our citizens. the uniform visa system applied over the past 20 years has been a key instrument in the achievement of one of the main elements of the internal market: the area of free movement of goods and persons. however, during this period there has been a steady increase in counterfeiting and fraud in several member states. this has made it necessary to take action to further improve the security of our citizens by introducing a new visa format, which is more secure and technologically capable of responding to the criticisms that have emerged in the application of the previous models. a clear union response to the fight against the falsification of documents, made even more necessary by the increase in visa applications registered in connection with the increase in migratory flows. the fact that we have taken action to change the uniform model with more security features in order to make the sticky visa more secure and to prevent its falsification will also help to combat illegal immigration, as well as the phenomenon of so-called overstayer, that is, those third-country nationals who reside in our territories beyond the limits set by law or visa-free agreements. we also know that visa forgery is a very sensitive area in which the interests and activities of organised crime have been concentrated, and that this has also provided support for terrorist organisations. the uniform model certainly makes it easier for the border guards to detect forged documents. i am convinced, however, that the union can be even more ambitious in terms of internal security and therefore i believe that we must continue to work towards full harmonisation of the whole visa system. i thank my colleagues for their work.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the visa system in force in the schengen states is now obsolete, it is a system which has been in use for over 20 years and which no longer provides a sufficient degree of protection against counterfeiting. at a time like this, with the threat of terrorism, we cannot afford to have any loopholes in the visa control system. a new uniform model for european visas should be adopted, which has higher technical characteristics in terms of security and anti-counterfeiting devices, without, however, entailing increased costs for administrations, let alone inconvenience for legitimate visa holders. in recent years there has been a marked increase in cases of forgery, especially in some member states, which has also been confirmed by the competent authorities who have verified the existence of counterfeit european visas in circulation. the commission has therefore taken the necessary steps to ensure that the secret technical specifications for the production of new adhesive stickers are updated and that the legislation is adopted as soon as possible.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the protection of vulnerable people is a matter which deserves our attention. these are adults who are temporarily or permanently unable to provide for themselves and whose protection requires increased attention. it is now generally accepted that the weak subject must be considered to have special legal positions which must be coordinated in the framework of interpersonal and international relations. many countries in the union have ratified the 2000 hague convention on the protection of vulnerable adults, but it is necessary for all member states to ratify it in order to make the protection of these individuals uniform across the union. unfortunately, eu countries have their own specific legislation and there is not always legal uniformity between member states, obviously creating considerable legal difficulties for vulnerable adults. it is therefore necessary for europe to work on identifying best practices in order to ensure that the hague convention is fully implemented and that the problems and delays experienced so far are overcome.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, every year the european commission prepares a report on fishing opportunities for the following year, and every year we read data on the mediterranean which unfortunately are similar. we see that there are some stocks recovering in some parts of europe and others reaching maximum sustainable yield, and we keep reading that in the mediterranean, however, about 90 percent of fish stocks are overexploited and therefore well beyond the limit of maximum sustainable yield. i must acknowledge - and i did so personally a few days ago in new york at the united nations conference on the oceans - that commissioner vella has succeeded in bringing the mediterranean to the forefront of attention with a series of initiatives over the last year and a half, and we are very pleased about that. we started in catania, where we finally had a meeting of technicians, politicians and scientists on the situation in the mediterranean. it was followed by interministerial meetings and finally by the malta declaration a few months ago and the medfish4ever project, launched by the european commission itself. we therefore thought that the european parliament too should have its own position and voice on this very important and sensitive subject and on this rather complex situation, and so we have tabled this own-initiative report and have expressly asked for an open debate here in the plenary, because this is a subject which requires the efforts of many people and policies. the report was the result of very well coordinated work with the shadow rapporteurs and it has produced a fairly broad picture. we have tried to cover a little bit of everything, to give a picture of the situation in the mediterranean fisheries, which is different from any other european basin, both in terms of the stock we have, the basin we have, which is shared with other non-european third countries, and also in terms of the type of fishermen, since 80% of the fishermen in the mediterranean are small fishermen with boats of less than 12 metres. we have tried to paint a complete picture and then we have also tried to give some ideas, proposals and solutions to try to deal with this situation. the points in the report are numerous, and i shall not be able to recall them all. the report has been seen by everyone in this house and everyone knows it well. i am only reiterating two or three concepts. we cannot think of a solution for the mediterranean without involving third countries. that is why we welcome the interministerial meetings organized by the european commission with great satisfaction, because we insist on the same basin, we insist on the same stocks and third countries must work with us to try to make these stocks sustainable. there is no socioeconomically sustainable fishery without healthy stocks. so we have to achieve this balance. the situation is very complicated now, and that is why the solutions are not unique, but different. we also dealt with a few difficult issues such as illegal fishing, which is still very much present, especially in some mediterranean countries. we also discussed possible conservation measures, including the problem of quotas, which seems to be a taboo in the mediterranean, without proposing it or even forgetting about it, but only as something that is there and could be useful. i am waiting to hear the commission's and my colleagues' comments and i believe that we have done a good job and that it is important that this report be voted on tomorrow to have parliament's voice on this issue.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank my colleague, mr marco affronte, for his valuable work on this dossier. with its 17 000 species, the mediterranean is a sea of great biodiversity. it is therefore important that fisheries management policies have a multispecies and ecosystem approach, based on scientific research and data exchange. but that's not enough. it is necessary to take account of local particularities through the principle of regionalization, which in my view remains the best instrument and on which we are working in the committee on fisheries on a great many dossiers, starting with technical measures. to achieve maximum sustainable yield by 2020, work needs to be done on several fronts, from safeguarding marine ecosystems to strengthening cooperation with third countries, including to combat illegal fishing, from greater involvement of fishermen in decision-making processes to investing in food education starting in schools, so that an aware consumer does not eat more fish but eats more fish. we must not simply reduce fishing effort, but we must act in all sectors with transversal policies. the mediterranean is the sea where shipping is greater than all the seas in the world and it is therefore on this that we must work, on land-based urbanisation and on marine waste. i mean, we have a lot of issues to discuss in a lot of committees. the mediterranean is therefore not without its artisanal fisheries, which account for 80% of the fleet. it employs hundreds of thousands of people, including many women. and then we are not just talking about fishing, but we have to think about who sells the fish, who is the caterer, who is the processor, who produces and markets the equipment, and so on. in short, to ensure a sustainable future we must combine environmental, social and economic considerations, otherwise, in a few years, we will be forced to find ourselves here to prevent the extinction of another species, that of the fisherman.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the overall level of overfished fish stocks in the mediterranean is considered to be twice the maximum sustainable yield. but the mediterranean sea is also subject to other threats, such as pollution, maritime traffic, climate change and oil and gas extraction. the mediterranean must be protected by sustainable multiannual management of resources, with more selective fishing gear, respect for the minimum size, greater control of illegal fishing and, where and if scientific studies require it, also biological stocking. at the same time, however, european fishermen must be guaranteed a decent income. member states should set up a fixed income compensation fund to cover fishing closure periods. the lack of a common regulatory framework for the fleets of the european union and third countries operating in the mediterranean is creating unfair competition to the detriment of our fishermen. it is therefore essential to encourage greater cooperation with third countries bordering the mediterranean sea.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am particularly excited today to tell you a story that has never been told before, at least in this house. this regulation introduces into european legislation certain concepts relating to the energy efficiency of electrical equipment and its potential dynamic interaction with electricity grids. i learned these concepts ten years ago when i was a dentist and, for the sake of publicity, translated environmental sustainability essays into italian. i could never have imagined that one day i would be standing here representing millions of citizens and having the honour of transposing into european legislation what were at the time some experimental proposals by lester brown and others. smart appliances are appliances, such as dishwashers and washing machines, that can be programmed by the user to start running at times when electricity is available in the most abundant and cheapest quantities. the widespread use of smart appliances will not only save users money, but also make a significant contribution to the balance of an electricity system powered by increasingly renewable sources. imagine a citizen producing wind or solar energy. some of the equipment in his house will be able to come into operation and carry out its work when self-production is more abundant. imagine the old, outdated electric water heater, which by its nature is not particularly efficient in purely thermodynamic terms, but if the water heater will heat water when electricity is cheaper and more abundant, the accumulated heat will be a low-cost form of energy source. smart appliances are a new frontier in energy efficiency, not just in quantity but also in quality, not just in how much energy is consumed, but also in when it is used. that's why i'm excited, because behind this text is a little piece of utopia that is becoming a reality for 500 million citizens. the proof that you can believe in an idea, however far-fetched it may seem, and piece by piece, with persistence and determination, get it done. this regulation, for the first time, gives manufacturers the possibility of indicating on the label the ability of equipment to be energy smart. this little thing allows the new labelling regulation to keep pace with the times and to fully integrate into the new dynamic, decentralised and renewable energy model we want to pursue with the energy union. an energy union whose stated objectives include putting the citizen at its centre. the new labels will be accompanied by an open data database which can be accessed directly via a mobile phone, a qr code, a link or similar on the paper label and will be able to provide buyers, in the 24 languages of the union, not only with a series of information that cannot be found on a piece of paper, but will also allow the development of smartphone applications which will allow citizens and businesses to make instant comparisons between different models and to choose the one which offers the best result in terms of initial investment and savings over time, not in relation to a generic average but in relation to personal usage habits. i've listed two things i've fought for and i'm proud of, and there's more. however, if i'm to be intellectually honest, as i am in my habit, i also feel obliged to share a bit of a pain with you. at the beginning of this process, i made a promise that i would be guided by three key words: smart, paperless and trust. we are certainly facing a smart regulation, in which the use and importance of paper is being reduced in favour of a more fruitful use of digital technologies of documents and online databases. it is true that this regulation undoubtedly strengthens the national market surveillance authorities, but we would have liked more. we would have liked to see a compensation from the manufacturers if it were found that the energy performance of a product was lower than the declared one. parliament wanted it to be a compact one, but unfortunately we found ourselves faced with a wall, the council's wall, which prevented it. it has prevented eu citizens from having the same rights as, for example, us citizens who were defrauded by volkswagen and who were reimbursed. we have, however, obtained from the european commission, to which i am grateful, a written undertaking attached to this regulation to study the possibilities of removing this absurd legislative vacuum, which we consider to be a real scandal. i am sure that the people of europe expect this absurdity to be brought to an end as soon as possible.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner cañete, in europe we produce very little of the energy we consume and a large part of our energy still comes from fossil fuels. we know then how important it is to take action to promote the energy transition, through increased use of renewable energy, but we also know how important it is to reduce energy consumption and thus increase energy efficiency. with the new regulation on the energy labelling of household appliances and electronic equipment we are taking a step in this direction. we have seen that consumers are very careful and, thanks to the label system, they choose more advanced appliances and also save money at the end of the month on their bill. on the other hand, thanks to this system, industry is developing increasingly effective models to remain competitive on the market. experience has shown us that in several cases, such as washing machines and refrigerators, almost all products have moved into the highest efficiency classes within a few years. for this reason too, it is necessary today to update labels, as we have done, by redefining them in a clearer way, without all those a+s, and understandable to consumers.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the energy efficiency labels of electrical products such as refrigerators, televisions and washing machines are finally changing, adapting to the digital revolution by linking to an open data base and being made available through the use of qr codes. it will thus be possible, also in europe, to compare the electricity consumption of different appliances at the time of purchase in an efficient and effective way and thus to promote a more conscious and sustainable consumption, based on usage habits and the price and availability of electricity. it is a small, but concrete and important step towards improving the use of resources. however, further work is needed, introducing stricter criteria for the electrical appliance market and obliging manufacturers to use smart technologies that can adapt to energy consumption and availability. the introduction of transparent and clear labelling, which moves from confusing a++ to a simple a to g scale, is a clear step forward in protecting consumers and industry. however, appropriate checks must be carried out to ensure that those labels actually correspond to products with the characteristics indicated.

adopted by the committee on the environment, public health and food safety (envi) includes a requirement for member states to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in effort-sharing sectors by 80% by 2050 compared to 2005. it is true that consistent and long-term emission reductions are a cornerstone of european union climate policy. however, i think it is too early to set national targets and emission trajectories for 2050 now already, without any thorough impact assessments and even before the intergovernmental panel on climate change (ipcc) has provided its special report. we must also consider emissions. the commission will address the long-term issues in the context of developing the european union mid-century strategy, which, in accordance with the g7 commission, is to be delivered well ahead of the 2020 deadline. secondly, i note the proposal for a biennial compliance check instead of every five years. this would significantly increase the misery burden of implementation and would not constitute a good example of better regulation. the commission fully supports the efforts of parliament and the council to agree on the ets and non-ets proposal this year. on the ets file, we are conclusion with your support.

thank this house and especially alojz peterle for its strong support for the eu election observation mission. this observation mission was deployed in record time. the european parliament has significantly contributed to making it possible. in most of kosovo, the election day passed calmly and peacefully. it is a sign of kosovo’s democratic maturity that people generally were able to cast their ballots freely and without hindrance. however, we do share chief election observer peterle’s concerns about several aspects of the elections. any incidents of intimidation and pressure as witnessed during the electoral campaign are unacceptable. it will be essential for kosovo’s democratic development that the findings of the observation mission are taken seriously and implemented as a matter of priority. now that elections are over, kosovo has no time to lose. based on the democratic will of the people, we expect a new government to be formed and begin work without delay. a new governing coalition will face huge expectations and challenges. the dialogue with belgrade needs to move ahead. the people of kosovo expect decisions on visa liberalisation. the rule of law, economic development and education need to be given the highest priority. broad societal consensus on the eu reforms will be necessary to navigate through these various challenges. one of the most important priorities the government will have to tackle immediately is delivery on the conditions for visa liberalisation. kosovo has made progress on its track record of high-level corruption and organised crime cases. this must be a continuous process and one in which momentum must be maintained at all times. i can assure you that we know how contentious the border demarcation agreement with montenegro has become. it will now be for kosovo’s new government and parliament to deliver on the expectations of its people. we are ready to support kosovo every step of the way. once kosovo has fulfilled these conditions, the commission will give its green light to the european parliament and council. beside these political challenges, kosovo’s priorities should remain the rule of law, economic development and education. kosovo needs to become an attractive place for business, provide citizens with high quality education and reduce the very high unemployment levels, in particular amongst young people. the incoming government will need to show strong commitment to addressing the systemic weaknesses in the rule of law, as we have frequently pointed out in our reports. the commission is providing strong support for the implementation of these priorities through substantive financial assistance and technical advice. for its part, kosovo needs to keep pace with the rest of the region, to promote economic growth and foster political stability, which is essential for the security of the western balkans as a whole. to achieve this, we have jointly agreed programmes with kosovo: the european reform agenda and the economic reform programme. these should serve as guidelines for concrete deliverables. this is the priority for now and the immediate future.
i would like to thank mrs lunacek for her work. this report, in addition to describing the state of our relations, is particularly useful in focusing our attention on the various crucial points which still prevent kosovo from full integration. the result of the important elections last sunday saw the so-called war wing, as the local media calls it, composed of a coalition led by haradinaj, get the largest number of votes, but it would not seem sufficient to support a government without alliances with other political forces. our expectations are, of course, to see the birth of a government that will guarantee the country the stability necessary to continue the process of political stabilization and integration of kosovo into the european context. however, we must be aware that haradinaj's victory will not make relations with serbia easier, a country which, as we know, has issued an international arrest warrant against the former commander of the kosovo liberation army. the european union will play an important role in this context. as the report rightly points out, there remains a high level of concern about corruption and organised crime, two factors that are a serious problem for the country. in addition, despite the appreciable economic improvement and the increase in tax revenues, it is essential to promote structural economic and social reforms, especially as regards employment and education. finally, i would like to ask you to consider the fact that the failure of five member states to recognise kosovo is in fact hindering the process of integration. a change of course could be useful and would allow for an improvement in relations between kosovo and serbia. i think that the european parliament needs to show more courage, because that would help the european union's political action in kosovo and the balkans even more.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, today it is still difficult to define the collaborative economy. yet it moves, it grows, it transforms our society, our way of living and working. it creates extraordinary opportunities and at the same time risks undermining established legal and social categories. thanks to the digital revolution and online platforms, with a click, we can rent a room anywhere in the world, share a ride with someone, buy a meal from a neighbor, find a gardener to cut the hedge. opportunities that consumers increasingly value and use. the collaborative economy is born, on the one hand, from technological innovation, but, on the other, from the increasingly widespread need for a better use of resources, with the effect of stimulating the biodiversity of the economic forms of society. a mosaic of different experiences involving large platforms, now truly multinational, and small start-ups strongly rooted in the territory and the communities of reference. in recent years, the collaborative economy has developed in europe more through court rulings and often contradictory national and regional rules than through a shared strategy, resulting in a fragmented market and provisions that are difficult for operators to interpret. the commission's attempt to define a common approach in its communication is therefore to be welcomed. our report goes further, calling for a european strategy. first of all, we invite the commission to examine the existing legal framework, considering whether it is appropriate to introduce general principles and specific rules which can promote harmonious development. the objective should be to avoid different rules applying to similar services between the traditional and the collaborative economy, both in terms of market access and taxation, thus ensuring fair competition between online and offline operators and between them and prosumers. the distinction between professional and non-professional is an essential point for the definition of fair and balanced rules. the evaluation of market access criteria can be a great opportunity to simplify the rules for operators in traditional services as well. we also believe that a common legal framework can foster the growth of european platforms, which today see uncertainty and fragmentation of rules and the unavailability of venture capital as the main obstacles to growth on a global scale. this is demonstrated by the fact that only one of the top ten platforms producing economic value in europe is european. the online platforms, the engine of the sharing economy, will have to assume greater responsibility towards consumers through clear information, towards service providers by ensuring the reliability of ratings, and towards public authorities through fair tax cooperation. finally, the sharing economy can be a stimulus to new employment, particularly for those with lower employment rates. however, it is not conceivable that in this sector workers, whether employed or selfemployed, should have fewer rights and protections than everyone else. let me conclude by thanking all the shadow rapporteurs, the rapporteurs of the committees of inquiry, for the excellent cooperation they have had in recent months, not without a frank and thorough debate, which i believe has been fruitful in the preparation of this final report.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, one in seven people living with hiv do not know they are hiv positive, and the estimated time between infection and diagnosis is on average four years, which increases the risk of transmission of the virus by almost four times. in 2015, around 30 000 new hiv infections were diagnosed in the 31 eu/eea countries, with no clear sign of a global decline. besides aids, tuberculosis and viral hepatitis are also widespread, progress more rapidly and cause a high mortality rate. a comprehensive eu strategic framework for hiv, tuberculosis and hepatitis b and c in particular, taking into account the specific challenges faced by member states and neighbouring countries with higher hiv and tuberculosis incidence rates, should be provided. multi-sectoral cooperation is therefore needed to ensure the necessary resources to strengthen prevention and care activities for vulnerable communities and individuals.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, we must start with a fact: the "use and throw" model of production is no longer sustainable. it's no longer ethically sustainable, because of the enormous waste of raw materials. it's no longer economically sustainable, because the materials we use are neither infinite nor biodegradable. and it's not sustainable for citizens, who are tired of buying things that don't last. we want to create an economic model where goods last and can be repaired. we are calling for sanctions against those who resort to planned obsolescence, that is, those manufacturers who design goods to be short-lived. we call for the use of construction techniques and materials that make repairs easier and cheaper. a citizen must be able to replace the damaged part of a mobile phone or a household appliance at reasonable cost, without having to throw away the mobile phone or the household appliance. we call on the european commission to come forward with a legislative proposal to put an end to the throwaway culture.

importance of longer-lasting products if it affects all of us as european citizens. i am sure that many of us have experienced frustration when domestic appliances have broken down and the price of repair costs as much as – or more than – buying a new product. also, when it equipment and software updates are no longer compatible, we can waste a lot of time sorting out these issues. however, we all need to recognise that our products are becoming increasingly sophisticated and more reliant on it, as well as more efficient. there are trade-offs to be made in keeping a product for 20 years regarding eco—design and energy labelling actions, in november 2016 the commission adopted an eco—design working plan for the years 2016—2019, setting out its working priorities and its eco—design and energy labelling framework. the working plan has a stronger focus on supporting circular economy objectives. the commission has committed to explore the possibility of establishing more product—specific and horizontal requirements in areas such as durability, reparability, upgradeability, information and ease of re—use and recycling. the implementation of the working plan is currently under way. regarding european standardisation action, a massive horizontal european standards effort has been mounted since december 2015 by a joint technical committee. this work looks at product—related legislation and standards. regarding the role of member states, your report acknowledges that member states could also play a role in promoting repairs, for example by putting lower conclusion, we welcome mr durand’s report. we are already acting on some of its suggestions and will reflect in further detail regarding others. we need to work on this together to make changes that make sense for our lifestyles, for businesses and for the planet. so i welcome your support from all relevant committees.
in writing. the realisation of a circular economy model requires the involvement of policy-makers, citizens and businesses, and implies changes not only in the design and sale of products and services, but also in consumer mindsets and entrepreneurial activity. a balance must be struck between extending the useful life of products and converting waste into resources, between innovation and consumer demand. issues such as product durability, commercial warranty extension, availability of spare parts, ease of repair and interchangeability of components must be part of the manufacturer's commercial offer. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of life of the elderly, and has recently launched a new initiative to combat the problem of the elderly. i am in favour of the definition of minimum durability criteria, which include, inter alia, robustness, repairability and ability to evolve, for the different product categories, from design, to the establishment of an independent system, capable of testing and detecting the obsolescence embedded in products.

depend on fishing. europe's coastal areas attract millions of visitors every year and there has been a recent upsurge in interest in sustainable tourism. diversification of activities will therefore not only help a sector in crisis to recover, but also help fishermen and tourists to meet and get to know each other through an ancient, difficult and complex craft. not only that: the meeting will help to raise awareness of responsible consumption, starting with the knowledge of the different fish species, including those that are less well known, which are often cheaper but not necessarily less good. to make the most of the economic and social potential of this sector, action is needed on several fronts: the commission has also proposed that the member states should harmonise the definition and legal basis of fishing tourism, which varies considerably from one member state to another. for example, in italy it is considered a professional activity, while in france it is considered a casual activity. it is also necessary to harmonize european safety standards so that small-scale fishing vessels can be used for tourist trips or for direct fishing experiences, while ensuring the safety of those on board. finally, investment at national, regional and local level should be encouraged to improve services, from better internet connections to the renovation of facilities and the promotion of local cultures and traditions. the resources made available by the emff should be better used, while at the same time the collaboration between public administrations, flags (i.e. local action groups), tourism experts and stakeholders should be strengthened in order to promote sustainable growth and to develop innovative products that meet the expectations of visitors. the issue of seasonality could be addressed through information and promotion campaigns that offer visitors different activities throughout the year, for example through the organisation of events. tourism linked to fishing, in particular fisheries tourism and hunting tourism, is thus a real form of integration and diversification of primary activity in many european regions, and is economically beneficial for fishermen and environmentally sustainable. unfortunately, however, they are still too little known to the general public and too little valued by the institutions. this requires a joint and shared effort involving all stakeholders and enabling coastal communities, fishermen and tourists to benefit fully from the great opportunities this sector has to offer. i would like to take this opportunity to thank all my colleagues, the shadow rapporteurs, for their help and their interest in the work we have done together.

vice-president of the commission. – madam president, the commission has made fair taxation one of its priorities. and, naturally, since recent disclosures have once again underlined the magnitude of the problem, calls for action have gained force. we have put forward a raft of measures to tackle tax abuse and to make sure that companies pay their fair share of taxes in the countries where their actual economic activity is taking place. in addition to measures addressing directly companies’ tax affairs and the work of tax authorities we are convinced that corporate transparency is part of the equation. parliament has been vocal and pivotal in calling for a valid answer to the widespread public discontent. the commission responded timely in a constructive way. the public country-by-country reporting, which we are examining today mainly aims to address two issues. first, a growing public distrust in the fairness of the tax system, and second, the accountability of multinational companies towards our citizens. the proposed corporate transparency measure is an ambitious and unprecedented move, a move that requires striking a delicate balance between, on the one hand, the public’s legitimate demands for information, and, on the other, legitimate calls for our businesses not to weaken their world-wide competitiveness. the commission also paid attention to complement, but not undermine, the existing system of exchange of a country-by-country reporting by tax authorities. this system is gaining remarkable traction globally under the aegis of the oecd and g20 and with the full support the european union. it is easy to see the importance of the issue. due to corporate tax avoidance, our governments miss out an estimated eur 50 to 70 billion a year. in view of the fiscal efforts they are making and the investment demanded by the economies, these amounts are unacceptably high. so, honourable members, we trust in your support to get this proposal agreed as quickly as possible.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank my fellow rapporteurs for their excellent and valuable work on this important dossier. state-by-state reporting is a key measure for transparency and against tax evasion and avoidance at global and european level. the commission is proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the european union's internal market, and to extend it to the european union's external borders. this will also enable developing countries to obtain valuable information on multinational companies operating within their borders. the poorest countries, in fact, are the ones paying the highest price for these practices, losing hundreds of billions of dollars every year, a vital resource for development. the fight against poverty and inequality also passes through here. unfortunately, there are some people in this house who preach well and preach badly, and they want a safeguard clause which would allow multinational companies to avoid publishing information which they consider sensitive. without at least the retroactive publication of this information, this becomes a very dangerous loophole to continue hiding profits. i therefore appeal to my liberal and popular colleagues to remember that partial solutions are not enough in the face of a global phenomenon. we can pass a historic measure, and when history passes, it's good not to be found elsewhere.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, italy is a country which, because of its tourist vocation and its almost 7 500 kilometres of coastline, is more than any other able to exploit the full potential of its sea. the climate and the fact that the fishing is mainly artisanal and seasonal make our country one of the main targets of the own-initiative report voted on today. coastal regions and islands are suffering from severe economic decline due to shortages of fish resources or overly restrictive or even wrong policies. in recent years, so-called 'fish tourism' has helped to create new jobs, but it is not the solution. the report is therefore generally positive, but it does have some criticisms. we must make the best use of the funds available, all of them, not just the emff, and we must make sure that fisheries tourism and other alternatives are not the solution. these proposals must not be a means of covering up the holes created over the years by wrong and unsuitable policies for our seas, but merely represent forms of economic integration which are necessary at certain times of the year and in well-defined circumstances.
the coastal areas are suffering greatly. the increasing constraints imposed by the common fisheries policy, the scarcity of resources and competition from products coming from abroad have brought the traditional productive activity of these areas, namely fishing, to its knees. so how do we enable coastal communities to survive, to maintain their traditions, to respect their vocation and to have a decent income? coastal areas are naturally a tourist attraction. it is therefore necessary to create spaces for fishermen in the services offered to tourists. boat trips or fishing trips offered to tourists by chance and left to their own devices - and sometimes disorganized - are certainly not enough. with the right incentive policies and an organic development strategy, tourism can also become a stable source of income for fishermen. we need to invest in infrastructure, in overcoming seasonal tourism, in connections. we need a connection with the business owners, the tour operators, the caterers. it's about teamwork and politics all rolled into one.

in writing. the report under discussion deals with a very important and complex subject. when it comes to international and cultural relations, i believe that we must avoid maintaining an ethnocentric and self-referential attitude. this would not only be contrary to the founding values of the european union and the very idea of aiding and developing the poorest countries, but would also be counterproductive to that end. the european union should promote its own culture in terms of reciprocity, thus avoiding the imposition of its cultural hegemony, which is too often used as a crutch to impose precise economic and legal choices. the choice too often has concealed, and continues to conceal, economic and human misfortunes. culture and cultural heritage are common goods that belong to everyone and as such must be safeguarded and managed. only by example, and not by aseptic export, can the european union make known to other countries the importance of its own values and culture, while respecting the values and cultures of others.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner jourová, commissioner oettinger, i first of all thank the rapporteurs for the difficult but important work they have done through years of intensive negotiations to define the text of the pif directive which, together with the forthcoming establishment of the european public prosecutor's office, represents a key step on the road to the harmonization of criminal law and will form the backbone of the new criminal justice system to combat fraud and corruption, which have cost the eu budget some eur 1 trillion. among the most significant provisions of the directive is the reference to the union legislation on combating money laundering and corruption, which is essential to tackle the activities of criminal groups that, through these offences, obtain money to use in their illicit activities. the introduction of vat fraud in the legislative text is also particularly important, as has been said, and represents a fundamental step forward in ensuring more comprehensive protection against financial crimes against the union.
in writing. the union's financial interests can only be effectively protected in an integrated manner. the criminal law in this area must therefore be adopted at european level and this report is a first step in that direction. vat fraud is an important part of the fraud in question and is facilitated by the very existence of the internal market (so-called 'carousel fraud'). the fact that these are included in the scope of the directive is very important, as is the fact that the relevant threshold is part of the aspects subject to review in three years' time. the same applies to fraud in the management of public contracts, another major problem for many countries, including our own. the text is therefore, as i said, only a first step, but it is certainly going in the right direction.
