the agenda includes the report by mr mihai ţurcanu, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council laying down rules for the making available on the market of ce marked fertilising products and amending regulations (ec) no 1069/2009 and (ec) no 1107/2009 (com (((2016) 0157 - c8-0123/2016 - 2016/0084 ((cod)) (a8-0270/2017).
the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a fire. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too am here to witness the hard, long and complex work that has been done. we have welcomed this regulation very warmly, because it will bring a wide range of fertilisers under the ec mark, which were previously excluded, but we also have some concerns. we, as the environment committee, had exclusive competence with regard to contaminants and the subject on which we had the most debate was certainly that of cadmium, as the rapporteur, mr ţurcanu, has already mentioned. my concerns are very acute because even in the commission's fact sheets it is estimated that going to a limit of 40 milligrams would require great efforts and greater investment in technology, etc., etc., but the commission itself acknowledges in these documents that going even to 20 milligrams, as the commission has proposed and as the environment committee has also confirmed, would involve such and greater investment in decadmification and probably even require a general reshaping of the fertiliser market. that is why i think caution is important and that perhaps it is right to give ourselves a little time to think, considering that already at 60 milligrams we are halfway to the lowest limit we find in the world. you know, from 120 to 150 to 160 we're talking about the united states, we're talking about canada, we're talking about australia: we are not talking about countries that do not care about the environment. so i join the call of the rapporteur, mr turcanu.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the regulation we are going to adopt tomorrow will give us a regulatory framework that is finally harmonized in a sector, that of fertilisers, which - i would like to remind all of us - represents 100 000 jobs in europe, hundreds of small and mediumsized enterprises, with an annual turnover of between 20 and 25 billion euros. i would like to stress three important results that emerge from this text. the first is the visible, legible and comprehensive ce marking, which will ensure greater protection for consumers and, above all, for farmers. the second: we have ensured that the use of recycled and organic materials is promoted for the further development of the circular economy and the reduction of dependence on imports of certain raw materials from third countries. finally, there is the most sensitive aspect of the regulation, namely the definition of harmonised limit values for certain contaminating products such as cadmium and chromium. i believe that the approach which our group has put to parliament is one of reasonableness and balance. on the one hand, attention to the health of citizens and to environmental safety, and on the other hand, the need for a reasonable period of time for the industrial system to adapt to the new limits envisaged, new limits which, i would remind you all, in most european countries are clearly below the starting limit of this directive, namely the 60 milligrams which we have set as the starting point. i think some people might argue that the timing could have been quicker to arrive at a harmonised framework at european level. however, what matters - i think, ladies and gentlemen - is to set europe on a course which, through investment, research and development, will make this sector more competitive and our policies more environmentally sustainable.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the food we eat is the main source of heavy metal contamination, including cadmium, which is classified as a carcinogen. this is stated by efsa, which has also set maximum acceptable intake levels in its scientific opinions. a 2015 study by the institute for experimental zooprophylaxis in venice found that those who follow a mediterranean vegetarian or vegan diet are also more exposed to high levels of cadmium and thus to contamination. by introducing strict limits for cadmium and other heavy metals such as mercury, arsenic and lead in this new regulation, we can safeguard the health of european consumers. not to do it today would be foolish and irresponsible. we also have another great opportunity to seize, that of the circular economy, to make something that has been abstract until now, something concrete. this regulation seeks to turn waste into resources and create a market for organic fertilisers to encourage natural and clean fertilisers. and in this way we could achieve a twofold result: the commission has already taken a number of measures to reduce the number of people who are unemployed, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. on the other hand, we would be encouraging a real transition towards sustainable and natural agriculture which is beneficial for ecosystems, the environment and, of course, people. we are talking about a ce mark and we are talking about stringent criteria for creating a new market. those who do not respect them can stay out and continue business as usual, but we must aim for the maximum and the improvement of the health of european citizens.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, european agriculture is called upon to play a leading role in the increasingly pressing global challenge of access to food. in this sense, the availability of quality fertilising products is one of the conditions for the development of more productive and at the same time more sustainable agricultural models, which in the future will have to be able to produce more, using less inputs. for these reasons, the regulation under discussion cannot be merely an opportunity to harmonize the rules on traditional fertilisers at european level. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's policy on climate change and its impact on the environment, and will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's policy on climate change and its impact on the environment. the european parliament's ambitious position will therefore have to be able to confirm the union's role as a leader in sustainable development, while ensuring the availability of fertilising products at fair prices, without creating further distortions of competition to the detriment of our farmers.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the fertiliser regulation is certainly a step forward. finally, there is harmonization of standards, finally, access to the market for innovative fertilisers is facilitated, the use of organic and recycled materials is promoted, and finally, clearer labels. unfortunately, there is still no agreement on the limits for cadmium. on cadmium, some colleagues have urged us to be cautious and reasonable. i think it is not reasonable to minimize or ignore the fact that cadmium is a heavy metal that is a serious carcinogen that contaminates water, soil and food. i think it is not reasonable to ignore the fact that in many european countries the national limits are lower, in the east and in the west: 20, 22 of them. italy, which excels in agriculture, has a limit of 50. and then it's possible, we're not proposing the moon. we are determined to apply the precautionary principle. let us not be divided: the proposal we have put forward is reasonable.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal for a regulation is a step in the right direction, by encouraging the large-scale production of organic fertilisers from waste, in line with the circular economy model, and by facilitating their access to the single market on equal terms with traditional inorganic fertilisers. the maximum limits for impurities, such as microbial contaminants, and the new minimum nutrient content per functional product category, to ensure the quality of ce marked fertilisers, are also positive. however, more could and should be done to ensure the safety of fertilisers and to reduce the limits for heavy metals, in particular cadmium, for each functional category. i think the envi proposal is reasonable and i think the executive committee's proposal is acceptable, but the compromise that has been advanced for 16 years to reduce cadmium to 20 milligrams per kilogram of product is more a gift to the producers than a serious and responsible position to protect the environment and consumers.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are facing one of the great tragedies of our time: the use and dependence of psychotropic substances that threaten the health and lives of millions of people. this theme crosses the existential drama of young people and adults, threatens their mental balance, becomes an opportunity for crime and illicit trafficking. the number of substances is growing rapidly and therefore i think it is no longer advisable to postpone the decision to strengthen the monitoring and warning system, making it even more widespread, and to accompany the monitoring systems with research into the effects and outcomes of the increasing use of mixed substances. finally, and i will come back to this again, the marketing of psychoactive substances via the internet should be strictly prohibited, because it is accessible to everyone and because it is also, perhaps, cheaper.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the rapporteurs on the two dossiers under discussion today, which update the european legislative framework for the fight against drugs by criminalising the illegal trade in new psychoactive and psychotropic substances. the subjecting of the illicit trafficking of these new substances to criminal law provisions is certainly a deterrent, aimed also at limiting the availability and consumption of substances which are sometimes extremely dangerous to the health of our young people. however, in addition to the measures to be taken to enforce the law, there is a need for measures to prevent and inform people of the harmful effects of the use of new psychoactive substances. it is therefore necessary to take coordinated action between the member states to harmonize national substantive legislation and, of course, as the proposal for a regulation rightly advocates, to ensure the most rapid exchange of information on new substances which could be classified as psychoactive.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the rapporteurs on the drugs package. new psychoactive substances are a relatively new phenomenon and europe has been the first to move in this direction. however, today the phenomenon must be seen as a global one and new measures must be taken to respond quickly to the new challenges. we certainly cannot be satisfied with the silence that has been so far; the commission is also proposing to establish a european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction (emcdda) to monitor the implementation of the new drug control and control measures. we cannot ignore the society that is asking us to discuss openly and without taboos the derivatives of cannabis, a substance that commits our law enforcement agencies to 80% of its resources. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the health of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens. the important pharmacological properties of this substance have also been too often underestimated. i therefore think it is appropriate to launch an open debate in parliament in the coming months on the role of the union in the un and the need to give cannabis a status that is more in line with the times.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in the last five years there has been an unprecedented increase in the number, type and availability of new psychoactive substances in europe, with over 100 new drugs identified for the first time. the world health organization states that the new psychoactive substances available in europe are particularly dangerous because of their toxicity, interaction with other substances and influence on mental processes. the rapid increase in new psychoactive substances presents a new challenge for the definition of an effective policy to combat the use of such substances, in which the european union must be at the forefront, both through europol's coordination action and through the eu rapid alert system, an essential tool to enable national authorities to identify new substances and to act promptly to intercept and remove them from the market. a joint effort by the european institutions, an economic, logistical and political effort is therefore necessary to ensure that the national and community authorities are equipped with the appropriate instruments to combat the spread and development of the new narcotics, which are increasingly difficult to detect and, unfortunately, increasingly dangerous.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, for several years now the fundamental role played by whistleblowers in revealing serious breaches of the public interest has been highlighted by a series of scandals in very different areas, such as the protection of public health, the environment and tax evasion. the protection of whistleblowers is one of the most important tools for safeguarding the public interest. unfortunately, the protections offered, where they exist, are inadequate or too fragmented to ensure a coherent framework within the european union. a number of international standards on the protection of whistleblowers have been developed, on which european legislation should therefore be based. in accordance with those rules, the definition of whistleblower should be sufficiently broad to cover a maximum number of situations and thereby protect public and private sector employees, consultants and the self-employed. the case of journalist and blogger daphne caruana galizia, who has been dubbed the "wikileaks woman", also forces us to do everything we can to protect whistleblowers who work to expose wrongdoing.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the panama papers, swiss leaks and lux leaks are just the latest major scandals to have exposed tax evasion, transnational fraud and corruption, which have become known thanks to the courageous initiative of those who felt it their duty to denounce criminal behaviour aimed at harming the community. i think that the european parliament should be given credit for having brought such a sensitive and topical issue to the fore, and also for having highlighted the differences between the national systems of the member states, in some of which whistleblowers are not protected or are sometimes criminalised for their actions. i thank mr rozière for his work in highlighting the need for a regulatory framework with minimum standards to harmonise the treatment of such cases and to protect whistleblowers by establishing specific legal rules, so as to recognise their fundamental role in the public interest.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are talking about the protection of whistleblowers, of informants, and so we are talking about a real fight against corruption, a real fight for transparency. but beyond words, the reality of the facts tells us about a heterogeneous system of norms, which varies from country to country: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's information system is not undermined by the fact that it is not able to provide the information it needs. it is therefore necessary to guarantee the possibility, even for anonymous informants, to be able to operate, it is therefore necessary to protect them from any form of retaliation by employers and the institutions for which they work, and for this, in my view, it is essential to achieve a reversal of the burden of proof. in the case of dismissals, in the case of potentially discriminatory behaviour, it is those who have done it who have to prove their good faith and not the whistleblower, on the contrary, who has to prove that he has suffered a wrong. in addition, perhaps we should also think about funds to help with the economic consequences. this is what we have to do if we really want to talk about protecting whistleblowers, otherwise the courage of their words will only be followed by the silence of our indifference.
member of the commission. – mr president, once again i would like to express my thanks to the rapporteur for this report, which is an important contribution to our debate. the commission strongly believes that protecting those who raise the alarm helps detect serious violations of the law which would otherwise be difficult to identify. whistle—blowing is an upstream component of the chain of actions necessary for an effective enforcement of the law and the safeguarding of the public interest. let me underline that we should protect responsible whistle—blowing which genuinely seeks to protect the public interest. it is essential to safeguard the rights and interests of entities affected by whistle—blower reports, such as their right of defence. the question is how best to achieve this objective, and how we can contribute at eu level. as you know, the commission is currently finalising its assessment of the scope of such eu action. our open public consultation conducted this year attracted a lot of interest. we received some 5700 replies, of which around 200 were from stakeholder organisations. the full results are available online, but let me underline that respondents were overwhelmingly in favour of protecting whistle—blowers. asked specifically in which areas the european union should support member states to better protect whistle—blowers, the top four areas they cited were: the fight against fraud and corruption, the fight against tax evasion and avoidance, the protection of the environment and the protection of public health and safety. to feed our assessment, we have also commissioned an external study. we are carrying out a detailed mapping of the legal situation across the european union, including through targeted consultations with national authorities and other stakeholders. the commission will consider further actions in the first part of 2018. in this context, your report is very timely, and the solutions proposed will be taken into account in our work.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, citizens, it is clear to everyone today that poverty is a european problem, caused precisely by the policies that this european union has perpetrated for years. the last hope for putting a stop to the poverty crisis is the willingness of all countries to adopt a minimum income that will restore life and dignity to the almost 120 million european citizens who are no longer able to make ends meet and are struggling to survive. with this document europe will no longer be able to turn a blind eye to the suffering of its citizens. europe must no longer remain deaf to the requests for help that households and businesses have been making for years. the european commission should address the issue of the minimum income without delay and present a proposal for a binding directive as soon as possible. today, according to the european social observatory, various forms of income support already exist in 26 member states, and i regret to add that in my own country there is no minimum income. we want europe to act immediately with a common framework of rules which will allow the harmonization of the different existing schemes with common and valid access criteria for all, such as, for example, basing the calculation of the income to be paid on the poverty threshold, which eurostat sets at 60% of the national average income. there are no 'b' citizens, everyone must be able to benefit from minimum income schemes in the same way. it is not enough to say that the budget lines of the european social fund and the european programme for employment and social innovation should be made available to help member states implement minimum income schemes. it is a strategic approach and a vision, which allows for real social integration. it 's not just about the money . the citizens do not ask for alms, but for policies of dignity. if money is found to save the banks, i demand all the more that resources be found for the children of this europe which is too often the victim of vicious interests. our continent must regain its human face, providing health care, housing, education and dignity through expansive economic policies that benefit everyone. i would like to conclude by thanking the commissioner and his fellow rapporteurs, but also by saying that this work, this document, bears my signature, bears the signature of the five star movement, but it contains the names of all the 120 million european citizens for whom it was written. our commitment, our dedication and our work have been, are and mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the figures on poverty in the european union are very worrying, and the austerity policies of recent years have exacerbated them: 119 million people in the european union, about 25% of the total population, are at risk of poverty and social exclusion, and to this must be added the high rates of unemployment, especially among young people. one of my first initiatives as a member of the european parliament was to ask the commission about the plight of millions of european citizens who are unable to meet their basic needs. the minimum income of citizenship is one possibility, although it varies with varying degrees in the various member states. europe must be able to build a common welfare system based on the centrality and the role of each european citizen. an integrated poverty reduction strategy, based on objective indicators and with a clear timetable for implementation, is needed to ensure that the europe 2020 targets are met.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ten years after the last update of the legislation on carcinogens, we are finally making progress. the work of the rapporteur, mrs ulvskog, is truly remarkable. with the agreement reached at the trilogue, we can say that we have added a new element to the fight against cancer, which remains the second leading cause of death at work in europe, as commissioner thyssen rightly pointed out. in dealing with many substances affecting different production sectors, we have been obliged to make an effort to ensure the balance of the various interests at stake, starting of course with the health of the workers. it will be essential to ensure that the rules are properly implemented, involving the social partners. a good example is the nepsi agreement, an excellence in social and sectoral dialogue. the health of workers is not to be taken lightly and we will therefore continue to do our part as a european parliament.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we too support this commission proposal because it actually improves the protection of workers at the workplace against exposure to carcinogens and mutagens. we therefore also support the proposal by the empl committee of the european parliament to include substances which are harmful to the reproduction of workers in the scope of this directive. we must remember that we are talking about substances which have a threshold effect and therefore, in fact, even minimal exposure to these substances creates a not negligible risk for those workers to develop cancer diseases in the course of their lives. unfortunately, the data is alarming, as you said before: 53% of all deaths at work are attributable to cancer, but there are 100,000 or more cases in the european union. so we are faced with a real health emergency, which must see us engaged with the utmost effort, without any uncertainty or hesitation. until now, unfortunately, the experience of the workers has preceded scientific research: this has happened in the coal industry, it has happened in the asbestos industry but also in the handling of radioactive substances. enough now, the workers can't be treated like guinea pigs. so we invest in finding innovative solutions, alternative solutions that can protect workers and their families from the curse of cancer.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am convinced that one of the most important objectives for the european institutions and for this parliament is that of work: the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of life of the people of europe, and i am pleased to see that the commission is now proposing a number of measures to improve the quality of life of the people of europe. there 's no doubt about it . exposure to carcinogens is the leading cause of illness and death among unprotected workers. i would also like to stress the risk to pregnant workers and all workers if they are exposed to endocrine disrupting mutagens. the principle of the precautionary approach is therefore a sensible choice, apart from, of course, stressing the need to promote an assessment of the costs which have a heavy impact on health expenditure, but also on social expenditure.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, cancer is the leading cause of work-related death in the european union, at 53%, a very worrying figure in an advanced society such as ours, which should ensure the health of citizens and workers. the protection of health at work must indeed become a priority on the european agenda. i therefore welcome the revision of the directive on carcinogens and mutagens, as it is essential for better protection of workers. however, i believe that the precautionary principle should be applied more forcefully in our legislation. individual potentially carcinogenic substances not yet included in the exposure limits should also be assessed more closely: i think, for example, of endocrine disruptors. there is a need for closer cooperation between the european union and the member states, which should provide clearer and more comprehensive data to enable the union itself to promote best practice. finally, the scope of the directive should be extended to include toxic agents, which are treated too lightly in the directive on chemical agents, despite the fact that they are very dangerous to human health.
member of the commission. – mr president, once more, i would like to thank the rapporteur and the shadows for reaching a balanced compromise that will clearly make a difference for workers’ protection from now on. as always, we take note of your questions and remarks and, as i said, our work will not stop here. this legislative proposal is a first step in a series of forthcoming initiatives in this area. i am pleased that in june this year the council reached a general approach on our second proposal to amend the directive. this confirms the political commitment of both the commission and the member states to fight occupational cancer. i count on the european parliament to adopt its position on this second batch so that the interinstitutional negotiations should start as soon as possible. dear members of parliament, some of you mentioned diesel engine exhausts and that this is one of the 25 chemical agents evaluated that are of a major concern for causing occupational cancer. why have we not yet proposed an occupational exposure limit (oel)? diesel engine exhaust is a complex issue, in particular in terms of defining exposure and identifying adequate measurement methods. it contains different components depending on the type of engine used. identifying the engines that produce carcinogenic exhaust requires further analysis. the commission is continuing its efforts to find the most appropriate action, and has the intention to include diesel engine emissions (dee) in its forthcoming second phase consultation of the social partners with a view to considering to address dee in the fourth batch. work—related cancer is a real tragedy for workers and their families, and is at the same time a heavy burden for the whole of society. we now have a chance to make a real difference in people’s lives. the commission counts on your support on these legislative files that aim to further fight occupational cancer. i invite you also to continue our constructive cooperation. thank you very much, and congratulations on the results of the trialogue.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, speaking in this very room yesterday, the president of the european council, president tusk, said that protecting our external border is the cornerstone of resolving the migration crisis. there are many aspects to this, but the fight against irregular migration and people smuggling has been at the forefront of agendas of both the european council and the council for a while now. it remains at the top of our agenda even though we have seen a dramatic reduction of almost 70% in the number of irregular migrants since spring 2016. our aim is to ensure the effective control of our external borders and stem illegal flows into the eu. we are determined to break the business model of smugglers and reduce the high number of human beings losing their lives while crossing the mediterranean sea in unseaworthy boats and flimsy dinghies. to achieve these aims, we reaffirm our commitment to strong cooperation with international partners, as well as with countries of origin, transit and destination. on both the central and the eastern mediterranean migratory routes, the eu and its member states have taken decisive action to reach these objectives. since spring 2016, we have implemented the eu—turkey statement to address the flows from turkey into greece. we have taken a number of measures to reduce the irregular migratory flows, to break the business model of smugglers and human traffickers, and to advance the effectiveness of returns. at the peak of the crisis, in october 2015, 216 000 arrivals from turkey to the eu were registered over a period of one month. subsequently, average monthly arrivals into the eu in the period from april 2016 to september 2017 were reduced to 2 465. on the central mediterranean route, we commend the significant contribution made by italy, including on a bilateral level. over the summer, a number of initiatives were taken by the presidency, the member states and the commission to complement the bilateral actions taken by italy. i refer here in particular to the commission’s action plan of 4 july and the respective presidency implementation plan. let me highlight some of the achievements so far. we have intensified efforts to train the libyan coastguard so that the government of national accord can improve the control of its territorial waters. the extension of the mandate of eunavfor med operation sophia until 31 august 2018 enables us to continue this task in a sustainable way. in the eur 46 million eu trust fund programme for border and migration management in libya, adopted in july this year, about eur 30 million are dedicated to the training, equipment and maintenance needs of the coastguard. we continue to promote the development of local communities across the migratory routes in libya. under the eu emergency trust fund for africa, projects worth eur 42 million have been contracted for this purpose. since last year, we have more than doubled our financial support for the work carried out by unhcr and iom to provide adequate reception conditions for migrants and persons falling under the international protection mandate in libya, and to coordinate assisted voluntary returns from libya and niger to countries of origin. we wish to reinforce our support to the most vulnerable groups by setting up a voluntary resettlement scheme, as presented by the commission in september in its recommendation on enhancing legal pathways for persons in need of international protection. six countries along the central mediterranean route are among priority countries for resettlement, including libya. some member states have already submitted ambitious pledges. there are many more strands that we are working on. i think it is important to bear in mind that they are nearly all medium- to long—term measures, for which patience and resilience by the eu are required. another limitation we should take into account is the unstable political and security situation in libya, preventing our full presence in the eu delegation and eu border assistance mission in tripoli and in the field. we are working very closely with our libyan interlocutors to bring about change in this country. in addition, our aim is to intensify our cooperation and, based on the european council conclusions from 19 october this year, to rapidly establish a permanent eu presence in libya. let me mention some of the actions to fight people smuggling. in the framework of the malta declaration of 3 february 2017, we now have a very efficient system for the monitoring of departure points in third countries. furthermore, the identification, detection and tracking of suspicious vessels has improved. frontex complements the eunavfor med operation sophia, to which it provides solid intelligence. europol’s european migrant smuggling centre focuses its activities on the central mediterranean route in order to target and disrupt supplies to smugglers. in an effort to further disrupt the business model of people smugglers and human traffickers, the council introduced restrictions on the export and supply to libya of inflatable boats, also known as dinghies, and outboard motors. finally, the council adopted the eu’s priorities for the fight against organised and serious international crime between 2018 and 2021. this was done in may 2017. they will include the fight against the facilitation of irregular immigration. in conclusion, despite the encouraging developments mentioned, the eu remains vigilant on all migration routes and continues a comprehensive, pragmatic and resolute approach by using all the relevant eu policies, instruments and tools.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, the fight against illegal immigration and people smuggling is, and remains, one of the key features of our comprehensive migration policy. as outlined in the mid—term review of the european agenda on migration, the implementation of the action plan on smuggling adopted in may 2015 and of the measures to address illegal immigration remains a priority. we all know that while the irregular flows towards europe are decreasing overall, we have to remain vigilant. this is why we will pursue our actions to build a proper management of migratory flows to the eu to prevent irregular immigration and fight smugglers. to tackle illegal immigration along the central mediterranean, cooperation with the libyan authorities remains an important element. the training and equipment of the libyan coastguard prevents illegal immigration and helps save lives at sea. this year alone, the libyan coastguard brought back to the libyan shores more than 16 000 migrants. the eu has also engaged with the libyan authorities to allow international organisations, mainly the iom and the unhcr, to assist vulnerable migrants in libya before they embark to europe. as a result, this year the iom has assisted 8438 migrants to return safely to their countries of origin. the commission also supports the unhcr’s plan to evacuate vulnerable migrants out of libya for onward resettlement. we also continue to help sahel countries to better manage the borders and enforce their capacities in relation to the fight against migrant smuggling and trafficking of human beings. the niger project is very encouraging. more than 100 offenders have been arrested and brought to justice in the first half of 2017. more generally, in the first quarter of this year, we proposed a revision of immigration liaison officers regulation to support actions to counter migrant smuggling in third countries. this will allow exploiting the full potential of the network of european immigration liaison officers, who have been deployed in 12 priority countries to coordinate closely the work of member states on the ground. to prevent smuggling and illegal immigration, we also have to use all our leverage to improve the readmission rates of countries of origin and show more solidarity with africa to address the root causes of migration. to this effect, eur 2.85 billion has been made available by the eu trust fund for africa. the refugees who need protection will be offered alternative solutions to smuggling. by enhancing safe and legal pathways, persons in need of protection will no longer have to rely on smugglers and risk their lives to find protection in the eu. this is why the commission recommends that member states increase their resettlement efforts by at least 50 000 persons over the next two years. we are also exploring how we could enhance the legal pathways for migrants who are not in need of protection. the commission is ready to coordinate pilot projects with select third countries in 2018. moreover, to clamp down on migrant smuggling networks, member states need to increase their capacity to investigate this crime, for which timely and practical information sharing is key. national investigators must talk to each other and fully use the resources provided by the european migrant smuggling centre at europol. indeed, the european migrant smuggling centre at europol, launched in 2016, has shown substantial added value in providing operational support to member states in fighting smuggling. it has provided support and conducted proactive high—profile investigations against criminal networks, with 68 cases reported this year so far, and 93 cases in its first year of operation leading to 147 arrests in 2016, and over 167 so far. finally, we must address all the factors in our system that fuel irregular immigration, such as undeclared labour, by better enforcing the employers sanctions directive. to conclude, let me stress that we will continue to fight this ruthless business in order to save lives, to prevent irregular immigration, and to provide protection for those in need.
i would like to ask the commission and the council three questions about the battle to stop the arrival of forced migrants in europe. the first concerns the priority fight against smugglers, agreed with libya, niger and chad. we're starting to see the results. fearful of the nigerian authorities, smugglers dump migrants in the desert or lead them on roads where there is no water. the result is that the deaths in the desert increase exponentially, they don't reach the mediterranean. according to danziger, iom's head of central west africa, the number of deaths at sea has now doubled, to around 30 000 in four years. the second question concerns the libyan coast, where there is a gang war. how can we distinguish the smuggler from the militias or the coastguards that the union and italy train and pay for? according to the un high commissioner, the abuses in detention centers are appalling. the third question concerns guarantees for the assistance of the unhcr in libya. the high commissioner in tripoli said that assistance was very precarious. libya has not signed the geneva convention, nor does it have a memorandum with unhcr. the union is responsible for this africa which has been turned into our prison, for these deaths. i think we're gonna pay for the guilt we're staining ourselves with one day. i would like to say to mr salvini what you know: in the eu you have more support than you say you have.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, thank you for this debate. there seems to be a broad consensus on the need to step up the fight against smugglers and irregular migration. we are on the right track, but we have to remain vigilant and implement all actions to stem irregular migratory flow towards europe. we can assure that the commission will continue its work to save lives, to put in place safe and legal pathways, to fight smuggling and to protect our external borders and return irregular migrants. to that end, we will strengthen our cooperation with key third countries. at the same time, let me stress that we also need to make progress on managing migration within europe. in this respect, member states will have to notably streamline their return procedure, in line with the return directive. we also have to work on the reform of common european asylum system. as you know, there is no single, no simple solution. we have to work on all sides.

answer to a blue-card question. i believe that there are many differences between member states, but i do not think that the reforms being pushed by the european commission, which are very often aimed at wage devaluation in peripheral countries, are a right way to solve the imbalances within the eurozone. this is the policy that is being perpetrated. we have a truly scandalous level of underemployment, especially in countries like italy where labour market reforms have been implemented. the moment there is a reversal in monetary policy, we will see the usual imbalances of the euro area emerge, so it would be appropriate to put an end to these imbalances with concrete measures towards the currency area to make it optimal, which is very difficult.
on behalf of the enf group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are discussing the economic policies of the euro area. i believe that the only reform worth discussing in the euro area is the dismantling of maastricht. maastricht, what came after it and what was done in preparation for this treaty and for european economic and monetary union, are now the main problem not only for the southern states but for the whole of europe. the euro and economic and monetary union, by their very nature and by their very architecture, fuel differences not only between member states but also within the various social classes of the member states. this is borne out by the votes in various countries: that's what happened in germany, where the poorest and most defeated population of these east german policies voted for parties considered extremist. i believe that the time has come to sit down and think about how to dismantle this single currency, which is not working, and to put europe back on a path of growth and development in a harmonious way and in cooperation between sovereign states.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the report indicates that the rules of the stability pact must be interpreted intelligently. i say this because flexibility is the rule, not a nice concession. in recent years, the european semester has shown its limits, as macro data remain uneven. if we want to return to convergence, we must put economic growth, social inclusion and convergence at the heart of the semester. the rules of the pact and the single currency cannot, of course, solve the structural problems of the euro area on their own. it is therefore crucial that clear decisions be taken at political level. there are several: in particular, given the theme, a positive aggregate budgetary orientation of the euro area; a budgetary capacity for the euro area to support investment and an unemployment mechanism, the latter financed from the union's own resources, to avoid an excessive burden on national budgets; the commission's proposal is to re-think the institutional architecture of the euro area. this is also the time to recognise that during the negative phases of the cycle we need the possibility for the european union to run a deficit and to issue zero-risk government bonds. i say this because at this moment the risk is to decide not to decide and this could risk plunging us back into the crisis from which the exit has been laboriously started.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the economic policy of austerity has shown all its limits. achieving significant growth levels requires linking greater investment and structural reforms to the stabilisation of national budgets, and modulating intervention measures for individual member states. but, as president draghi said a few days ago, if the structural reforms are to be socially acceptable, they must be accompanied by inclusive economic policies with redistributive effects. the euro area remains short of investment. in some countries, investment has already exceeded pre-crisis levels, but in others it is stagnating or not progressing at the same pace, particularly in southern europe, where the unemployment rate, especially among young people, is a cause for concern. further measures are therefore needed to close the investment gap accumulated since the outbreak of the crisis. strengthening and making the youth guarantee programme more efficient, but also investing more and better in training, research, young talent and innovative start-ups are the essential coordinates of an effective economic policy in the euro area.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as a citizen and spokesperson for the five star movement in the european parliament, i am particularly proud to be able to present this ambitious but realistic report on the implementation of the environmental liability directive. there is a very close and very strong link between the fruit of this work and the reasons why i, along with millions of other italian citizens, are politically committed to changing the things that we believe are wrong, both in italy and in europe. one of these reasons, symbolized by one of the five stars of the movement, is precisely the protection and respect of the environment in all its forms, as a unique and fundamental asset for life and also for future generations. i am therefore very pleased that this commitment has been shared by my colleagues in the other political groups, whom i thank for helping to make the proposal we are making to the european commission even more ambitious and advanced. the first consideration to be made in the area of environmental liability is that the implementation of the directive, which has been uneven and superficial, has not achieved the desired results. more efforts are needed to make possible a standardisation of environmental liability rules in the european union and, to this end, a clear interpretation of the concept of significant environmental damage threshold and the introduction of standard administrative procedures for reporting threats of environmental damage are needed. we are particularly concerned that the directive should be updated as soon as possible, extending the concept of environmental damage and its scope of application, in particular with regard to the criteria for determining adverse effects on protected species and habitats, the risks of damage to water and soil, but also to human health and air. this concept should be updated in order to make it sufficiently effective and consistent and to keep pace with the rapidly evolving pollutants produced by industrial activities. we believe that the costs of repairing environmental damage borne by operators can be reduced by using compulsory financial instruments such as insurance or similar guarantees, which we call for. it is also appropriate to establish a european fund for the protection of the environment against industrial damage, governed by the directive, to deal with the risks of insolvency and only in cases where the financial guarantee markets fail. this fund would also be useful in cases of environmental disasters caused by industrial factors when it is not possible to identify the operator responsible for the damage. on the other hand, action is needed on the prevention side, with information, awareness and accountability actions based on the 'polluter pays' principle. the committee also calls for the introduction of a system of civil liability for damage to human health and the environment. the same is true of the proposal to set up a register for operators carrying out dangerous activities and a financial monitoring system to ensure that operators are solvent. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of accidents. we also believe that citizens should play a non-secondary role in the system of environmental responsibility. therefore, they should be provided with adequate means of complaint, both to call for action by the competent authorities and by introducing mechanisms for collective redress for breaches of union environmental law. we also call for the adoption of a system of compulsory secondary liability which extends liability to those who buy a company which causes damage. all this, as well as the proposal to set up independent authorities with management powers, we believe can help to protect the environment and the health of citizens.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the need for the implementation of the environmental liability directive has been felt for some time. i come from a wonderful land, for centuries called the "land of work", which today is sadly known as the "land of fires", a land poisoned by the burial of toxic waste from companies all over europe, and especially from northern italy, which for decades have been using the illegal disposal services offered by organized crime to eliminate, at low cost, the waste of their production activities. first of all, the definition of environmental damage needs to be reformulated to extend its scope to include fauna, flora, air and landscape and to extend the objective responsibilities to other dangerous activities not currently envisaged. rules should be introduced to facilitate operators and insurance companies in order to increase the spread of an insurance scheme for environmental damage. finally, the provision of a more adequate financial control system and the establishment of a national and european register for operators carrying out dangerous activities could also improve the framework for guarantees for environmental damage.

author. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, we wanted to start a debate on the subject of compulsory vaccination because recently in italy a measure was introduced for the compulsory administration of six new vaccines, which are added to the four already compulsory vaccines, for a total of ten compulsory vaccinations at present. the data available on the global vaccine action plan portal shows that this was done despite not facing a real epidemic emergency that could have justified such a coercive measure. the italian ministry of health justified this measure on the basis of measles incidence data from the first months of the year in italy; these figures were indeed worrying, also taking into account the fact that measles in italy still remains endemic. however, many parents are concerned about this drastic decision by the italian ministry of health because they did not understand why, if there was an emergency for measles, no specific measure was taken to combat measles alone. they did not understand why the obligation was extended to ten mandatory vaccinations and, unfortunately, what aggravated the fears of the parents was the fact that such a sensitive issue, which concerns the health of our children, was brought to the centre of the political debate and treated as if it were two opposing fan clubs, with obvious instrumentalisations that we find very dangerous. that is why we wanted to discuss it here in the european parliament, outside the national context and outside the time of increased media attention, so that we could discuss it calmly in the interests of those concerned parents. the majority of citizens, and we with them, recognize the importance that vaccines have had in reducing, and in some cases eliminating (think of smallpox), the incidence of serious infectious diseases. however, those same citizens, and we with them, want above all that medicines, especially when administered to healthy people and especially children, be effective and safe. citizens want to know what the real risks are for their children when they agree to vaccinate them and the role of the institutions should be to provide this information in a clear and transparent way. we therefore believe that policy should be concerned with making all regulatory bodies, such as the european medicines agency and the national regulatory agencies, independent and free from the pressure of the (profit-seeking) pharmaceutical industry, and that they should be able to express their opinions on a purely scientific basis. we know that this is not always true and it does not help that relationship of trust with the institutions that is the basis for achieving the goals of national vaccination plans. because, for those vaccines whose efficacy and safety have been tested, the question then arises as to what strategy to adopt to achieve greater vaccination coverage and, if we look around, we see that most member states, including those with the greatest economic and social development, have adopted an approach based on persuasion and accompanying families to vaccination, and not an approach based on compulsion. we therefore ask the commission: is it possible to say from the information you have that a coercive approach based on mandatory vaccination is more effective than an approach based on active recommendation and informed guidance of families to vaccination? question number two: can the fact that the obligation to vaccinate a total of 10 children aged 0 to 3 years is unprecedented be considered a valid reason for invoking the precautionary principle? and to finish: in the context of the priority of industrial strengthening contained in president juncker's letter of intent, juncker himself indicated a joint action plan on national vaccination policies. we wonder how vaccination policies can be a means of strengthening the internal market and industry, because we believe that health should be completely outside the logic of the market.
member of the commission. – madam president, vaccination is one of the most effective public health measures. vaccination saves lives. vaccination protects our societies, reduces illness and helps achieve long life expectancy rates. vaccination not only leads to better public health outcomes, but it is also beneficial from a socio—economic point of view. before vaccines existed, many children would die young or be crippled for life. our generation has no memory of this. thanks to vaccination, such diseases have almost – i stress almost – been eradicated. as president juncker mentioned in the state of the union speech, today in the eu children are still dying from diseases such as measles that can easily be prevented with vaccines. this is unacceptable. so i want to thank members for raising this major interpellation on a subject of great importance to all of us. vaccination programmes have become increasingly fragile in the face of the low uptake of vaccines, vaccine hesitancy and vaccine shortages. many people in europe live and work in different member states throughout their lives and have trouble in comparing vaccination calendars and vaccinating their children on time. each country in europe has its own vaccination schedule. they are the result of long traditions and therefore vary widely across the union. some countries opt for mandatory vaccination and it is their legal right to do so. honourable members, i would like to address each of your questions. the first question is whether the obligation to carry out the 10 vaccinations for young children should be considered a reason to invoke the precautionary principle. first, 12 member states currently have at least one mandatory vaccination in their national vaccination programmes and some have many more. italy is one of seven member states that prescribe between 10 and 14 mandatory vaccinations in their vaccination programmes. as such, the new italian law does not constitute a so—called precedent in europe. the precautionary principle can be invoked when there is a suspected danger to human health and scientific knowledge does not permit an evaluation of the situation and of the risk. in the case of vaccination, we have scientific evidence—based knowledge on the benefits of vaccination. in this context, when considering vaccination programmes, it would not be appropriate only to take into account the small risk of potential adverse reactions to vaccines while ignoring the solid evidence—based benefits of vaccination. it would be misleading, in fact, at a time when people in europe are dying from measles – a disease that should have been eliminated long ago because the european union had obligations to eradicate measles by 2014, but we are not there. we need to strengthen our approach to vaccination. we need to encourage everyone to be vaccinated and protect the most vulnerable in society, leaving no one behind. moving to your second question: can the commission gather evidence on the effectiveness gap between mandatory and non—mandatory vaccination policies with regard to immunisation rates? the commission can play a key role in facilitating the collection, analysis and dissemination of evidence—based research on the best ways to increase vaccine coverage. to this end, we will work closely with the european centre for disease prevention and control and the member states. some studies show that, in the case of healthcare professionals, mandatory vaccination has indeed increased vaccination uptake. our studies point to mandatory vaccinations not being decisive in determining childhood immunisation rates. as such, more data is needed to understand if, and how, changes in vaccination policies have influenced immunisation trends. further research would help us to better appreciate the relationship between voluntary and mandatory vaccination programmes and vaccine coverage. i do not want to enter into a discussion on the benefits of voluntary versus mandatory programmes. they are all working towards the same goal of improving health. to do so, we need to analyse the implementation of the national programmes. do we have appropriate surveillance in place? is data available and used to inform future vaccination policies? how are targets met and what are the attitudes of health workers? that is very important. these are some of the issues we need to look at. finally, your third question: how can the eu coordinate action to improve the effectiveness of vaccination policies and increase immunisation rates? as you will know from president juncker’s letter of intent to the parliament, the commission intends to present an initiative to support member states in strengthening cooperation on vaccination. our aim is to help counter vaccine hesitancy and increase vaccination coverage, address shortages and prepare for emergencies, ensuring cooperation between member states, involving stakeholders and ensuring a comprehensive research agenda on vaccination. we will work closely with a broad range of stakeholders from the health workforce, industry, academia, ngos and patients’ organisations. in addition, next year i intend to launch a new joint action with member states. this action builds on the results of the discussions with stakeholders that i held earlier this year. i hope it will pave the way towards a shared vision to improve vaccination coverage in the eu. this action, which will be co—financed by the health programme, will focus on the convergence of national policies on vaccination schedules and the evaluation of the effectiveness of vaccination policies. the aim is to increase intersectoral cooperation, promote cross—border interoperability and increase the consistency of communication on vaccination. together we are working, first, to increase trust and confidence in vaccines, which is very important, through vaccination programmes and health systems, and to enhance the effectiveness and sustainability of vaccination programmes and improve electronic vaccine registries. these efforts must be underpinned by effective communication and enhanced public engagement. we need to foster an understanding of the importance of vaccination as a key tool for preventing diseases. this issue is one that affects us all, irrespective of borders or nationality. it is one we must address collectively and strategically. i count on members to support these efforts and help increase vaccination coverage in europe.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the spread of the disease, and it is therefore proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of vaccines. do we or do we not agree that conveying messages that are outdated, patently false and lacking scientific validity is a way to create confusion and alarm that lowers immunization rates? on behalf of the enf group. mr president, the true lungs of the mediterranean, the posidonia herbaceous plants convert carbon dioxide into oxygen and are therefore vital for the survival of all species. but today, about 34% of the grasslands are threatened by wastewater discharges, nitrogen discharges, invasive species such as caulerpa taxifolia, extraction of sea sands and ship anchorages. in view of these threats, should new marine protected areas be created that would exclude fishermen, who are the ones most often blamed for the destruction of posidonia? i believe that this is a simplistic and ineffective solution because trawling cannot, in principle, harm the posidonia grassland. why would you do that? because trawling is prohibited within three miles of the coast in france and above a depth of fifty metres in italy and spain. the grasslands are less than three miles from the coast and less than fifty metres deep, which means that they are not suitable for trawling. so rather than seeking to impose new constraints on fishermen, i would advocate investing in wastewater treatment. i think that is the most effective solution. for example, in the calanques de cortiou in marseille and cape sissi in toulon, the grasslands have been rebuilt as soon as wastewater treatment has been improved. of course, this solution must be applied throughout the mediterranean. i would like to remind you that the union for the mediterranean, from its creation in 2008, has identified the cleanup of the sea as one of its main objectives. this cleaning up therefore necessarily involves reducing the discharge of land-based pollutants into the sea. that is why, commissioner, it would be interesting to know what progress has been made in this area by the union for the mediterranean, whose projects are financed by the eib and the ebrd.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr commissioner, the posidonia oceanica is part of our heritage of biodiversity. it is not an algae, it is a superior plant and it is endemic to the mediterranean sea, where unfortunately its presence is decreasing. due to its particular sensitivity to environmental conditions, it has been considered a true bioindicator. posidonia, for example, combines some features of land plants with those of algae. it is precisely because of this peculiarity that it has had considerable commercial importance in the past. suffice it to say that, as it is not flammable, its leaves were used as insulation, for example on roofs, or to supplement certain animal feed, or to pack fragile objects, and it was even called the glassmaker's algae. so it has a great tradition in our mediterranean culture as well. its uses were not limited to commercial purposes, and the leaves were also used to treat irritation and inflammation. posidonia today is essential not only to protect coastlines from erosion, but also to preserve the health of the seas by helping to convert carbon dioxide into oxygen. the effects of climate change on marine and coastal habitats will inevitably have negative consequences also for human activities linked to these environments, such as fishing, and it is certainly human activities that we must act on. the commissioner has already given me some answers, i am thinking for example of coastal erosion, but also of large-scale construction. i remember when i was in the liguria region, i had to fight hard to prevent the construction of a small harbor that would have wiped out from liguria the only grassland of posidonia that still flourishes. so for these reasons we have to work and i wanted to ask the commissioner some questions, but let us say that in his introduction he has already answered.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, coastal marine habitats are essential for the conversion of carbon dioxide into oxygen, for the productivity of marine resources, for the protection of the coast and for other fundamental ecological functions that these habitats perform for humans and other species. however, these habitats are under severe anthropogenic pressures, either directly caused by humans or as a consequence of global climate change. posidonia oceanica, an aquatic plant endemic to the mediterranean sea, is one of the most resilient and productive species in the biosphere, is part of an important ecosystem for the conservation of biodiversity and plays a fundamental role in coastal defence, as it acts as a shock absorber to wave action and hinders the erosion of the coasts by the sea. nevertheless, its population has declined dramatically over the past two decades due to dredging and trawling, coastal development, eutrophication and other forms of pollution, climate change, and mechanical damage caused by boat anchoring. this species is characterized by very slow growth and, if destroyed, requires a long time to replenish itself. it is therefore necessary to ensure its rebuilding by financing european conservation programmes and by raising awareness in the other mediterranean countries so that they follow the example of italy, spain and france, where legislation already exists.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as in all post-industrial societies, the european population is characterized by a high life expectancy and a low fertility rate. there is also an increase in population in most urban areas and a decline in most rural and remote areas. these imbalances represent major challenges both for areas affected by depopulation, and southern italy is one of them, and for those affected by population inflows. cohesion policy has the right instruments to help tackle demographic change, but the esi funds need to give the problem a priority dimension and there needs to be greater coordination of european union instruments. a change of approach is needed if the european union is to integrate demographic aspects into all its policies in order to enable development, particularly in cohesion, employment, agriculture, the environment, research, employment, education, social policy and transport.

president-in-office of the council. – madam president, honourable members, we have witnessed a series of revelations in respect of tax evasion and avoidance over the last years: offshore leaks, luxleaks, swissleaks, the panama papers, and now the paradise papers. the council attaches great importance to such investigative journalism. not only have these revelations been instrumental in providing bases for informed policy-making, but they have also helped in creating political awareness. it might be the case that many of the practices described in the paradise papers are formally legal; however, we cannot exclude that certain schemes exist with the sole objective of reducing the taxes that would otherwise be due. this is unfair for those citizens and enterprises who are paying their fair share of taxes. against this background, member states are working very hard to change the legislation so that unwanted practices leading to loss of tax revenue would become illegal. here, we have to work in the context of 28 different systems of national law which, strictly speaking, fall into the area of national competence, but progress is being made. the council and the commission have worked hand in hand. the commission was quick to present new proposals to tackle the problems identified and the council swiftly found necessary compromises and has adopted tax legislation. the list of eu legislation that the council has adopted against tax evasion and tax avoidance over the last four years, under the unanimity rule, is impressive, especially compared to the previous decades. clearly, our response is picking up speed. just to name a few: the revision of the savings taxation directive and of the parent subsidiary directive, the adoption of four successive revisions of the directive on administrative cooperation in tax matters, the adoption of a new anti-tax avoidance directive and of amendments concerning hybrid mismatches, the adoption of a new directive on dispute resolution mechanisms and, lastly, the conclusion of eu agreements on automatic exchange of information with five ‘third countries’ to the european union. in some of the cases, for instance with regard to hybrid mismatches, the measures are just about to be implemented by member states. their impact on the tax avoidance practices highlighted in the paradise papers will therefore only be visible in a few years’ time. we have also adopted conclusions at the ecofin meeting in november 2016 setting out the process for establishing an eu list of non-cooperative third country jurisdictions for tax purposes. this important work is led by the council’s code of conduct group for business taxation and has been particularly intense over the past months, including in terms of dialogues with a number of countries. at this stage the code of conduct group is seeking commitments from jurisdictions to address the issues that were determined by our experts in the areas of tax transparency, fair taxation and the implementation of anti-base erosion and profit shifting standards. this work of promoting good tax governance standards is also carried out in coordination with the oecd and g20 agenda. the code of conduct group also continues to perform other important non-legislative tasks such as peer review of our member states’ potentially harmful tax regimes, development of new guidance to enable fairer tax competition between member states, dialogue with our immediate neighbours (recently switzerland and liechtenstein), and an update of the tax good governance clause to be included in eu agreements with third countries. all in all, these legislative and non-legislative initiatives just mentioned have been politically important steps for the eu. among the results achieved so far, we have seen bank secrecy de facto coming to an end, a shift of our policy focus from removing double taxation to tackling double non-taxation, development of new eu policy instruments to combat tax avoidance, and steps taken towards harmonisation of our national practices affecting the functioning of our single market. however, we cannot be complacent. more work will be needed, since tax planning methods are evolving constantly. we are currently examining several proposals, inter alia the revision of the mandatory disclosure rules directive, which would require tax advisers to disclose aggressive tax planning schemes to their tax administration. in addition, work is ongoing on several vat legislative proposals, where we hope to adopt the vat e-commerce package at the next ecofin meeting on 5 december. the presidency has also initiated a debate on the taxation of the digital economy, which should provide input into oecd discussions. we are also happy that the commission has announced that it will put forward a legislative proposal on this matter next spring. on this front, we will need the cooperation of our global partners so that international tax rules could be revised and adjusted to the reality of digitalisation. we are, in this respect, closely monitoring international developments. the council is taking the paradise papers revelations very seriously and is moving fast to deliver progress. a fairer tax system is what our citizens expect from us.
member of the commission. madam president, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, like all of you, i am deeply outraged by the recent revelations of the paradise papers, which follow other scandals of the same nature. every day, new news in the newspapers of all our countries sheds a little more light on what we can call a perfectly oiled global circuit of aggressive tax planning. a very aggressive tax planning system. i'm shocked, but i'm not surprised. we have long known that multinationals, wealthy taxpayers, consultancies and banks are working hand in hand to avoid taxation of huge swathes of income, and to do this they spare neither money nor imagination. we are not dealing with isolated incidents, but with practices that are systemic, global and organized. these aggressive tax optimisation schemes are all the more shocking as many of them - this remains to be verified - are apparently legal. we must therefore respond to a defect in the law by means of a new regulatory framework. if it is legal, as some claim, then the law must be changed and that is what i want to do with the help of this parliament. that is why, from the beginning of my mandate in the european commission, i have emphasised transparency, because i am convinced that transparency is our first weapon. it will put an end to the culture of secrecy and the feeling of impunity of those who practice and benefit from tax evasion. these are a bit like vampires, in a way: they fear nothing but light. we're the ones who have to make that light. today, there are three major proposals to be finalised to ensure greater transparency in our tax systems. as regards the first, i proposed to you last june new rules on transparency for tax intermediaries, that is to say lawyers, bankers and consultants who sell these tax optimisation schemes. the reason for this is purely commercial. if my proposal is accepted, they will have to systematically declare these arrangements to the tax authorities of the buyer's country. if these schemes are illegal, then the tax authorities can prosecute. if they are legal, the tax authorities will be able to identify the fault and correct it. i hope, and i say this with firmness, that the council will adopt the proposal on tax intermediaries within the next six months. it is an easy proposal, which is simple, and it is therefore primarily a matter of political will. there's no time to lose. there is really no reason to delay this adoption. in parallel, as you know, my colleague, vera jourová, has proposed more transparency on beneficial ownership in the context of the anti-money laundering directive. this information must be made public to combat the opaque structures that the paradise papers have revealed. today i have to admit that the negotiations are struggling to find a satisfactory answer and outcome. i deeply regret this and encourage the co-legislators to do everything possible to ensure that these new rules can be implemented as soon as possible. the citizens would not understand our inaction after the new warning shot of the paradise papers. the second proposal i am basically in favour of is to target companies through the publication of mandatory public information, country by country. what would this publication change? it would give every citizen a power of control and pressure that they do not have today. if this is achieved, we will have a publication accessible to all, citizens, the media, ngos, and you parliamentarians yourselves, of accounting and tax data which today are made available - this is already a progress - to tax administrations, but only to them. because it is through the pressure of the press, it is through the pressure of public opinion that we can change the rules. these paradise papers, like all these scandals, are both good news and bad news. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. i would like to say again to those who are hesitant in the council: i do not believe that transparency and competitiveness should be pitted against each other. on the contrary, i believe that transparency is a factor in the competitiveness of companies and that it is always in a company's interest to behave as a good citizen, as a good taxpayer ex ante rather than being denounced ex post in revelations or leaks. let us not be afraid of this publication of information country by country, i insist on this notion of publication. that's what i've been saying since the first day i was here. finally, this is my third proposal, we must have a european blacklist of tax havens that the member states have wanted to establish under their own responsibility, the minister said. i undertook to complete this list quickly after the panama papers scandal and the commission quickly made its proposal. i urge the member states to adopt it this time, not in six months, but at the next ecofin council of finance consumer markets, which has also increased possibilities for illegal and unfair practices. unfortunately public enforcement systems in most member states date back to the pre—digital era, and in all member states the reach of public authorities is limited by national jurisdictional rules. it was therefore high time that we modernised the public enforcement of consumer laws in the eu. we have authorities will get more leverage in their joint negotiations with multinational players. equipped with the power to accept traders’ commitments on remedies to consumers, as foreseen in the
