madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the agreement reached in the trilogue is moving in the right direction. in order to determine dumping, especially in the case of severe distortions of competition, it is essential to refer to costs and prices of production in third countries. the circumstances in which significant distortions can be inferred, which may affect free market forces, are defined and a new methodology for calculating anti-dumping duties is established, which takes account of both so-called micro distortions of prices and costs and macro distortions linked to, for example, subsidies and investments. in assessing unfair trading practices, due consideration shall be given to compliance with environmental criteria and, with reference to the standards of the international labour organisation, to compliance with labour law. finally, european industry and trade unions will be able to report distortions to the commission without any additional burden on them. this is a very good result for the european union, for european industry and for european citizens. i congratulate the rapporteur, mr cicu, on his report.
member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank all the members; it has been a very useful debate, and it has shown a very broad support for this new piece of legislation – a legislation that will protect our industry from unfair practices, from unfair trade, especially when it comes from market distortion. it does so in a country-neutral way. with this, we go away from our old system of dividing countries into non-market and market economies. the new methodology will look at all countries to see if there are distortions. this is not – and i would like to repeat that – this is not about giving market economy status to china. it never has been. the historical writing here should be revised a little bit: it has never been about this; it has been about respecting our commitments in the wto. china is not a market economy – if it were, it would be much easier. this is not about china – it is about any country. the anti-dumping methodology is to capture market distortion; it is linked to intervention in third countries or in sectors of the country. it will ensure a smooth transition to the new methodology for the measures already in place, the grandfather with a clear time frame, and we strengthen our anti-dumping instrument to increase our ability to capture the full magnitude of subsidisation by making it possible to address subsidies identified in the course of the investigation. also, as you have mentioned, it is taking into account social and environmental standards in a trade defence context for the first time. the draft reports for a country or for a sector where we find distortions will be made public – there are no secret reports. this is a trade defence instrument that is efficient, and where we comply with international obligations. trade is good; it leads to a lot of advantages – growth, investment, jobs. but trade has to be fair, and we have to have a fair, level playing field, and with this we will assure that we can contribute to this. the trade defence instrument is also an important piece of legislation. i know that there are two more trilogue plans in the coming weeks; i am sure that we will make good progress if we cannot finish this. we are closer to each other than has been insinuated here, and i am sure that – together with the council, the commission and parliament – we will do our utmost to get an agreement here before christmas. i would again like to thank the rapporteur mr cicu, his team and all the shadow rapporteurs, and all the teams in the trilogue for making this such a good piece of legislation, and i hope for a very strong endorsement tomorrow at the vote.
the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i think that after ten months of intensive work, which i believe has been fruitful and effective, we should remember that this is a very important step forward, but now we must look at the application of this new methodology after tomorrow's vote. so i would like to convey two thoughts to the commission and the commissioner. the first is that parliament's role will be to monitor the application of a methodology which is in line with the work we have done, which i think is extraordinary, in an effective, highly effective way. the other aspect, madam commissioner, is that your statements, which are extremely important, concern the fact that our companies and our industry should not have any additional burden in applying this methodology. so no bureaucracy, but above all, as you said, fairness and a chance to prove that there must be a guarantee, a protection, a defence of fair competition. of course, the application of this methodology cannot be less effective than the present one. so i think that if we continue to work towards these goals, we will certainly bring home an extraordinary result in terms of our project, our 2020 programme. i would also like to thank, and especially president lange, i would like to thank the members of the inta committee for the extraordinary work they have done, and indeed everyone for the contribution they have made in this capacity and to achieve an extraordinary and important result which is truly strong. so i think tomorrow's move will be the most decisive and effective.
member of the commission, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, i would like to start by thanking the rapporteur, mr ponga, for an excellent and very useful report. we are very glad to see that the arguments and priority areas set out in your report concur with the thinking outlined in the joint communication for a renewed impetus of the africa-eu partnership from may 2017 and the june council conclusions. the key priorities under the heading ‘resilience’, referring to improved political security as well as environmental, economic and social resilience, are duly reflected in our work with african partners. the resolution underlines the critical role of african youth in light of a significant population growth. more than half of global population growth between now and 2050 is expected to occur in africa. according to projections, sub-saharan africa needs to create around 18 million new jobs each year up to 2035 in order to absorb new labour market entrants, compared to the three million formal jobs created today. it should be a priority for both africa and europe to turn demographic developments into a dividend. we require inclusive development and sustainable growth for large-scale job creation. the leitmotiv of the fifth au-eu summit taking place on 29—30 november this year in abidjan, côte d’ivoire, will be investing in youth. more broadly, this will provide a critical opportunity for the eu and africa to build a stronger political partnership and increase our cooperation in the international arena, guided by: the un’s 2030 agenda and its sustainable development goals; member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank mr demesmaeker and the house for this opportunity to discuss with you the commission action plan for nature, people and the economy. as you know, the plan is the result of a comprehensive and participatory evaluation process and a fitness check on the habitats and birds directives. the findings of the fitness check were fully endorsed by the college of commissioners during an orientation debate in december last year. the conclusion was clear: there is no essential problem with the legal framework of the habitats and birds directives. it remains fundamentally sound, but there are problems with the application of the framework, and that is why we do not get the results that we want. there are funding shortages and we need more knowledge and more commitment. these are the key issues and that is why we prepared a strategic plan to address those gaps. let me turn to the specific questions you have tabled for today’s debate. your first question is about the links between the action plan and the 2020 biodiversity strategy. the action plan includes 15 concrete actions. these reflect the findings of the fitness check on the habitats and birds directives and address the main shortcomings revealed by this evidence-based evaluation. the aim of the plan is rapidly to improve the practical implementation of the directives, to accelerate progress towards the eu 2020 goal of halting and reversing the loss of biodiversity and ecosystem services, and to improve consistency between the habitats and birds directives and broader socio-economic objectives. implementation of the action plan is essential in order to make progress on target 1 of the eu biodiversity strategy, to – and i quote – ‘fully implement the birds and habitats directives’. it will also contribute to achieving other targets in this strategy, namely targets 2, 3 and 4, on restoration, agriculture, forestry and fisheries. most of the actions are being launched in 2017 so that the commission can report on their delivery before the end of its current term of office in 2019. we are aware that further efforts are needed to reach the 2020 biodiversity targets. the upcoming initiative to address the decline of pollinators is just one example of the commission’s response to the calls made by parliament to achieve the 2020 targets. since you also asked about the commission’s intentions from 2020 onwards, i can tell you that the nature directives provide a solid and long-term legal foundation for eu biodiversity policy. the commission plans to evaluate the eu biodiversity strategy and to report on its finding by 2020. the outcome of this evaluation will feed into thinking on the follow-up to the current eu biodiversity strategy, along with a global biodiversity framework for post-2020. let me now address question two, which concerns specific initiatives on the trans-european network for green infrastructure (ten-g), and also pollinators, access to justice and the illegal killing of birds. on ten-g, i referred to action 12 of the action plan which consists of providing guidance to support the deployment of eu-level green infrastructure, including through improving connectivity of natura 2000 areas by mid-2018. a strategy framework to facilitate a more integrated approach to green infrastructure will be proposed under the current multiannual financial framework (mff), providing some lessons for future inspiration. in addition, action 1(b) of the action plan will motivate decision-makers to invest in green infrastructure through the provision of deeper guidance and appreciation of the value of ecosystem services. on pollinators, the commission intends to launch a dedicated initiative to complement the action plan. on access to justice, as a previous legislative proposal did not prove successful in council, the commission adopted in april 2017 an interpretative notice, presenting and explaining the substantial body of case law of the court of justice on the subject, including on the nature directives. the commission also undertakes many measures to eliminate illegal bird trapping, killing and trade, in cooperation with international conventions, and enforces the provision of the birds directive prohibiting trapping, killing and trade. financial support is provided through the eu life programme funding. the commission assists member states in fulfilling their obligations under the birds directive, for example through the ongoing life european social enterprise training (euroset) project, which is developing action plans and management plans for 16 threatened bird species. the third question is about mainstreaming natura 2000 and wider biodiversity measures with other policies, especially with the common agricultural policy (cap). as regards the current funding framework, natura 2000 and wider biodiversity measures can be co-financed under several eu policies. as decisions on the allocation of eu funds under shared management rest primarily with the member states, they are not obliged to take up the opportunities for financing natura 2000 from the eu budget. actions 9 to 12 of the action plan aim to facilitate full and effective use of the financial resources allocated for biodiversity protection and natura 2000 sites in the period 2014-2020 under the various programmes and, where feasible, to promote increased allocations and uptake. in the context of action 9 under the action plan, the impact of the cap on biodiversity will be addressed in a specific evaluation scheduled for the second half of 2018. in accordance with the commission guidelines, such an evaluation includes an assessment of consistency between the various policy areas concerned. let me now turn to a specific issue which is also the subject of the third question: large carnivores. the return of large carnivores, especially the wolf, to areas where they have been absent for a long time represents a significant challenge, especially at local level. the action plan envisages a series of measures to help address these challenges. for example, the commission will update and actively promote, in all eu languages, its guidance document on species protection rules, which will include clarifications on flexibility within the existing legal framework. the commission will also bring together experts from different member states at bio-geographical level to address common challenges. this may also cover large carnivores whose populations are often transboundary. action 13 of the action plan specifically proposes providing further support through the involvement of local and regional authorities, in order to inspire dialogue and help find solutions at a local level. the commission will encourage the full and effective use of the financial resources under the european agricultural rural development fund (eardf) to support coexistence through rural development measures and, in this context, support can be provided to farmers for preventive measures aimed at mitigating the risk of damage by large carnivores to livestock farming. lastly, in question four, you ask about the next mff. here, i will be very brief as the commission is now preparing its proposals for the post-2020 mff. the indicators and the results from the ongoing financing period and the measures taken under the action plan will inform the debate and the reflections on the next mff. it is too early to give indications of how natura 2000 and wider biodiversity measures will be taken into account. i thank the members for their attention and i look forward to any further thoughts they may have on this broad, but important, topic.
i am speaking on behalf of the ppe group. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the natura 2000 guidelines are now almost exactly 25 years old. and if you look back over these 25 years, you can say: on the one hand, a lot has been achieved, but on the other hand, there are perhaps few guidelines in our legal texts that provide for such friction on the ground. this is because natura 2000 guidelines are very often top-down, meaning that member states feel that they are being forced to do something, and on the other hand there are still major gaps in the management of natura 2000 sites. that is why my group, commissioner, supports the action plan presented, because we believe it is a step in the right direction and because we believe that the natura 2000 guidelines must be implemented in a subsidiary and cooperative manner. subsidiary with those who are affected on the ground with the administrations in the member states and the regions , cooperative above all with those who are really affected, and these are usually the land owners. but let me return briefly to a question which you, commissioner, have just raised, namely the question of large carnivores, particularly the wolf. where the wolf returns today, it usually creates problems, and that's because it's not returning to a natural landscape, but to a cultural landscape - a cultural landscape where there are farmers, where there is breeding of small animals, where there is tourism, where there are people, and where then it usually leads to massive problems. i am afraid, commissioner, that we are not necessarily done with a multilingual information sheet and that we cannot necessarily satisfy the farmers by saying: 'ok, we will pay for this from the agricultural fund.' this means that the farmers can pay for themselves. that is not the purpose of compensation for damage that is undoubtedly occurring. i think we have to recognize that the wolf is no longer an endangered animal today, that there are certainly populations that are in good conservation status, and that perhaps it is our job to think about taboos, to think about the question: how can we manage wolves even where good conservation status has been achieved, and do wolves really need to return to europe in a widespread way? i think that's our job. only then will we be able to give a reasonable answer to those affected on the ground.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, common values such as human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and human rights are the cornerstone of the european union. each member state must therefore respect, protect and promote them. after the debates in january and september 2016, this is the third time that the council has been asked to intervene in this house on the situation in poland. the continued debate on these issues shows again that the protection and promotion of the rule of law and human rights are a constant challenge. this challenge requires unwavering attention and efforts across different policy areas. the presidency – and, indeed, all of us – agree that the protection of the rule of law, democracy and fundamental rights in our union cannot be taken for granted. we also agree that there is never a time to be complacent about the state of fundamental rights protection in europe. our core values are put to the test every day as we are facing multiple interrelated crises, be they in the area of migration or internal security. ensuring the rule of law is an absolute priority and has to be our joint commitment, of the member states and eu institutions together. equally, fundamental rights need to be upheld and defended as our best guarantee for sustaining stable, open and free societies. only one month ago, on 12 october, the justice and home affairs council had an exchange of views with the director of the fundamental rights agency, michael o’flaherty, on the priorities in the protection of fundamental rights. after this debate, the council adopted conclusions on the application of the eu charter of fundamental rights in 2016. these conclusions reaffirmed that democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights lay down the foundation of the european union and our societies. a few days later, on 17 october, the council held its annual rule of law dialogue. this year, the specific focus was on media pluralism and the rule of law in the digital age. let me assure you that the rule of law, including the independence of the judiciary and the balance of powers, are at the heart of our concerns, and the eu is not alone. our strongest partner is the council of europe, which is fully engaged in the promotion, protection and development of human rights and the rule of law. according to our information, the polish authorities are in contact with both the venice commission and the european commission, following the opinions and recommendations issued. the council has already been informed twice about the situation in poland by first vice—president timmermans, and i am looking forward to the update he will now present to us on the latest developments. from the council side, it is worth mentioning that on 11 july this year, the ecofin council adopted country—specific recommendations in the context of the 2017 european semester, of which one specific recommendation concerning poland addressed the issue of the rule of law. the issues raised go to the heart of our commitment to the union. we therefore trust that all sides will act responsibly and constructively to reach a swift solution that leaves no doubt about our core values.
first vice-president of the commission. – mr president, i want to start by thanking this parliament for its strong engagement on this issue, and especially the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, which i had the honour to update on the issue on 6 november. it is not my intention to repeat everything i said then, it would take too much time, but let me start by saying that an issue pertaining to the rule of law never affects only the country concerned: it affects the whole construction of the european union. that is the basis upon which i believe this parliament’s engagement is so important. i want to recall that on 26 july the commission adopted a third rule of law recommendation addressed to the polish authorities. this was necessary after four laws adopted by the sejm would have had a very significant negative impact on the independence of the polish judiciary and would have increased the systemic threat to the rule of law. two of the four laws were sent back to parliament by the president of the republic. the recommendation also recalled the situation of a systemic threat to the rule of law, resulting from the changes to the constitutional tribunal, which have led to a serious undermining of its independence and legitimacy as the result of its complete recomposition, contrary to the normal constitutional process for the appointment of judges. moreover, the polish executive persists in its refusal to publish a number of the tribunal’s rulings. unfortunately, the polish reply regarding the third recommendation did not announce any concrete measures to address the issues raised by the commission. we have now sent four letters to the polish authorities since july, inviting them to meet. sadly, these invitations were not accepted. i have not had the opportunity to talk to polish ministers about the issue. so our exchanges have essentially been in writing. that said, my invitation still stands, and i hope i can have a dialogue with the ministers of justice or foreign affairs as soon as possible. in parallel to the rule of law recommendation, the commission has also initiated infringement proceedings in relation to the polish law on the common courts organisation, which discriminates against individuals on the basis of gender. this is contrary to article 157 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union and to the 2006 directive on gender equality in employment. in our reasoned opinion, the commission also raised the issue that giving the minister of justice discretionary power to prolong the term of office of judges who have reached retirement age, as well as discretionary power to dismiss and appoint court presidents, would undermine the independence of polish courts. to be very clear: the minister of justice in poland is also chief prosecutor and the chief prosecutor now has full discretionary powers to appoint and dismiss presidents of courts. just let this sink in for a moment. the commission understands that, on the basis of this law, a considerable number of court presidents have already been dismissed. the commission is currently finalising its assessment of the polish authorities’ reply, with a view to deciding on the next step. president duda also presented two new draft laws on the supreme court and on the national council for the judiciary. the commission is now analysing these new draft laws very carefully and will follow closely the related developments. at this preliminary stage of our assessment, the commission already notes that certain issues in connection with the new draft laws could raise serious concerns. the commission will continue to assess these issues thoroughly and objectively, including in the light of the venice commission opinions which will be forthcoming in december. the commission is not alone in its assessment of the gravity of the situation. other critical opinions have been issued on the draft laws, not only in poland by the supreme court, the council for the judiciary and the ombudsman, but also at european and international level. i would refer to the recent opinions of the european network of councils for the judiciary and the consultative council of european judges. i would refer, too, to the preliminary observations by the united nations special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, who also takes the view that the independence of the judiciary is under serious threat in poland today, and has expressed serious concerns about the two draft laws on the supreme court and the national council for the judiciary. every member state carrying out judicial reforms must respect the rule of law as one of the fundamental values to which all member states signed up when joining the eu. it is up to the member states to organise their justice systems, including whether to establish a council for the judiciary, or not. however, where such a council has been established to safeguard judicial independence, as in the polish constitution, the independence of that council must be guaranteed, in line with european standards. so let me recall for the record what it is that the commission expects from the polish authorities to avoid further escalation. first, the polish authorities should restore the independence and legitimacy of the constitutional tribunal as guarantor of the polish constitution. second, the polish authorities should bring the law on the common courts organisation into line with union law by abolishing gender discrimination and by abolishing the minister of justice’s influence on judges through the retirement regime and the dismissal or appointment of court presidents. third, the polish authorities should bring the law on the national school of judiciary into line with european standards on the independence of the judiciary by eliminating external influence on assistant judges, notably, again, by the minister of justice. and finally, the polish authorities should bring the two new draft laws on the supreme court and on the national council for the judiciary, proposed by president duda, fully into line with eu law and with european standards on the independence of the judiciary and the status of councils for the judiciary. the legislative process on these two draft laws, which is about to commence, will provide a key test for the polish authorities, to show to the outside world whether or not there is willingness to respect the rule of law and take full account of the commission’s concerns and the forthcoming opinions of the venice commission. the commission is looking for real, constructive dialogue in order to redress the situation in poland with regard to the rule of law. this parliament’s support for our efforts is essential if we want to succeed.
i would like to say that i am very pleased that the commission has taken the initiative to present this report to the council. i am well aware that your government will try to pass this debate off as yet another attempt to harass poland. it's not true. we love your people and we love your nation. we have done everything possible, as vice-president frans timmermans rightly pointed out, to keep the dialogue with the polish authorities open, and we continue to do so today, as timmermans said, ready for dialogue. but dialogue is a two-way street, and if you're deaf on one side, it's hard to have a dialogue. we are always open to comparison, as long as the principle on which our living together is based is not called into question. the first principle: freedom, democracy and the rule of law. the european union is not a restaurant, where you go in and serve à la carte, but a living democracy, a community of values to which all its members are bound. i would have liked to have discussed this morning how to defend the rights of polish citizens in the face of the consequences of brexit, how to prevent so many young poles from having to leave their country to go abroad, and instead we are all hostages of the polish government, which does not come to brussels to deal with the problems of its citizens and which continues to provoke us with a closed-minded attitude. i ask the polish authorities: you say you represent the majority of poland - you got the votes, yes of course - but your fellow citizens never gave you any mandate to attack the independence of the constitutional court, to reduce the autonomy of the judiciary, so why do you do this? the truth is that your attempts to undermine the independence of the judiciary are a weapon of mass distraction from the difficulties you have in government. you lied to your constituents and you don't want to confront the real issues. but behind your plans there is something else, something deeper. there is contempt for liberal democracy, hostility to human rights and constitutional rules, the cult of the law of the strongest, and seeing the streets of warsaw on saturday guarded by the squads of the extreme right reminded me of the darkest pages of european history. to all poles, to those who oppose this government today, but also to those who voted for it, to all poles, i say that we will not leave you alone. the socialist and democratic group and its polish delegation stand by the polish people. we are not against poland, we are against deviating from the linear path of the rule of law. we want this path to be corrected. we want poland to live fully as a central member of the european union. answer to a blue-card question. it is ridiculous to compare the situation in malta with that in poland and to compare the situation of the maltese prime minister, who has always shown his willingness to engage in a concrete dialogue with the european institutions, to be present in the european parliament and to correct the shortcomings and problems in malta, with the situation in poland. so let's not compare! this is another weapon to distract from real problems. to equate malta with poland is a false historical statement.
i would like to address my polish colleagues, and in particular the representatives of the ruling party. i would like them to understand that we are not punishing a member country, that we are respecting the multiple sovereignties that the union will increasingly have to be made up of. the reason why we are going to adopt a third resolution on poland is to recall together the reasons which unite us, the legal bases which all the member states have subscribed to. i mean rule of law in the deepest sense of the word. i would ask you to read recital e to the resolution. the rule of law is distinct from the rule by law. rule by law means government by law, where law is the act used by those who exercise power on the basis of a parliamentary majority. the rule of law is a notion that includes a substantive concept of law, such as a set of fundamental rights, the independence of the judiciary, the separation of powers, free expression, the rights of refugees and women. whoever wins the election obeys this set of rights, not grants them. once elected to this parliament, we all have the task of representing all the citizens of the union, without distinction of nationality or constituency, and at the same time the primary duty to ensure that the foundations of citizenship, fundamental rights and freedoms, are fully guaranteed. in asking for article 7 (1) to be activated, we are asking only for this commitment to be honoured and for us to take responsibility for continuing the open dialogue with the government of a member state. on the other hand, it is the only instrument that the treaty has given us as a parliament.

mr president, we are talking today about the rule of law in poland. if you want to play football you abide by the rules of the game and you accept the fact that there is a referee who makes sure that those playing the game abide by the rules. if you join the european union, you do this as a sovereign decision. you sign and ratify a treaty. once you have signed and ratified a treaty, the rules of that treaty apply to you. then if you simply say "i am a sovereign nation, i don't care about the rules", it's like saying "i want to play football but i will determine for myself which rules i will apply and which rules i will not apply". then you cannot play football! the european union cannot function if member states start saying "we pick and choose which rules we have adhered to, are applicable to us, yes or no". i think this should be the starting point of our debate. in particular, in article 2 of the treaty, all member states have said very clearly that they will respect the rule of law. one of the fundamental elements of the rule of law is that you accept and maintain a separation of powers. an independent judiciary is essential in the rule of law. you can't pick and choose and use the argument that you have the majority to simply ignore the law. you can use that majority to change the law. you can use a majority to change the constitution if you have one, but you cannot simply say "i ignore it because i have a majority". you cannot use democracy against the rule of law and this is the argument that is often used in this debate. just imagine, i would say to those of the european conservatives and reformists group (ecr) who still remained in the room, just imagine the shoe were on the other foot, and in this parliament a majority would say, "hey, we have the majority, we don't care about the rules of procedure of parliament, we have the majority, we dictate what happens!" in what position would you then be? the rights you now claim for yourself as a majority might not be granted to you once you are no longer a majority. this is a fundamental problem for europe because, as some of you have said, once you have destroyed the independence of the judiciary, even if you lose an election, the new powers that be will have no other option but to try and reverse it and then it becomes a perpetual machine of not respecting the rule of law. this will never stay limited to one member state. if it happens in one member state it affects the union as a whole, and this should never be disregarded. had mr legutko still been here i would have said to mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to greet commissioner bulc and commissioner šefčovič. we're finally starting to work on the mobility package. the time is right, road transport is, as has been said, the most widely used mode of transport in europe and action is needed to prevent situations leading to distortion of competition, but also to address environmental and road safety issues. we are well aware that road transport is plagued by serious problems, such as undeclared work and social dumping, and it is our task to provide the right solutions. in europe, the cost of labour varies from country to country. many companies take advantage of this to enter national markets at the expense of workers, their safety and with very serious repercussions on the national labour market. in italy, to take an example i know, under the present conditions many transport companies have to close because they cannot compete in labour costs, with many companies in other countries taking advantage of regulatory loopholes to offer the same work at cheaper costs. abuses and distortions must be corrected. i would also ask everyone to pay close attention to the definition of cabotage, because that is where the future of many small and medium-sized transport companies is at stake.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome the commissioners. as has been said on many occasions, we are very much in favour of the ageing of the traditional transport system, which is still based on technology that is over a century old. however, no matter how much we try in terms of research and technological applications, we will not be able to make co2 emissions acceptable by using a combustion engine and going beyond euro 6. we have to be realistic. so we have to decarbonize the industry, we have to move away from fossil fuels, but we have to do it in a smart and thoughtful way, because the decisions we make today will have an impact on the industry for decades to come, with important social and economic consequences. we cannot afford to make radical changes, as has happened, for example, in the case of biofuels, and we must prevent unscrupulous companies from tampering with their products in order to make them falsely conform to existing directives, as in the case of volkswagen, which we unfortunately know. the transition to alternative propulsion systems for vehicles cannot be one-way, but must take account of all new technologies and develop them in an equivalent way. this means that it is good to push for electricity, but let's not forget about hydrogen and other types that are already widely tested, because until the source of electricity generation is totally sustainable, we cannot talk about true decarbonization. until the environmental cost of producing an electric vehicle over its entire life cycle is actually lower than that of a conventional vehicle, we cannot be satisfied and talk about a real energy transition.

president-in-office of the council. – madam president, first of all, i would like to thank parliament for the interest it is taking, through this question and its resolution, in the new environmental implementation review initiative. i can confirm that this interest is fully shared by the council. in terms of addressing implementation gaps in eu environmental legislation and policy, this initiative has a high potential. in addition to contributing to the environment ministers’ input into the european semester, the environmental implementation review process is meant to become a distinct and consistent process. it would involve several important elements: the preparation of environmental implementation review country reports and bilateral discussions with the member states, as well as the identification of common issues and their discussion in the environmental council. on 28 february 2017, the environment council held its latest exchange of views on greening the european semester. the economic system depends largely on the availability and sustainable use of limited natural resources. keeping this in mind, greening the economy and advancing the transition towards a resource efficient circular economy becomes essential to secure future competitiveness and long-term sustainable and inclusive growth. in this context, ministers also discussed the commission’s communication on the eu environmental implementation review. they welcomed this initiative as a useful tool to help improve implementation of eu environmental policy and legislation at national level and contribute to the greening of the european semester. in doing this, they underlined the need for national findings to be based on sound scientific data. ministers also welcomed the opportunity for member states to engage in dialogue and cooperation with the commission and among themselves, peer to peer, with the aim of reflecting on their respective priorities, addressing common challenges and sharing best practices. as regards the specific questions that you have raised at this early stage of the environmental implementation review process, i would like to limit myself to the following comments. we agree with the identified root causes of the implementation gaps and we are willing to address them further. it is to be expected that the different strands of the implementation process of the environmental implementation review, and in particular the dialogue with the member states on the basis of the country reports, will allow us to carry out a structured dialogue in council. member states are generally responding positively to the environmental implementation review process. bilateral dialogues have already taken place in five countries since march this year. these countries are belgium, the czech republic, estonia, luxembourg and slovakia. i also encourage other countries to organise action-oriented country dialogues and to hold forward—looking debates on environmental challenges. i trust that these dialogues will be inclusive and that the relevant stakeholders get an opportunity to contribute as appropriate. the current environmental implementation review cycle is already very ambitious and covers a large number of complex and very significant areas. in terms of broadening the scope of the environmental implementation review to other policy areas in the future, we find it essential that environmental challenges are tackled in a comprehensive manner and that all relevant policies are taken into account. the real added value of the environmental implementation review will come from in—depth impartial analysis. however, if broadening the scope is considered, due attention should be given to avoiding a disproportionate administrative burden. as regards the involvement of the council – although i cannot speak on behalf of future presidencies – currently, the idea is to bring the structural problems and common challenges identified in the course of the two-year period to the attention of the council. the council would then discuss environmental implementation review-related issues at regular intervals in line with the cycle, also ensuring complementarity with the discussion on the greening of the european semester and the relevant post—2020 strategies.lastly, in many areas environmental policy is interlinked with other domains. in addressing the cross-cutting issues, we should avoid working in silos and ensure that all relevant parties are involved in discussions. the respective dialogues should not be held at council level only, but start from expert groups and other working formations. hence the effort of engaging colleagues from other policy areas is welcome at all levels in order to achieve a coordinated and informed outcome. i thank parliament once again for these questions.
member of the commission. – madam president, i want to say how glad i am to take this point on behalf of commissioner vella. commissioner vella wishes to thank the author and all of the people involved in the interest in the environmental implementation review (eir) and for your support for this important initiative. the eir puts implementation in a broader context with a view to finding practical solutions by looking at integration with other sectors and by identifying possible root causes for implementation challenges. this helps to improve the knowledge and sharing of good practice. the main goal of the eir was to draw attention to the need for improved implementation in order to attain the european union’s environmental objectives. the environmental targets and deadlines which need to be achieved by the member states are included in the legal obligations set out in the environmental aquis and are being monitored per directive and regulation. the eir encourages cooperation, dialogue and the search for solutions involving a wide range of stakeholders at national level. it is not feasible, but neither is it the commission’s intention, to rely on a name-and-shame exercise. this could, at any rate, jeopardise the achievement of goals. the commission has included in the country reports both good practices and good examples, as well as implementation challenges. the data used in the country reports are comparable. the commission’s ongoing initiative in streamlining reporting requirements in eu environmental law is expected to improve the quality and completeness of the data significantly. the eir takes a holistic approach, reflecting the spirit of the sustainable development goals. and the commission is taking steps to ensure that the second review cycle will be even more comprehensive by including chemicals, industrial emissions and the implementation of climate change policies. the nexus with climate change and other policies will also be developed as much as possible. the commission encourages member states to organise national dialogues under the eir in a cross-sectoral approach. the first five countries’ dialogues succeeded in doing so, and further dialogues are being planned. the commission has also asked member states to involve all relevant stakeholders during their country dialogues. we firmly believe that discussions will result in tailored solutions and mount some pressure to fill in the implementation gaps that are identified in the eir reports. the eir inspires learning from good practice. on 7 september 2017, the commission launched a peer-to-peer tool with the committee of the regions. it is intended to support concretely the member states at all administrative levels to share experience and expertise. this will lead to a database of good practices. the eir has not changed the commission’s policy as regards infringements, and there is no formal relationship between the voluntary approach and the legal procedures. in most cases, the infringement procedures will run in parallel where necessary. however, if the eir succeeds over time in improving implementation, as is expected, fewer infringement procedures will be needed and, therefore, fewer resources will have to be spent on legal proceedings, and we should have enhanced environmental protection due to upstream and systematic solutions. i wish to conclude by thanking the author and all of the people that have been involved in drawing up this report.
the european union is leading the world in environmental protection, and so the regulations we have set for ourselves on air quality, water quality, waste management, and i could go on. but we must not only boast of having ambitious regulations, we must also be able to enforce them, which, unfortunately, is not always the case. this is essential not only for the union's credibility, but also for the protection of the environment and the health of our citizens, and also for the economic benefits. we see this very well, for example, with the circular economy impact assessment, the benefits in terms of employment and economic growth that effective and efficient waste management can bring. the commission has therefore put in place a tool to assess the performance of the member states in implementing environmental legislation. having a map allows us to understand how far reality is from the objectives set by law, the areas where we are still behind, why we are still behind, and then identify the causes, and what tools to put in place to achieve the objectives. you will understand that, first of all, data must be more comparable in order to facilitate the exchange of best practice, as we ask in the resolution. we must also have as accurate a picture as possible, including other elements in the evaluation. let's think about the energy efficiency resolution, the transport sector, climate change. i am glad to hear that there is already an opening, as the commissioner said, also because it is unthinkable today not to consider the impact of climate change. and now i turn to the council. this cannot be a mere exercise in style, but the member states must then make a concrete commitment to achieve the objectives, and we ask the council to make a concrete commitment to fully participate in the review and to take this instrument very seriously.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, we will support this resolution of parliament because we believe that the review of implementation is an essential tool for getting the most out of environmental policies in the european union, but also for defining and charting that path, those milestones that we need to reach the sustainable future in europe. however, we believe that all this can only happen if we really tackle the paradox of very strong european environmental legislation on the one hand and completely ineffective implementation on the other. then we need to do three things. first of all: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of sanctions which are really effective for those member states which fail to enforce the polluter pays principle. second thing: the infringement procedure mechanism is not functioning. they can't be the citizens who pay twice: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is not damaged, and that the environment is not affected. they must pay the people responsible, who are very often the environment ministries of the individual member states, who are sitting in their chairs, although they are responsible. third thing: we must put an end to the triangle of hell in which the polluting industry also funds representatives in the european institutions and in local and regional authorities who then appoint the directors of the control institutions. if these three things are not done, europe will never have a sustainable future.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, europe, as it is still imagined, cannot but take on the most affected human capital, wounded by inequalities and hence imprisoned by its many poverty. so inequalities create poverty, and fighting inequalities means giving everyone a plurality of tools that are essential to defeating them. the basic choice is therefore to ensure that the rights are enforceable. it is time for politics to take on the full responsibility of rethinking its development model, placing the issue of the dignity of persons and the value of human capital at the centre, without delaying the easy reading that links, in a cause and effect relationship, the impoverishment of opportunities to the economic crisis. so this is the time to decide not to contract public spending, but to reorient it to guarantee rights, to fight inequalities, to combat poverty. this is the time that leads us to generate a new sense of community within an idea of social cohesion that links the public chain to the actors of the territory, to think about new welfare models within the workplace and in the places of life, to respond to the demand for accessibility to new lifestyles, care and prevention, at every age and in every corner of europe, to allow every child to be able to grow in the awareness of being able to compete as an adult in a scenario that we want more and more generous of opportunities for everyone, imagining that they can build their own life project through work, certainly equally paid, but of quality and safety. in short, the europe of development and sustainable and inclusive growth can only start from here, from the europe of opportunities for all and for all.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, in his excellent report mr lópez has rightly pointed out that the crisis presents us with two major blocks of issues in relation to inequality: the first is social, the second is economic. over the years, some european countries have countered the crisis with senseless austerity policies, reducing social protection, reducing the effect and the amount of welfare available, in the idea that the economy would be divided up in this way, making the cost of labour cheaper, while competition from weaker parts of the world's population has prevailed. on the other hand, old, but already ineffective, redistributive instruments have also been broken. the systematic scandals over taxation, which has remained largely intact as an element of negative pressure on the poorest part of the european population, the working and self-employed, and has allowed companies, on the other hand, to escape from obligations and loyalty to the states, have destroyed the elements of cohesion which also guaranteed an adequate competitive capacity for the economic system. when work becomes precarious and unprotected and individual and collective rights are not recognized, productivity inevitably suffers. so what we are called upon to do today is to try to put in place fair, just redistributive policies to protect the weakest and to fight poverty. for this reason, i believe that a minimum income is the right tool, it is a universal tool that gives everyone the same protection and the same opportunities. then we must improve working conditions, because better working conditions make people work more. today, however, we are faced with a world in which those who work are penalized and forced to undergo conditions that inevitably affect the quantity and quality of their work.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i firmly believe that anyone who cares about the european union must insist that the priority is to reduce inequalities on the continent, not only inequalities between its countries, but also within them, starting from a basic concept: the european project and the political and economic integration of its member states and peoples must serve the objective of regaining sovereignty for decisions concerning the social and economic spheres. sovereignty that has been progressively eroded by the dynamics of uncontrolled globalisation and financial capitalism. the data clearly show that the crisis of recent years has had a dramatic effect on the growth of inequalities in their various forms: we have to look at the different types of people. the differences have increased more than proportionally for the weaker groups, and it is therefore imperative that the european union take charge of reviving a social agenda that can reverse this trend. in a few days' time, the heads of state and government will meet in gothenburg to conclude the agreement on the european pillar of social rights. we must be able to turn this solemn event into a real movement, capable of finally equipping the union with a social strategy adapted to the challenges of modernity. we are starting from concrete initiatives, not just from a list of principles. we are starting with the european institutions, applying a more extensive version of the quality framework for traineeships, including a guarantee of remuneration, and finally banning unpaid and low-quality traineeships in europe. i would also like to remind you that this parliament has proposed a framework directive on decent working conditions for all forms of employment. so let the european commission show us, also on this front, that it really wants a triple-a social europe.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the subject we are debating tonight, as has just been mentioned, should be the guiding principle behind all the work we do in this parliament. a parliament which, in my view, should put the fundamental rights of european citizens and the fight against poverty at the forefront of its initiative. unfortunately, we are faced with an unprecedented growth in economic, social and cultural inequalities, and this situation is at the root of the enormous difficulties and social malaise that european citizens are experiencing. it is enough to think that since 2005, income poverty has been steadily increasing and that, according to a report by oxfam, in 2015 there were 342 billionaires in europe and 123 million people, almost a quarter of the european population, at risk of poverty or social exclusion. regressive labour market reforms in several member states, including, alas, in my own country, have weakened workers' representation and bargaining power, leading to increasingly precarious working conditions and lower wages. social mobility has practically disappeared. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one. that is why i believe it is imperative to address social spending, to address the problem of poverty through family support, to ensure universal access to free health care and to introduce a decent minimum income for all. equally vital is the refocusing of public policies to promote employment and investment in infrastructure, as well as improving the quality and efficiency of education systems and accessibility to public services.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, after years of economic crisis, the fact that i have seen in my own group is that social inequalities threaten the future of the european project, erode its legitimacy and damage confidence in the european union as a motor of social progress. while brexit has opened a window of opportunity for europe, reducing inequalities must be a top policy priority, not only to tackle poverty or promote convergence, but also because it is the prerequisite for economic recovery, the creation of decent jobs, social cohesion and shared prosperity. equality and fairness are an integral part of european values. we need a genuine european pillar of social rights, which promotes upward convergence, and a deeper and fairer social dimension of the european union, economic and monetary, providing the citizens of the european union with the necessary legislative, institutional and financial instruments to ensure the social progress that must be the next stage in the process of european integration.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the import ban imposed by russia has deprived european fruit and vegetable producers of one of their main export markets and its extension until 31 december 2018 will cause further damage. for three years now, european union fruit and vegetable producers have been suffering significant losses, as they have no alternative outlets comparable to russia. i agree that the commission should promote studies on the effectiveness of the reorientation towards other markets and on the development of production, distribution and demand in the agricultural sector since the embargo began, but above all solutions that are of practical support to the sector must be found urgently, structural measures must be found. the fruit and vegetable sector should be supported by increasing the quantities eligible for aid under the new eu aid scheme, the level of compensatory aid for withdrawal from the market should be increased, giving priority to alternatives to free distribution, and, above all, it would be important to ensure that the deadlines for payments to farmers are shortened.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the rapporteur. the european parliament's recommendation to conclude a partnership agreement with new zealand was a positive one. new zealand, it was said, is one of our closest neighbours, sharing the same democratic values and principles, respect for human rights, and fundamental issues such as peace, security and the environment. a common culture and common sensibility, therefore, has made it possible to establish a close partnership with the european union and the member states, which has been embodied in common policy choices. i am referring to new zealand's contribution to un peacekeeping operations in bosnia, kosovo, sierra leone and afghanistan, to the training of iraqi security forces fighting daesh, to its role as co-sponsor of un security council resolutions on syria and the middle east peace process. the union's contribution to the implementation of the paris agreement is estimated at eur 5 billion. it is therefore good that this agreement has been concluded, which also includes the fight against terrorism, in particular commitments on the exchange of information on terrorist networks and groups, on methods of preventing, countering and combating terrorism, radicalisation and cybercrime, but also agreements on scientific, academic and technological cooperation. this is consistent with the opening of negotiations on the eu-new zealand free trade agreement, which must be conducted in a spirit of reciprocity and mutual benefit, taking into account the sensitivity of certain agricultural and other products. a major agreement, a coherent policy framework for the future, within which relations and cooperation on a wide range of issues will be further developed over the years, in the interests of the citizens of the union and of new zealand.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, new zealand is linked to the european union and its member states by a close and long-standing partnership and has already concluded bilateral free trade agreements with important countries such as australia, thailand and china. new zealand is a country with high standards of civilization that promotes sustainable production methods, particularly in the food sector, and has promoted global climate and emission mitigation agreements globally. but we must not make the same mistakes as in the past, because every free trade agreement involves some risk, especially for our agricultural and food production. the protection of european agri-food products, which are sensitive products and have already been put at risk by agreements such as ceta, must therefore be clarified as a matter of priority. new zealand is an important partner. the free trade agreement can bring benefits to both countries, but europe must be able to protect its assets and specificities with the utmost care.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with this text we have reached a political agreement to avoid a significant increase in the level of budgetary provisions due to the new approach to depreciation provided for in ifrs 9. in particular, we have achieved good results with regard to the so-called phasing-in. we have avoided the sudden increase in provisions for expected credit losses and the consequent reduction in the capital ratios of banks, especially small banks, and we have envisaged that these measures could be adopted with transitional provisions to prevent any unjustified impact on the system. moreover, such a transitional period should also provide an appropriate measure to avoid any procyclicality effects. finally, the text agreed by parliament and the council is appropriate to minimise the disadvantages for all those institutions using the standardised method compared to institutions using internal models. this is therefore an important measure to support, above all, the small banks, which are the main actors in investment in the real economy, and the small and mediumsized enterprises of our continent, which would have had greater difficulties in adopting these measures without these transitional provisions.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, to avoid a new crisis it is essential to reduce risks within the banking union and this is a precondition for the reform of the euro area. the introduction of the new international accounting standards ifrs 9 will bring major changes for banks, in particular on the crucial issue of credit risk and provisions. the new scenario will require increased interaction between risk management structures and administrative structures, and will imply the need for managerial choices and estimates, the desirability of a conscious attitude also on the side of credit demand and the consequent attention to customer information. this is therefore a major challenge for the banking sector, also in view of the risks in terms of future profitability and volatility. transitional provisions are therefore essential, especially for small banks, to prevent any undue impact of the introduction of ifrs 9 on the regulatory capital of banks in the european union, for example by allowing them to add to their core capital a part of the provisions for expected credit losses.

the commission's proposal for a regulation on the common organization of the market in cereals, which is to be adopted by the council on 1 january, is a very important one. the omnibus has in fact given us the opportunity to take action on the current structure of the cap, an opportunity which has been made possible mainly thanks to the determined and decisive contribution of the european parliament. the small adjustments and timid openings presented in the commission's initial proposal were certainly in the right direction, but they did not seem to be up to the challenges facing agri-food systems. that is why we felt it was our responsibility to give the citizens and farmers of europe answers that were more than just a touch-up, with an ambitious initiative, through which we were able to strengthen and supplement the ideas offered by the commission. the scale of the innovations introduced in the field of simplification, risk management and market measures make this work a genuine medium-term reform of the common agricultural policy. a mid-term reform with a double value: on the one hand, it is a response to the now certain postponement of the cap reform to the next european parliament and the next commissioner. on the other hand, it has been able to set a starting point for reflection on the future of agricultural policies, also providing a significant direction for the recent commission communication on the cap post-2020. the large number of amendments tabled by parliament has generated intense debate, but the balance achieved is welcomed by all european farmers and is a good example of the work done by our three institutions, in full compliance with the ambitious time-limits initially set by the committees responsible. i would therefore like to thank the estonian presidency, commissioner hogan and his services, and all the shadow rapporteurs and colleagues for the extraordinary work, including from a procedural point of view, in having succeeded mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the rapporteurs. i am personally very pleased with the positive results we have achieved with the omnibus regulation. the first is that we have been able to speed up the approval procedure so that we have the operational regulation as of 1 january, and this is proof that when there is the political will, bureaucracy can really be simplified, and i hope that this approach will become more and more frequent. the second positive result is that with the omnibus regulation we are implementing a small reform of the cap which is in the process of being implemented: we are going to correct, adjust, those rules that have proven to be lacking, complex and inefficient, thus moving towards supporting farmers, improving the agro-food production system and protecting the environment. the third positive result is that the regulatory framework has been improved after listening to the criticisms and suggestions of european farmers, those who apply it and live it every day, and this is important because the institutions need to listen more to the citizens and to those who work in the specific sector. we have already seen that decisions simply taken from above do not work, and we want the same shared approach to the definition of the new cap.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the agreement reached offers the prospect of real reform in the medium term: the definition of an active farmer has been retained, the role of young farmers has been enhanced, direct payment schemes and greening have been simplified. access to insurance instruments, mutual funds and income stabilisation mechanisms for farmers is also improved. the agreement reached on the omnibus is therefore an important achievement for european agriculture, and i congratulate the rapporteurs dess and de castro on the work they have done. the main part of the market measures was given greater force by the contractual arrangements of the op and aop farmers. however, this is not enough: solutions must be found to ensure a more equitable sharing of risks throughout the agri-food chain in order to combat unfair practices. we do not yet have european legislation, and it is essential that european competition law takes account of the specific characteristics of agriculture in order to ensure the well-being of european producers.
in writing. finally, we have achieved positive measures to simplify and protect our farmers. the common agricultural policy should now be more closely geared to the needs of farms. i am very pleased with the work done by our group, especially by mr marco zullo, and with the fact that our amendments to the original proposal were adopted by a favourable vote. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one. the result is that producer organisations and associations of producer organisations will be able to derogate internally from the competition rules governing the production, sale and processing of agricultural products, in order to give them greater management autonomy. a very important achievement for us, because it represents an important innovation for our agriculture, is to have achieved accessibility to traditional weather insurance.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the report focuses on the issue and management of licences for european vessels operating outside union waters, and especially for third country vessels fishing in our waters. cooperation between the european institutions has resulted in a new regime with transparent and harmonised rules, aimed at optimising governance and improving monitoring and implementation. great attention is paid to all measures to protect against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, which is one of the main threats to our professional fishermen. the new set of rules achieves many of the objectives related to the environmental and economic sustainability of fishing, but without punishing the operators in the sector. unlike the current situation, where small fishermen are exempt from any form of financial support, even in the event of a biological freeze, if they have committed infringements in the period after the disbursement of the fund, they now have to prove that they are not on the list of illegal vessels in order to be authorised to fish in third countries' waters. so yes to compliance with the rules, but without burdening the fishermen with a blind and pretentious bureaucracy.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the agreement reached on the new legislative framework for the sustainable management of external fishing fleets is certainly a very good achievement, and i congratulate the rapporteur on that. the new regime provides for strict, transparent and harmonised rules for the issuing and management of fishing authorisations for eu vessels operating outside union waters and for third country vessels fishing in union waters. these are essential rules to improve governance, increase transparency and optimise monitoring and enforcement of the rules, especially in specific cases such as direct authorisations, transhipments or flag changes. the new, more transparent rules will make the eu better able to tackle illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. it was a necessary revision to ensure that fishing activities outside union waters comply with rules and principles similar to those applied within the european union, and it is important in this context to provide for lists of vessels engaged in illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, aviation is a huge source of greenhouse gas emissions, and if no action is taken to reduce them, they are expected to quadruple by 2050 compared to 2010. for these reasons, the overall reduction of national greenhouse gas emissions is a key objective of european union policy. in this sense, the ets is an essential tool for a cost-effective reduction of these emissions. pending the establishment of the details of the mechanism of a market-based agreement to address the increase in missions globally by the world civil aviation organisation, it is necessary for the european parliament and the council to approve the revision of this regulation. a swift approval by the end of the year will avoid any legal vacuum for european aircraft operators in relation to the ets legislation in the current year. this will ensure legal certainty and clarity and allow compliance with the compliance obligations of the european union ets for aviation and the extension of the derogation until 31 december 2023 for flights outside the european economic area. finally, i would like to stress the importance of the full implementation of the single european sky. this will avoid the fragmentation of airspace and optimise the flow of traffic, resulting in reduced emissions.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, greenhouse gas emissions from aviation are increasing rapidly and, if no action is taken, could reach four times the level of 2010 by 2050. the increase in aviation emissions risks undermining the efforts of the european union and the world to effectively address climate change. i too express my support for the extension until 2020 of the current eu ets, which reduces emissions by some 17 million tonnes of co2 per year, until there is sufficient clarity on the nature and content of the legal instruments adopted by icao for the implementation of a global measure, the so-called corsia. this means that within the european economic area, the aviation sector will continue to contribute, like every other economic sector, to efforts to reduce domestic emissions. however, work within icao must be accelerated with a view to the effective adoption and implementation of a comprehensive measure capable of solving all the problems related to international traffic.

one, bulgaria is second, greece third, portugal fourth, and spain fifth. our idea was to address market failure and it seems to be functioning as we planned. let me give you some concrete examples of efsi projects. in poland the eib is providing a loan of over eur 30 million for the construction of 1 300 affordable houses for low-income earners. in greece, the eib is lending to a telecoms operator to roll out high-speed broadband, bringing better internet access to rural and remote areas of the country. in finland, efsi supports the first ever social impact points scheme in europe. the scheme continue to match the high expectations which we have set. this efsi extension will increase the target of investment to be triggered to at least eur 0.5 trillion by 2020. efsi 2.0 comes with a number of enhancements as a result of the input and commitment of the co—legislators. let me outline some of them. first, there is a more precise definition of ‘additionally’, and, second, investment decisions will be better explained and the scoreboard on which they are based will be published. this is a measure of transparency and also of increased accountability. thirdly, technical assistance to project promoters at a local level will be strengthened so that even more regions and sectors can benefit from it. finally, efsi 2.0 will better focus on eu political priorities, such as climate change and environmental projects. i would now like to focus on three areas where the parliament’s constructive, but determined, pressure was key and take this opportunity to two rapporteurs, udo bullmann and josé manuel fernandes. the first relates to the report of the committee of inquiry into money laundering, tax avoidance and tax evasion. thanks to parliament’s efforts, due diligence on european investment bank operations under this regulation will include a thorough check of compliance with eu and international standards on anti—money laundering, the fight against terrorism, financing and tax fraud, and on tax avoidance. the second area where the european parliament has clearly left a footprint is increased transparency. thanks to parliament’s efforts, the scoreboard of indicators will be made public after the signature of each project and the investment committee will substantiate its decision on the granting of eu funding. finally, parliament’s efforts are also clearly seen when it comes to support for small—scale projects. as mr fernandes rightly pointed out, what is perceived as small in some countries or regions is actually a large-scale project in others. better use of platforms, a delegation model with national promotional banks and a reinforced advisory hub will help smaller projects to benefit from efsi more than they have been doing so far. before i conclude, i would like to highlight that much still remains to be done. efsi plays a major role in catalysing private investment, but the impact of these funds would be enhanced by further addressing barriers to investment in member states. i refer to the third pillar of the investment plan that is a joint european and national responsibility. thank you very much for the great cooperation.
